div.p: • A SONG OF REST. 0 weary Hands! that, all the day, L t. Were set to labour hard and long, • Vow softly fall the shadows gray, ,• • The bells are rung for evensong. • • V An hour ago, the golden sun Sank slowly down into the west; Poor, weary Hands, your toil is done; 'Tis time for rest !—'tis time for rest! 0 weary Feet! that many a mile )3ave trudged along a stony way, 3. tr At last ye reach the trysting stile; ,t•:•s No longer fear to go astray. The gently bending, rustling trees •• Rock the young birds within the nest,! And softly sings the quiet breeze: "'Tis time for rest !—'tis time for rest!" ▪ - 0 weary Eyes! from which the tears • Fell many a time like thunder-rain— " 0 weary Heart! that through the years Beat with such bitter, restless pain, To-night forget the stormy strife, And know, what Heayen shall send is best; • tr.* Lay down the tangled web of life; "'ls time for rest !—'tis time for rest! ......Woribers's Journal. ,

THE BELFRY PIGEON. Ike the cross-beam under the Old South bell Ike nest of a pigeon is builded well. liglinnarner and winter that bird is there, WO and in with the morning air. • • • Neve to see him track the street, With his wary eye and active feet; And I often watch him when he springs, 4113,relting the steeple with easy wings; across the dial his shade has passed, And the belfry edge is gained at last. "es a bird I love, with its brooding note And the trembling throb in its mottled throat. There's a human look in its swelling breast And the gentle cnrve of its lowly crest; Awl I often stop with the fear I feel— Ile runs so close to the rapid wheel. Whatever is rung on that noisy bell- 4111kime of the hour or funeral knell— Ike dove in the belfry must hear it well— When the tongue swings out to the midnight moon— When the sexton cheerily rings for noon— When the clock strikes clear at morning light— When the child is waked with " nine at night"— When the chimes play soft in the Sabbath air, Filling the spirit with tones of prayer. Whatever tale in the bell is heard, He broods on his folded feet unstirred, Or, rising half in his rounded nest, Me takes the time to smooth his breast, Then drops again with filmed eyes, And sleeps as the last vibration dies. Sweet bird! I would that I could be A hermit in the crowd like thee! With wings to fly to wood and glen. Thy lot, like mine, is cast with men; And daily, with unwilling feet, ].tread, like thee, the crowded street, • But, unlike me, when day is o'er, Thou canst dismiss the world and soar, *l, at a half-felt wish for rest, Oanst smooth the feathers on thy breast, And drop, forgetful, to thy rest.
N. P. Wards.

A bard-headed business man was among the guests at a recent fashionable gathering, where also was a very land and very obtrusive new-rich woman. "Humph," gasewled Hard Head as the very loud and so forth swept past him in the grand procession, "Too much money, and hasn't had it long enough." A gentleman in the west of Scotland, celebrated for his wit, was conversing with a lady, who, at last, quite over- powered by the brilliance and frequency of his bon roots, exidaimed, "Stop, sir; there is really no end to your "God forbid, madam" replied the humorist," that Mould ever be at my wit's end." "I think," said Mr. Bronson Alcott, once in conversa- tion, " that when a man lives on beef he becomes some- thing like an ox; if he eats mutton he begins to look sheepish, and if he eats pork may he not grow swinish ?" "That may be," said Dr. Walker of Cambridge, "hut when a man lives on nothing but vegetables, I think he is apt to be pretty small potatoes." "Let IA see some of your black kid gloves," said Mrs. Slangs to the draper's assistant. "These are not the kiteet style, are they?" she asked, when the gloves were predueed. 'Yes, diadem," said the man. "We have had them in stock only two days." "I didn't think they were, because the fashion-paper says that black kids have tan stitches and vice versa. I see the tan stitches, but not the vice versa." The assistant explained that vice versa was French for "seven buttons," and Mrs. Snaggs bought the gloves. BISHOP HANNTNGTON IN SOUTH APRICA.—TIIO labours and death of Lieutenant Shergold Smith and Mr. O'Neill at Victoria Nyanza in 1878 greatly stirred Hannington's imagination, and planted the germ of that impulse which nitimately led him to offer his services to the Church Missionary Society on terms which showed his perfect disinterestedness. His offer was accepted in March, 1882, and two months later a band of six men, with James Hannington as leader, left Gravesend for mission- ary work at Rubaga on the Victoria Nyanza. On his ar- rival at Zanzibar Hannington proceeded to the lake by way of Uyui, and it is not surprising that he should sub- , sequently have desired to open up the far healthier route I to the north. At the mission station at Uyui he was so ' ill with dysentery that he thought he was going to die, and actually chose a place for his grave- and when he arrived at the head of the lake he was so tormented with farm. and other ailments that the once "bright and buoyant figure," we are told, "became bent and feeble, Ipre that of a very old man." Yet during a portion of the rums- he 514070 great energy. He botanised in the Haagara mountains. He was a keen sportsman and had more than one exciting adventure when engaged in lion .or buffalo hunting. His biographer relates that once, at - 3 moment when he was dangerously near a lion and • lioness who were growling over their dead cub which he had shot, he saw an unknown flower. He plucked it, pressed it between the leaaes of his note-book, and clas- sified it to the best of his ability on the spot. His cool- ness and courage were indeed remarkable; and at the same time he showed great tact in dealing with the na- tives through whose territory he passed. The chief of Tfrima wanted a present, and Hannington had none to give excepa his blanket, which the chief coveted. The poor tray eller appealed to the better nature of the impor- tunate savage in these words: "The white man is cold; 12_2 wa'sts much clothes. If you take his blanket he will When the sun is gone to rest the white man grows I il. Leave him his blanket." His eloquence prevailed. BISHOP HANNINGTON'S DEA.TH.—The bishop determined to make another journey to the Victoria Nyanza. He was greatly struck with the superior advantages of the route to Uganda through Masai Land, it being a healthy highland country—very different from the inhospitable and malarious region through which he had made his previous painful journey. Sir John Kirk, Her Majesty's aonsul-General at Zanzibar, was also anxious that the new route should be opened up. The bishop, at the head a his caravan, left Rabbai on July 23rd, 1885, and his last letter to his wife is dated " Kikumbuliu, August 11th." He did not write in very good spirits, but his characteristic humour found vent in the following pass- ago:—"We are a little poor,' as Jones says. My watch has gone wrong. The candles and lamp oil were forgotten and left behind, so that the camp-fire has to serve in- stead. My donkey has died, so that I must walk every step of the way. Well having no watch, Ido not wake *pin the night to see if it is time to get up, but wait till daylight dawns. Having no candle, I don't read at sight, which never suits me. Having no donkey, I can judge better as to distances, and as to what the men can do; for many marches depend upon my saying, We will stop here and rest or sleep.'" At Kwa Sundu the bishop decided to leave the Rev. W. Jones, a native clergyman, in charge of the caravan, and to make the journey to Rubaga with fifty men. Mr. Jones remained at Kwa Sundu in great suspense from October 12th, the day on which he parted from the bishop, till lNovember Bth, when he heard that his brave and noble-hearted chief was dead. The happy recovery of the bishop's little pocket diary at Rubaga furnished authentic details of his capture and imprison- ment, and brought the story down almost to the moment of his execution. Mr. Dawson in his life of Bishop Hannington thus describes the bishop's death:—"ln that supreme moment we have the happiness of knowing that the bishop faced his destiny like a Christian and a man. As the soldiers told off to murder him closed round, he made one last use of that command- ing mien which never failed to secure for him the re- spect of the most savage. Drawing himself up, he ooked around, and as they momentarily hesitated with poised weapons, he spoke a few words which graved themselves upon their memories, and which they after- wards repeated just as they were heard. He bade them ten the king that he was about to die for the Ba-ganda, and that he had purchased the road to Buganda with his life. Then, as they still hesitated, he pointed to his own gun, which one of them discharged, and the great and noble spirit leapt forth from its broken house of clay, and entered with exceeding joy into the presence of the King." The circumstances which led to the murder are well known. Mtasa, Kin eof Uganda, was suc- ceeded by his son Mwanga. lie was jealous of the missionaries, and was so enraged at the progress which Glaristianity was making among his people that lie committed or authorised acts of atrocious cruelty. I Moreover, his fears were excited by reports of German intrigues; and when he heard that "a tall Englishman, who had lost a thumb," had arrived at Busoga, he regarded that as evidence of the intention of the foreigner to steal into the country by "the ie be putback door." He therefore ordered the poor bishop to death. We doubt whether a nobler or more pathetic story has ever been told in biography. THE KING OF MaN-INlir.t.nunts.—M. Worth, the Parisian king of dressmakers, is an Englishman about forty-five years old, good-looking, and of pleasant manners. He is said to have obtained admission to the salons and opera- box of a celebrated foreign princess and leader of fashion as a settlement of her long unpaid bills—a composition which so offended the Court dignitaries of her native country that she narrowly escaped social ostracism on her return home. The sae Madame de M—, it is de- clared, being anxious to make a grand display without a great outlay, arranged with Worth to hire hi .3 new dresses for one wearing, and then to return them for sale to those ladies who were desirous of imitating the , toilettes of her highness. He is a man of tireless activity; every department in his immense establish- ment is under his own personal supervision, and it is difficult to obtain more than a few moments' uninter- rupted conversation with him, so frequently is he called upon for advice; or, as he impatiently remarked to our inferma.nt, "the workwomen cannot so much as put a sleeve in a polonaise without coming to ask me about it." He buys the material, sees the customers, designs the style, and selects the colours himself, and his taste is said to be very good, only that he has "a weakness for arraying blondes in certain bright shades of yellow." The prices paid by unhappy husbands and disconsolate fathers for his productions are something fabulous. His charge for an ordinary silk walking or evening dress may be computed at fifty or sixty pounds; but upon grand occasions even this price is largely exceeded. Notwith- standing these exorbitant figures, he is literally over- whelmed with orders, his customers including not only Parisians, but large numbers of English and Americans. —Ca.q.cell's Saturday Journal. A GIANT TORTES SHELL—A party of English natural- ists, with several native attendants, recently penetrated into a hitherto unexplored portion of India. They had to take great care to guard against the dangerous animals that infested the jungle. For days they had been tavelling through a wooded region, when one even- ing they came upon a clear and undulating stretch of country that seemed, in the opinion of the officer in charge, favourable for the object of their trip, the estab- lishment of a station. A halt was ordered, the brush- wood cleared away, great patches that might have con- cealed the deadly cobra were burned, and the tents were pitched. In a few days the workmen had commenced their task of erecting a substantial building. It was necessary to have a large and deep cellar for the recep- tion of stores, and in a short time a deep excavation was made. The earth was dry and sandy, and was worked with ease; no stones were found, no hard substance that would have interested a geologist. Late in the afternoon of the 'first day's work one of the natives struck his pick against some resisting substance. Another blow, and his instrument broke through into a hollow space. The earth was at once scraped away, when a large smooth object was exposed of a strange 'appearance. As work went on their wonder and excitement increased. That which they had discovered began to assume the shape of a dome, and appeared to be rounded off. As more and more sand was cleared away, the thing, whatever it was, began to look like a hat; and from the hole made by the pick, they could see that it wds hollow inside. Some of , the natives said it must be the home of one of their far- away ancestors, that had in the course of time been ,covered up by the sand. But the English naturalists found a more simple explanation of the mystery; they knew that the curious bone was the shell of a gigantic turtle, Vlonging to an age. long past when there were mamino`th animals and reptffes on the earth. The shell was in very truth that of a rand tortoi3e. Hundreds of thousands of years ago the monster lived and died, and the dust, sand, and vegetation had gradually covered it up and preserved it as a monument of the animul won- ders of that ancient time. So enormous was the shell that when the sand and dirt were removed several of the men crawled into it; in facr,.it might have been used as a house, and on a subsequent occasion was so used by a party which took refuge- in it during a heavy I shower.

NATURAL LAWS AND SUPERNATURAL APPRARANCES.— With what awe the visit of a meteorite may be regarded. even in this nineteenth century, 33, unlearned' country- folk, may be gathered from the account of one which fell at, Juvenas, in Ardeche, on the- 15th of .Tune, 12/, and which formed the subject of a curious p7oces verbal' drawn up by the Mayor of the Commune. It was first seen at three p.m. as a fire ball, in a clear sky, while the sun was shining brightly; and it sank five feet into the ground. The inhabitants were so alarmed that it was , more than a week before they could make up their minds to search for this strange visitant. "They deliberated , for a long time whether they should go armed to under- take this operation, which appeared se dangerous; but Claude Serre, the sexton, justly observed that if it was the Evil One, neither powder nor arms would prevail against him—that holy water would be more effectual and that he would undertake to make the evil spirit fly after which reassuring speech they set to work and dug up the aerolite, which weighed over two-hundred pounds, We read in the classic poets that on certain momentous occasions, statues have been so affected as to perspire, as if they were living human beings. These stories have been passed over as mere poetic fictions; but probably they rest on a substantial foundation. The phenomenon is dobutless that which is observed when a fire has been lighted for the first time in a room which has for a lengthened period been allowed to remain cold; the walls and other objects are seen to run down with moisture, which appears as if exuded from their surface. The same thing occurs when a long-continued frost is succeeded by mild weather. The appearance is familiar enough to us, who are accustomed to sudden variations of temperature; but in warmer and more equitable climates, the requisite conditions are probably rare; and the appearance of copious moisture on statues composed of substances on which dew is not commonly found, may well have been ac- counted a prodigy. We may not be disposed to admit that the fiery cross seen by Constantine was a miracu- lous intimation; but we cannot set aside the account as necessarily apocryphal; for a celestial cross was seen in Migne, near Poitiers, in December, 1826'. It was ob- served during a religious service, and the preacher in his sermon had referred to the cross of Constantine. The awe-struck congregation, on perceiving the visible cross in the sky, of shining silver, edged with red, immediately fell upon their knees, accepting the sign as a divine tes- timony to the truth of what had just been told them. The source of the phenomenon was afterwards found in a wooden cross which had been erected near the chapel, the shadow of which had been cast by the declining sun on a rising mist. The Flying Dutchman was obviously another instance of atmospheric reflection, and similar phantom ships have been described by modern travellers. The Enchanted Island, or Isle of Ghosts, which had its' place in old charts in the mid-Atlantic, and so perplexed the mariners of the middle ages by its varying appear- ance, defying all attempts to reach its shores, has since been recognised as a fogbank. Among the wonders re- corded in the reign of William Rufus, it is stated that on a night in 1095, the stars seemed falling like a shower of rain from heaven to earth, or, according to the Chronicle of Rheims, were driven like dust before the wind. A tradition is recorded as prevailing in Thessaly that on a certain night in August the heavens were opened and burning torches were seen through the aperture. These are clearly but high?), coloured accounts by persons of limited knowledge of natural phenomena, of specially brilliant displays of shooting-stars. The last corresponds with the August meteors.—Chambers's Journal. CEEAPF.ST HOUSE in the eity for Glass, China, Oriental Wares, arhA Fancy Goods.-175, Oxtord-strect, Manchester.— Adr.t.

As the various breeds of poultry are derived from one, I or, at most, two original stocks, and as many of the varieties we have at the present time are of comparatively recent production, that is, they are only a few genera- tions old in their present form, the second of these two main causes is that which most of all faces the poultry- breeder, and he needs to exercise the greatest care in the choice of birds of other strains than his own, lest the introduction of these will develop long-lost and objec- tionable characteristics. In fact, many of the best breeders never think of introducing any absolutely foreign blood, but find out birds for their purpose amongst stocks known to be related to their own. Or, if they are compelled to find out absolutely fresh blood, they take the precaution of not introducing this directly into the main stock. This undoubtedly leads to a great deal of what is known as in-breeding, that is, the.mating of closely related birds together. By doing this merely external qualities can be more easily preserved and im- proved, and it is not too much to say that a very large proportion of the best show stock, both animals and birds, are closely bred. This of itself would be an evil, were it not for the fact that all the harm resultant from the high breeding can be overcome by the first cross, and that the undoubted benefits corning from the develop- ment of pure-bred stock in the development of the best qualities, more than overbalance it. And the law of the survival of the fittest works here, as everywhere else, for those varieties or families which are too much weakened by this system of breeding either die out, or a different system is adopted in reference to them ere they become extinct. The constant introduction of new varieties prevents poultry as a whole suffering, and, as these often contain the qualities really worth' preserving in the weaker kinds, they have not lived in vain. To secure, therefore, what are known as high class stock, a certain amount of close breeding is needed, but by this we do not mean in-breeding pure and simple. One of the most important factors in this consideration is that the highly developed parts are the most difficult to maintain. In fancy poultry and pigeons this is the every-day experience of breeders. Given any charac- teristic which is purely a spurt, or has been grafted on to the breed, and it takes all the efforts of breeders to keep it up. Constant and unvarying selection are re- quired or the characteristic would disappear. Take, for instance, the white face of the Spanish, the white ear-lobe of the Leghorn the globular crest of the Polish, the fea- thered legs of the Cochin and the Brahma, the lacing of the Wyandotte, and the cuckoo plumage of the Plymouth Rocks—all :these are artificial characteristics, or minor

MANAGEMENT OP MILK.—" Cream" asks whether, in order to obtain the greatest quantity of butter, the cream from spring and autumn calvers ought to be churned separately, or mixed together ?—We do not suppose that the "age," so to speak, of the milk has anything to do with this matter, though it is sometimes asserted that when butter will not " come " in churning, the addition of " young " milk meets the difficulty. PEDIGREE Pies.—The movement to maintain the purity and improve the breed of swine in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland is making pro- gress. Two Herd-books have already been published by the National Pier-breeders' Association, and the third volume will make its appearance early in the New Year. In addition to the pedigree of boars and sows. farrowed before the Ist of January last, it will contain a register of the produce of a number of sows already entered in the Herd-book. _ MANURE FOR GRASS LAND.—" Lox" askg "the best

form of manure to apply to pasture land—dissolved bones, quarter inch bones, or bone meal; and also when, and in what quantity it should be applied."—You will certainly get a large increase of grass if you apply 1 cwt. or 1i cwt. of nitrate of soda broadcast over it per acre in the months of March and April; whether you will get anything by bones or superphosphates is not certain. In Cheshire, half a ton of bone dust per acre is always sure to make its mark—the clover comes up, and every- thing (even rushes) gets sweetened, and is eaten up. But on other soils bone dust has no immediate effect. You had better apply 3 cwt. of superphosphates per acre over a portion of your land early next spring, and be guided by the result. The nitrate will produce grass; the phos- phate manure promotes the growth especially of clover. Trni SCIENCIEC OP AGRICULTURR.—The third year's course of lectures delivered by Prof. Hope, M.R.A.C., F.C.S. (who has given a series of lectures in Preston). during the session 1885-86, seems from Mr. Cundall's re- port as honorary secretary of the executive committee of the York Chamber ot Agriculture, to have been as usual a success. The classes which had been held in the previous year at Selby and Stamford Bridge were dis- continued, and arrangements were made for the forma- tion of advanced and elementary classes at York, Malton, and Market Weighton, and of elementary classes at Gan- ton and Sheriff Hutton. The usual course of twenty- eight lectures was delivered to each -class. The total number attending the various classes has been 100, of whom 80 per cent. are farmers and those connected with agriculture. At, the examination held in May last, 22 were examined; 10 passed in Class 1, two of them ad- vanced; and nine in Class 2, one honours, and four ad- vanced. Practical illustrations of the lectures have from time to time been given, and Messrs. Rowntree, Hills, and Co. allowed a visit by the students, accom- panied by Prof. Hope, to their dairy, and Mr. Wood, dairyman, Clifton, permitted them to inspect his silos. I The lectures have been well received in the district. It would surely be worth the while of the agriculturists of the Fylde to give their children the benefit of such lec- tures.

NORTH LANCASHIRE! NOTES.—MallgOld3 are mostly stored, but the land has been too wet for raising pota- toes or taking up swedes. There is fortunately less disease in the potato crop than was at one time feared, while prices have not yet risen above 6d. per 141 b. re- tail. Even on the driest soils the land is too wet for

autumn ploughing, and back-end manuring would be a waste of manure, for the fertilising properties of the manure would simply be w.ashed away. On November the 16th, we had the first foretaste of winter in heavy showers of hail. A week ago the tops of the Lake Mountains were tipped with snow, but in the valleys the weather has been abnormally mild,land roots are still making growth. I am afraid the year 1886 will prove the worst we have here experienced as regards the long spell of agricultural depression. In the first place the bulk of the barley crop was spoiled for malting, owing to the long-continued bad weather at harvest, and it will have to be used for stock feeding. This does not open out an assuring prospect, for the prices that fat beasts are now bringing are very low. We have fair crops of roots, and grass has lasted out late, but the prices the animals bring at the auction marts are simply ruinous to the feeders. The rise in the price of wool came too late to be of service, as the clips had been sold when it occurred, and only the buyers benefited from it. Altogether, I fear that 1886-7 will prove a hard struggle for many of our farmers.—R. EXERCISING HOUSE-Fen CATrLi.—A certain amount of exercise is necessary for all farm animals. Every stock- owner knows the value of exercise in maintaining the health and vitality of cattle that are highly fed; and those who provide loose boxes without ample room for the animal to move about in are courtinc, failure very directly. The fat ox that is intended for the shambles does not require more exercise than is necessary to keep him on his legs, but all other breeding animals re- quire more than this. A good many feeders fancy that their cattle are all right so long as they keep them from going wrong on their legs. They altogether forget that weakness in the legs is the last stage of collapse when an animal is over-fed, and very rarely indeed premoni- tory. There is, of course, much difference in the muscular

characteristics artificially developed, and as a conse- quence they have no real basis to work upon, or to resist the inexorable law of reversion. In process of many generations and the most careful breeding, they may be so fixed as to appear unalterable, but it will not be long, if neglected, or strange blood introduced, ere they will show themselves in some form or another. On this point Darwin says:—" If, in our domestic animals, any part or the whole animal be neglected, and no selection be ap- plied, that part (for instance, the combs in the Dorking fowl) or the whole breed will cease to have a uniform character; and the breed may be said to be degenerating. • . . There may truly be said to be a constant struggle going on between, on the one hand, the ten- dency to reversion to a less perfect state, as well as AA inuate teridelacy to new Yariotions, and, on the other hand, the power of steady selection to keep the breed true. In the long run selection gains the day." Now this brings us to a most important conclusion for those whose object is to maintain and improve the economic qualities of poultry, rather than the merely external characteristics, namely, that whilst the highly developed.parts are very difficult indeed to maintain, and need the greatest care in selection to prevent their loss, the less showy but more valuable properties, such as early maturity,, laying powers, and quality of flesh are much more tenacious, and do not readily lose their influence. We do not mean by this that even these qualities cannot be lost by neglect, but they are not se easily lost. This is a matter which can be proved by ordinary experience, and any old henwife will have some tale to tell of the influence exerted by a famous layer, whose blood was like that of the duchess tribe in shorthorns. The poultry breeder may feel, therefore, that his efforts for the improvement of his stock in the direction of economic qualities, are likely to be of a permanent nature, and that he is exerting an influence which will not be confined to his own yard. He is, in fact, after tha substance, not the shadow, and though he will be wise for many reasons if he uses pure bred stock, he will not be seeking some highly developed character- istic which will be difficult to maintain and easy to lose. SEASONABLE HINTS. In some poultry yards there may vet be a number of cockerels which it is well to get rid of. If this. be the case they should be fed well preparatory to being put up to fatten. About three weeks or a month is generally found long enough for the fattening process, but much can be done beforehand. The best way is to select the birds to be so dealt with, and to put them in an open run by themselves. There they should be fed on such foods as boiled rice, Indian corn, and oatmeal, and they will lay a good foundation. When the time comes for them to be fattened, they will be to some extent pre- pared. Fattening pens can be made very easily, and aTe best placed in a rather warm shed or room; if darkrit will be all the better, br.t it should be well ventilated.

strength and action of different animals; for one beast may be internally morbid without showing any outward sign of it, while another will fail quite early on its legs. The only safety lies in making certain that the animals do not lack exercise. The natural way of exercising by allowing them to feud out of doors is by far the best, Cows and calves ought al/ to be pastured in summer and have the run of a yard in winter. For young bulls there should be strong-walled paddocks, where two at a time can be grazed or take exercise for an hour 07 two daily. When the bulls get to be over a year old it is better to let them go out in the yard singly. In going out and in, the herdsman should take the opportunity of giving them a lesson in leading. If they have been taught to lead when calves, the training now is easy and light; but if they have been neglected at first, the work is too much for one man, and' requires an assistant with a \a hip. Old bulls are generally confined to closer quarters, with a small yard adjoining their box. If they have no yard to exercise in, theyshotdd be lead out with. a staff for at least two miles on the road daily. Cattle- that are being fattei ed for the butcher—and especially cattle that are being pampered for the Christmas fat stock shows, and having every comfort provided them (as many art at this season), should not be turned out of doors for ozercise regardless of the weather. When they are kept in warm quarters, not to say blanketed in the house, it is forty to turn them out into the yard, even with the sheets on, when the day is either wet or very cold. A chill may put them off their feed for weeks; their coats will stare, and the aniinalS will lose flesh ha spite of all; besides, there is great- danger of the illness in such a case- terminating fatally.. We have seen some good cattle lost through exercisiag on cold days when they ought toliave been kept indeors.--5.6. If there were only negative indbences at work in the breeding of anima and birds, the- breeder would find the selection of his stock a very much soupier business than it is proved to be. But, as everyone-discovers who the breeding of pure stock, there are positive' influences at work which must be reekoneell with, if any measure of success has to be attained. It is, as we shall presently see, to counteract this that the producers of high-bred stock resort to closerorinebreeding, as in. this way the risk of variation is greatly though that is often at the expense-of important quali,- ties, such as staraina and size. _ _ _

The first and most important or these positive infli ences is that known as the law of reversion, or avatism That this is a Ihw which needs to be reaconed with, every breeder can testify, and there- are recorded some most remarkable-oases illustrative of "it. It is not neces- sary, however, that these should be-given here, for the law of reversion, needs no proof, surprising though it undoubtedly is.. Dhrwin explains- it 8,3 follows :-- " When a breed has been crossed only once by some other breed, the- offspring occasionally show for many generations a tendency to revert to the foreign breed:L._ some say, for a dozen or even a score of generations. After twelve generations, the proportion of bleed, to use a common expression,. is coly one in 2,048 ; and yet, as we see, it- is generally be-- lieved that a tendency to reversion, iS retained by this remnant of foreign blood. In a timed which hanot been crossed, but-in which both parents have lost some character which) their progenitors possessed, the ten- dency, whether- strong- or weak, to reproduce the. lost I character might,,--as was formerly remarked—for allthat we can see to the contrary, be transmitted for almos e any number of generations. When a character, which has been lost in a breed; reappears atter a great number of generations, the most probable hypothesis is, not that one individual suddenly takes after an-ancestor removed by some hundred' generations, but that in each SUC3essive generation the character in question hasbeen lying)latent, and, at last, under unknown favourable conditions, is developed." And in another work the same famous. naturalist says- that "The cases of reversion may be. divided into two main classe,s, which, however,.in some instances blend into one another-,- namely, first, those oc- curring in a variety or race which has not been crossed; but has lost by variation some character that it formerly possessed, and which a,fterwarth reappears. The secand' class includes all cases in which an individualiwith some- distinguishable character, race, or species has at some former period been crossed, antic character 6iarived from this cross, after having disappeared during Gine or s..nreral generations, suddenly reappears."

' WELCOMING THE MEMBERS.—Prior to the Com- mencement of the business of the meeting Alder- man Harrison referred to the illness of the Mayor (Dr. Mackie) and asked the warm sympathy of the members of the association in the painful affliction that had befallen him. In the absence of the Mayor he accorded all present a very hearty wel- come to Warrington. He was delighted to see them, because they were all representatives of an impor- tant branch of science; which involved not only the comfort of the people, but the life and health of the nation. He hoped that the meeting would be pro- ductive of benefit and mutual advantage which would guide them in the development of the ad- vantages of sanitary science. In Wbtrrington dur- ing the last few years they had taken almost a leap in sanitary science, and they had not been niggardly in spending money to solve the great problem of how to get rid of town refuse. He believed they had succeeded in getting rid of it, and that they had one of the most perfect systems ever adopted. (Hear, hear.) He had especial pleasure in welcom- ing them, because he believed that fourteen or fif- teen years ago an important branch of the institu- tion was founded in Warrington. (Applause.) CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c. "The Land of Little People" is the title of a new illustrated book published by Messrs. Hildesheimer and Faulkner, of 41, Jewin-street, London. As the title suggests, it is a book for the little folks, and there are none, little or big, who set eyes on it that could fail to admire it. The firm seem to'have brought to perfection the art of illustrating books of this kind. They spend large sums of money in order to command talent of the highest order, and the money is well spent. The rhymes and poeins—for some of the pieces are entitled to be called poems—are from the versatile pen of Mr. F. E. Weatherley, who is always happy when trying to .u.ake the little ones happy. The illustrations, which are numerons and varied,are by Jane M. Dealy and Ernest Watson, and it is little enough to say of them that they are "simply charming." "The Historical Scrap Book" (Messrs. Cassell and Co.) is a new issue which is likely to be highly prized and very popular. It is a large and magnificent yol- time of nearly 200 pages, and every page is adorned with plates of historical picturee. Some pages, scrap- book fashion, have half-a-doxen or more of pictures or portraits on them, but there are many full-page engravings, and, as may be supposed, the effect is very fine. Only such a firm as that of Messrs. Cas • sell, with the thousands of elates which they have at their disposal, could offer a work of this kind, except at a price which would be beyond the reach of the general public. The illustrations embrace every' pe- riod of English history, and, as names and dates are given, it will be sem that the Scrap Book, while in the highest degree pictorially attractive, is of great value from an educational point of view, Young stu- dents have too often had to munch the dry hones of history, but in this case a real banquet is offered. Caseell's Illustrated Almanac, price fid., is cheap enough, but it always contains a number of excel- lent engravings, besides a mass of valuable informa- tion. A feature in the Almanac for 1887 is a batch of excellent portraits of the notable men of the year. "Euchre—How to play it," is published by Messrs Griffith, Farren and Co., London, and is sure to make headway. It is by the author of "Poker—How to play it," which has met with a good reception. In the introdaction the author says—" Euchre and Poker divide between them the honour of being the national card games of the United States of America, while. in Australia, Euchre takes the first rank. In England. Euchre has of late years been making its way among card-players, and in some circles " the right and left bower" are as familiar in phrase as "three by cards and two by honours." Messrs. Grant atid Co.'s Christmas Number bears the title of " Golden Bells, a peal in Seven Changes It is a continuoue story, and when we say that it is written by Mr. R. E. Francillon it is sufficient t) auggest that it neither lack power nor interest. Nor does it; from peal to peal the effect ia heightened until the reader is almost breathless. The story is sensational enough in some of its features, and yet it is not merely sensational ; it is literary in the telling and moral in the effect; and, which is more than can be said of many Christmas stories, it can be read a second time.

"The Devil's Cauldron" (Messrs. Pennington and Co.) is what it purports to be—" tale for Christmas time and all other times." The author is Mr. J. W. Nicholas; and he is to be congratulated on having succesefully accomplished his task. It is true his story here and there suggests some other story; but it is sufficiently original in the main to hold the reader's attention. There is no loose writing or fragmentary disquisition, so that there ia nothing tlaat can be skipped. Mesmerism is so much of reality that Mr. Nicholas has done well to make full use of it in fiction.

Messrs. Macmillan and Co issue the "English Illustrated Magazine" as a double number for Christ- mas, and it goes without saying that snecial pains have been taken to make it attractive. The frontis- piece is the study of a head from a drawing by Mr. Alma-Taderas, R.A., and Mr.. A. C. Swinburne fol- lows with "In a Garden "—a piece a charming verse—more charming perhaps because one does not expect Swinborne to be simple and natural ;an article on "Venice" effectively illustrated from numerous drawings by Clara. Montabella ; and by way of con- trast thera is an illustrated paper on "The Heart of London,' which sets the reader thinking of the social problems of the day. "The Surrey Mill-wheets " furnish beautiful subjects, and "Hops and Hop- picking "is also bright and picturesqze. Mr. George Meredith contributes a poem—" The Young Prin- cess ; " there are, besides, several interesting stories; and the number for December is therefore a strong one.

"The Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic News" offers a capital ebilling'S worth in its Christmas num- ber of " Holly Leaves." The enamelled illuminated wrapper is a work of art to begin with ; and there is a large coloured picture, " Rejected Addresses," by , Mr. CT. Garland. It represents egirl holding a bit Fof mistletoe over a pet dog, that rejects the proffered kiss. Then there is an eight-page coloured supplement ,humourously illustrating" My Grandfather's Ghost FI Story," and over a dozen striking engravings on wood, .to say nothing of sketches and stories by writers of repute.

" Myra's Journal of Dress and [Fashion "is double /nr December, and the price is, of course,double (1s). The cover is suggestive of the approaching season, with its display of holly leaves and berries ;: and there is, as a present, a large chromo-lithograph picture from the painting '4-Frozen Up," by Mr. T Blinks. BeBidea the current designs patterns, &a., we have an illustrated article on "Christmasl and New Year' Gifts." another on"-Christmas Cards and Books," and a third on "Suggestions for Tableauu Vivants." 'Mrs Leach's Family Dressmaker" is also double for December; and there is given with it an attractive oleograph picture with the title of " Beauty and the Beast" which is in itself well worth the fourpence -whieh is charged this-month for the journal. "Hood's Comic Annual for 1887 '" (le) is as comical as ever. There is an abundance of sketches, stories, and "quips and cranks "in prose and verse. The illustrations, which are very numerous, are for the most part exceedingly clever; the engraving is lir Messrs. Dalziel Brothers. Amongst the more noted contributors may ite mentioned Mr. G. /2.: Sims, Mr. G. Manville Fenn, Mr. Ernest Griset, and Mr. Georpe Dalziel. The annual has reached its nineteenth year of publication, and it is satisfactory to see that it is still thriving-. "-Bow Bells Lelinanao for 1837 "is a capital six- , pennyworth. The illustrations embrace portraits of.: eminent men and women, and some fine full-page plates of Rhine scenery. The information given has been carefully compiled, and it is as °onions as it is useful. The almanac is published by IKE. Dicks, 31.37, Strand, London.

div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

THE BULGARIA.N SITUArION. THE VACANT THBONI4 —PLOT AGAINST KING MILAN. CONSTAICTINOPLZ, SATCIRDAY.—Before General Kaulhars 'departure for Russia yesterday. the Order of the Med- jidie of the Second Clouse was conferred upon him by the Sultan. Vreetere. Seeruntr.—ln diplomatic circles here the can- didature of the Prince if Mingrelia is the only one seriously entertained, and it is expected that, notwithstanding the opposition offered by the Balgerians, it well receive the approval of the Powers, and be strongly recommended by them to the Bulgarian Government, provided that a settle- ment of the existing crisis be thereby effected. NONDAT NlGlUT.—lntelligence of a plot against King Mama of Servile has just reached here on what purports to be good authority, although so far there has been no confirmatioi of it. According to the pablished version a number of Montenegrin's had been hired to kidnap he King—pretty much as Prince Alexander was kidnapped by the Hessian hirelings—while Bis Majesty was hunting in the Vranys Mountains, and to carry him off to Monte- negro. Tei plot leaked out, however, and the King was warned in sufficient time to leave the mountains before the conspirators eauld execate their plans, His Majesty suddenly quitting Vranya leer. ilomoley night, TILE BULGeRIAN DEPUTATION TO THE POWERS. A Central Nees telegram, dated Sofia, Thursday, states: —The Bulgarian ciepuretion to the Powers left to-day. They are instructed to decline the Prince of Idingrelia's can- didatere, and to demard either Prince Waldemar or Prince Alexander of Battenberg. FRANCE.—THB FASTING MAN. French foreign policy was the subject of a statement made in the Chamber of Deputies, on Saturday, by M. de Freycinet. Osae of the prinsipal aims of the Government, the Pre ei,-r staid, had been to maintain peace, so necessary to the task of transforming an old monarchial repose into a republic. PARIS, SAITRLAY.—The medical men who are watching the case of Signor Merlatti. the Italian, who to day entered upon the 32nd day of his fast, state that his constitution is beginning to Cause them seam disquietude. The blood threatens to decompose, and the organic resistance of the stomach has reacuad its last stage. Nevertheless, despite the advice of his doctors. Signor Merlatti insists on con- tinuing his faast until the 50th day. The French Ceember of Deputies on Monday commenced the discussion of the credit tor Tocouin. The result of the debate was that the credit was sanctioned by 278 votes to 249. The Ceanuteer also approved the Tunis credit. The Madagascar vote will be diecusited to-day. EGYPf AND THE BOUDeN.—ATROCITIES IN THE It EBEL CAMP. CAIRO, SMIDAY NlQlllT.—easeording to an official report jvst received from Waey Haifa, large numbers of the black troops who originally formed part of the Egyptian army, and afterwards. from one cause or another, went over to the rebels, have latterly doseerted. Several of them, however, were recaptured before they reached our lines and were con- ducted beck to the rebel headquarters, where they were cruelly tortured to death by inueoernent and burning, the penalty being inflicted ae publiey as peersible so as to act as a deterrent Is, others. SPAINe—CBELTING A NAVY. MarralD. MOVIDATe--0013.graSS unanimoully voted to-day the Bill autherisiug an expenditure if £f1,000,000 en naval armaments to be distributed over Sine years besides £1,700,00 for the annual naval expenditure. THE BURNAM CAMPAIGN. Five additional native Indiem regiments have been ordered to Burraah. The troops forming the expedition to the ruby mines number 1,000. General Lockhart has goes in pursuit of the insurgents who fired from an ambush on a detach- ment of Madras infantry, killiug Lieutenant Green-Wood, who was in command. General White has been well re- ceived in the Shan country, whets military pests have been formed, cud trade caravans are being preparld. FIGHTING IN BURMAIL 'CYAN NIIYAT Lhro, TlitE4DAT.—The expedition to the Ruby Mines has encountered a force of 300 Share, who were, however, repelsed after sharp, close fighting. BELGrIUM.—ROMBERY OF MAALS. Burefsees, Sarttureeve—The *Eteile Beige" publishes the following telegram from Verviere of to-day's date : " On the at rival here of the exertion mail train from Ostend this morning, it was found that 22 packs, eentaining mails from England for Germany, Bessie, Austria, and the East, had been me open. All the registered lettees, the number of which is estimated at abant 150, had been stolen; but the ordinary correspondenee bad been left intset." The police believe that the thieves must have secreted themselves in the van before it was locked. An active inquiry is being made into the affair. The" Independence Beige" says that the mail especially included 40 pockets of diamonds from .New York. flue journal estimates the loss sustained by the State of Belgium, which is responsible for the-robbery, at one million francs. The Secretary of the General Post-office in London has telegraphed to the Peetmaeter of Liverpool as follows :—"Ac- cording to the lateet intelligenee,no registered letters posted in England have been stolen in the Belgian mail robbery. .All the lettere stolen were from the closed mail from New -York for Russia."

AUSTRALIA. NINE IME( SRN-PENCE') TO DEATH. SYDNAY, MONDAY.—S4ntenc,e of death has been passed upon nine young men convict d of outraging a servant girl, 16 years of age, near Moore Park, in the suburbs of this city, last September. The law of the colony prescribes death as ..a.eenalty for rape, but there is probably no case on record' where nine mu were sentenced to be hanged for outraging .008 girl. - BRIFISH .AND BELGIAN FISHERMEN. ,OSTHND, TIEMDA.Y.—The trial of the Belgian fishermen accused of cutting the nets of English fishermen in the 'North Sea has concluded. Three captains of Belgian fish- ing vessels who were charged with cutting the nets of the tfishing sloop "SurpriAe." of Lowestoft, and the " Fisher- man," of Yarmouth. were argo'oa..ed by the court, the evi- dence being ibsufficient to convict them, but other two dsber capt,ins were folly convicted of having cut the nets of the British fishing boats Leo and Airee. One of the prisoners was s.trateneati to pay a fine ef 15 francs, in de- fault, three days' imprisomnent and the other to one day's imprisonment Aid 25 figura fine. Botb were, in addition, ordered to pay for tne damage done to the British vessels nets. ,REPORTED LOSS Or A FRENCH TRANSPORT WiTh 100 TROOPS. ALGIERS, TRIIESDAY.—A despatch from Sidi Bel Abbas published here reports the total loss of the steamer Cban- dernagore, with 1,200 troops on board. The vessel is stated to have been oVertaKen hya cyclone, and to have fcundered immediately with all bends.

- - GOOD TEMP LARS' DEMONSTRATION AT WA,RRINGroN. A Good Templars' Demonstration was held on Saturday evening, in the Friends' Meeting House, Buttexmarket-street. There was a good attendance, spveral of those present wearing the decorations of the Order. The chair was ,r,ccapied by the ex- Mayor, Alderman Harrison, who took the position owing to the absence of the Mayor (Dr. Mackie.) In opening the proceedings, the Chairman said that he was pleased to be present to enjoy the concerts, and speecoes, and eecrtuets the object of that Association was the promotion of human good, but he was sorry to be present beceuee he represented the worthy Mayor under circumstances of a must painful character. The Mayor had been eti ieken down suddenly, and at that moment lay in such a hopeless, critical state, that he almost shrank from saying what he thought. The name of temperance, Alderman liarreson proceeded to say, was not in any way estrange to him. He did not think anybody could for one moment eneeeou the prepriety of people keeping sober. 'hey also knew that where a man was in the slightest dan- ger of falling into temptation, the only tning for him to do was to keep out of temptation's way. When a man suffered .from a cancer they hed, as a rule, to take off the limb to •sasee the body, and so it was with a naan who indulged in- temperately in intoricating liquor ; if he could not resist Atte terriptAtion, he should esiotosterd it altogether. The .Good Templare said, "Never tare the first glass, and you will never take the second." (Cheers.) That was A propo- sition he could not resist. There could be no two opinions as to the advisability by every possible means to do what ' they could to promote habits of sobriety amongst the people of :this country. He did not wish them to think that he was a teetotaler, for be was not. But, notwithetanding, he had the warmest sympathy with them. He could assure them that he did not underestimate the great advantage, and the benefit, to the human race, that was growing out of total abstinence secietiws. (Cheers.) He did not think therevas any positive sin in the drinking of a glass of beer cr spirite; the sin was the abuse of it, and he knew there was great abuse. The safest course. no doubt. would be to abolish it altogether. (Cheers.) They must indulge is moeeration with those ,vho differed froin them, for be believed that the tide of etoial abstinence had been rolled hack meny years by the intemperate language used by some of its advocates, who had been too zealous. He was satisfied net had been the means of keeping from the total abstinence 01085 many who woisid have taken a warm and hearty interest in it, He thought that on all occasions it was desirable to use temperate language. He had felt that the juvenile part of the com- munity were to lie the regenerators. If children could be taught from their earliest infeucy to abhor driels they would grow up to abhor ir, and the chancre were that they would remain so to the end of their lives. When a person became a teetotaller at.3o to 40 years of age he was esmeedinglv likely to fall back, unless the change in his habits arose from a pure and firm conviction of those habits being wrong. It appeared from statietics that the Geod Templars possessed 40 lees than 3,000 lodges, and had COO,OOO members scattered throughout the warld. In the district of South-West Lan- cashire the number of lodges was 66, and the number of members 2 50.1—(cheers)—and there were about the same number of juveniles, ituteteendent of the adult branch. He thought that it must be very encouraging to the Good Tem- plate in that neighbourhood to think that they could set forth figures of eucti magnitude ; they roust be satisfied that it was a cause that was making, and would make, pro- gress. He was inclined to believe that it would make more pro- gress by convincing people of the propriety of it, than it would by paseing any coercive measure to compel people. They could only bone that tie Legislature would, whenever pos- sible, do what they could to facilitate the teaching of tem. perauee habits to the people. Ho thought that they were in

div.head: LONDON MISSIONARY SOCIETY.
div.p: LONDON MISSIONARY SOCIETY.
BAZAAR AND MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

On Sunday sermons were preached in Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, in aid of the London Missionary Society. The pulpit in the, morning was occupied by the Rev. John Yonge, and the Rev. W. W. Stephenson, of Gooty, India, preached in the afternoon and evening. The collec- tions fat the day amounted to £l5 6s Od. On Monday afternoon a sale of work, the pro- ceeds of which are to be devoted to the special fund for the Zenana Missions in India, was held in Wycliffe Hall. Several stalls were nicely arranged with a variety of articles, and there were on view a number of Indian dresses and curiosities, that had been lent by Mr. Stephenson. The bazaar was opened at three o'clock in the afternoon, when, after the Rev. John Yonge had made a few intro- ductory remarks, the Rev. W. W. Stephenson briefly explained the object of the Zenana Missions. The missions were to the mass of women in India, I who lived in seclusion; a much better term than Zenana would be female missions, or missions to the women in India. The young men of India were be- ing educated, but the women of India were almost wholly neglected, and, in consequence of the cus- toms of the country, by which the women were kept in seclusion, it was found necessary to have lady missionaries, who visited them, and the work, although it was not many years ago since it was undertaken, was already showing good results, and promise of better. The sale was then proceeded with. The following ladies presided at the tables: —Mrs. Armitage, Mrs. Tonge, Mrs. Garland, Mrs. Barker, Mrs. Walker, Mrs. Henry Roberts, Mrs. Percival, Miss Garner, Mrs. and the Misses Legge, Miss Fanny Jones Miss Porritt, the Misses Kewley, Mrs. Birtles, and Mrs. Wallington. In the evening a public meeting was held in Wycliffe Church. There was a good attendance. Mr. R. Garnett presided, and addresses were given by the Rev. W. W. Stephenson, from Gooty, India, and the Rev. J. L. Green, from Tahiti, South Seas.—ln introducing • the chairman, the Rev. J. YONGE stated that it was the first time that gentleman had visited them for a purpose of that kind; but he hoped it would be by no means the last. (Hear, hear.) Those missionary meetings were opportunities for bringing upon the same plat- form memhers of various denominations. The claims of foreign missions appealed to their hearts. and whatever denomination they belonged to, they were desirous of showing their Christian sympathy by meeting together •to promote the extension of the Gospel. Mr. Yonge then read an extract from the annual report, which stated that the so- ciety was in a satisfactory condition. The total income of the society for the year was £142,016 3s. The expenditure had ex- actly equalled the income, and there was no balance against the society. (Hear, hear.) In W arrington £65 la 7d had been collected at Wycliffe Chapel and schools, and £5 7s lid from the Cockhedge Mission, making a total of over £7O. (Applause.)—The CHAIRMAN said they were under no obligation to him for his presence that evening, as it gave him a feeling of gratitude to be permitted in any shape or form to be able to do any thing for the Great Master. (Hear, hear.) There were people who made calculations from a business point of view as to how much it cost to convert the souls in a foreign land; but he thought that was a most miserable way of doing it. (Hear, hear.) The great and broad command was "Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature." (Hear, hear.) That command, which was given 1,800 years ago, was equally good to-day, and a man who refused to do anything towards the salvation of his fellowman was denying the obliga- tion which God had put upon him. (Hear, hear.) If they could put that question rightly before the people, what a wonderful difference there would be in their contributions and collections! There was an amount spent in this country in some things which if it were contributed for one year to the aid of missionary societies would put them in such a condition that they would not have to make collec- tions every year. (Hear, hear.) He asked them I to give freely, as there was much land to be encom- passed and much work to be done. (Cheers.)— The Rev. J. L. GREEN, speaking of mission work and the progress of civilization in the islands of the South Seas, referred to the increased commerce of those islands, and said that at the present time thousands of men and women rejoiced in the liberty wherewith the Gospel made them free. (Applause.) There were now living on those islands men and women consecrated to God in body and in soul, and delighting in his service. There was a vast improvement in the condition of the

Telford, Hackett, Ashurst, Nevins, Eyes, Holland; umpire, S Wright. WARRINGTON V. ROCHDALE HORNETS. A very fine game resalted from the meeting of these two clubs on Saturday, at Warrington, and it was witnessed by about 4,000 spectators. The home team were short of Jolley and Rigby. Fair Turner taking the place of the for- mer at three-quarters; and the visitors were minus Groves. The Warringtonians were first on the field, the visitore,how- ever, soon putting in an appearance, A start being at once made. The Rochdale team kicked off from the town end, Barnes returning. Gilbert was the first to make himself conspicu- ous by a run and kick to touch. Some excellent passing was next witnessed on the part of the visitors, a good scrim- mage being formed in neutral quarters. Fair Turner col- lared Hastings in fine style, Barnes doing likewise for No- lan and Griffith& Good kicking between Barnes, Smith. and Griffiths was indulged in, Smith in the end making a nice run and kick, and Appleton neatly returning. Little. wood next made a good collar, and then Gilbert a nice run from a kick by Beckley. The visitors' forwards next took the oval to the home 25, but Gilbert and Barnes by a good dribble were instrumental in bringing play te centre. Again the visitors' forwards by strong play took the leather to the /Arne quarters, and again Gilbert brought it back, this time to the Rechdele 25. Massey next got hold and made a sen- sational run over the line, but through some informality the point was not allowed. Dillon next put in a good dribble, and then the Warrington men rushed the ball over the line, a dead ball resulting. Fair Turner returned the kick out, and Davies neatly collared Hastings with the ball. Speakman next stopped a rush, and thee passed to Barnes, a dead ball resulting. Nolan, shortly after the kick out, made a very good run, and some good forward play and a run by Smith brought about half-time, with the score two minors to the home team, to the visitors nothing. On resuming Frank Turner kicked off, end there being little or no return play settled down in the visitors' quarters. Gilbert now passed to Fair. Turner, who struggled over the line, everyone thinking that the try was a fair one; but the referee de- cided otherwise. The Hornets now worked hard to notch a point, and took the ball pest the half-way flag, but Fair. Turner returned with a punt, and Massey following up col- lared Griffiths with the ball. Another dead ball resulted from a strong rush of the forwards. Appleton now took the oval in grand style and punted to touch. After a good run by Nolan, and a niee dribble by Gilbert, time was called, the score standing Warrington four minors, Rochdale Hornets nil. Commenting on the game a splendid exhibition of foot- ball was the result of the tussle. Warrington, as has been usual with them for some time, tried to make it as open as possible. Their opponents, when they found this out, were deficient in this respect, making the game slightly a packed one, the home team, however, having the best of it in the scrimmage. Nothing could be better than the grand com- bined play at times exlaibited by the home team, and it was only the hardest of luck which prevented them from run- ning op a score. Speaking of individual play, the full back Appleton quite justified his selection, playing a good sound game; one piece of play when he got the ball et top speed after running a good distance, quite pleasing the spectators. Barnes, the centre three-quarter, played a good sound game, tackling and kicking well. Fair. Turner bad a try at wing three-quarter, and was very successful, if we take into con- sideration that this is not his proper position. Massey, his partner on the other wing, again exhibited superior sav- ing form, besides putting in some good punts, and following up exceedingly well. Speakman played fairly well on the defensive, but his play was not up to the form of his brother half back. Gilbert, who was the best back on the field, and passed with excellent judgment, as well as dribbling and tackling in a very praiseworthy manner. Of the forwards. Davies quite pleased everybody by his bard work in the scrimmage. and by his good following up and tackling; Littiewood, Dillon, and Frank Turner also show- ing up well in this respect. In fact all the forwards exhi- bited good form. Coining to the Rochdale contingent, Buckley, the full back, several times had his hands full, and very successfully repelled the invasion. Griffiths was not quite a match for his opponent, Barnes, but nevertheless did his little in a masterly manner Smith and Has'ing both got in some nice runs, the former tackling with great de— termination. Nolan was the best of the two half hacks and did a vast amount of work, both running, kicking, and tackling in fine style. It would be hard to single out indi- vidual players in the ranks of the forwards, as one and all strove their utmost to beat the cup-holders, but could not manage the task. Teams :—Warrington : Back, Appleton ; three-quarter backs. Fair. Turner, Barnes. and Massey: half backs, Gil- bert and Speakman ; forwards. Frank Turner, Dayies, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, W. Povey, R. Littleweod, Hough. Ash- ton, and Hayes. Rochdale : Back. Buckley; Hasting (e4ptaita), Smith. and Griffiths, three-quarter backs ; half backs, Nolan and Beinford ; forwards, Rawkin, Wild, Milli- dew, Binas, Roe, Brierly, Ashworth, Leech, and Holt. Re- feree, Mr. Dewhurst.

NOTES BY THE WAY. Warrington and Rochdale Hornets on their meeting last Saturday, gave us an example of what might be fairly termed high-class football. The Hornets evidently believe in organised, or as it is sometimes called, scientific play, and their passing at times was much admired. At the same time the home team were fully equal to them in this re- spect, while they excelled them in strength and endurance. As a conssqaeace the Hornets were distinctly out-played. and it wag only due to the decisions on the part of the re- feree, which seemed inexplicable to ordinary people, that the home team score WAS not a very decided one. Three players were particularly conspicuous in the War- rington team, namely, Massey, Gilhprt, and &ppleton. The last-named was quite a success as back, always turning up at the right moment. Gilbert has often distinguished him- self lately, but on Saturday be was more than usually prominent, while Massey was brilliant in his tackling and quick tans. The new grand stand which has previously been referred to, though not covered in, was put to use on Saturday. It is well designed and strong, and was generally voted to be a great improvement. To-day it will be formally opened by the president of the club, Mr. R. W. Francomb, J.P. The match to-day, it may also be mentioned, will be under the patronage of Colonel Thackwell and the officers of the Bth ani 4.oth Legimental districts. The match on Eaterday between West Lancashire and Westmorland was a tough affair. Both teams played well, Lancashire having the best of the scoring up to the last five minutes, when the home team equalised matters, the gam ending in a draw of one try and five minors each. At Newcastle, on Saturday, 2,000 spectators witnessed the match between Lancashire and Northumberland. Lan- cashire had decidedly the best of the game, scoring three goals, one try, and six minor points to their oppanents one try and three minor points.

Wound conclusion—A dying echo. . frln studying character, do not be blind to the short- comings of a warm friend or the virtues of a bitter enemy. A man who went fishing in a private pond in a suburban town complains that he only got one bite, and that was from a dog whose master owns the pond. He who feels contempt for any fellow-creature, and expresses it by word or look or gesture, is guilty of an irremediable wrong to himself, to his neighbour, and to society. He is not only inflicting needless and fruitless pain, but he is loosening the foundations of virtue and the ties which bind society together. SNOWED Up.—Saow has been falling heavily over the northern counties of Sootland since Wednesday morning, and the roads and railways in exposed sit uationsare blocked Two passenger trains were 1' snowed up " on Thursday morning on the Highland and Great North of Scotland lines, and the general traffic is blocked. LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION IN EuINEURGFL—A great de- monstration was made in Edinburgh on 'I hursday night by the Liberals of the Scottish metropolis. The Earl of Aber- deen presided, and repeated the expression of his opinion in favour of Home Rule for Ireland. Mr. John Morley, who had a very enthusiastic reception, said the Liberal dissen- tients professed to be satisfied with the Tory programme, which was prepared by the Liberals ; but he declined to say grace until the dish-covers were raised, and he hoped he dissentient friends would not find that they who supped with Lord R. Churchill required a very long ladle. Mr. Morley went on to speak on the question of the extension of local self-government in Scotland. He strongly denied that any case for Horne Rule had been made out as far as Scot- land was concerned, but admitted that intolerable evils ex- isted, and predicted that in a short time a great part of the Scotch business which was now done at Westminster would he transacted in Scotland. When the proper time came, English members would not resist a sober, practical scheme of self-government fir Scotland. On the question of the Church, Mr. Motley said that religious equality was rapidly obtaining, if it had not already obtained, a place among the declared and active objects of the Liberal party in Scotland. Turning to the Irish question, the right hon. gentleman denied that he had " palliated lawlessness." He showed how deplorable it was that good legislation could not be obtained without lawlessness or the threat of it. He re- viewed the history of English rule in Ireland. sketched the " Castle system." and summed up the record of even our most recent dealings with Ireland as a catalogue of " va- cillations, precipitancies, and hesitancies." With wisdom, energy, and patience, in a free government, every good cause triumphed at last, and he believed that their cause would soon triumph. THE STATE OF IRELAND..

The Duke of Devonshire has announced by circular to his tenants in the Counties of Waterford and Cork that he will allow 25 per cent reduction on the present half-year's rent. The premises of the Belfast Constitutional Club have just been sold by auction. Conservatism has for some months past been without " headquarters " in the capitel of Ulster. The Earl af Erne (the Viscount Crichton of the House of Commons for many years) was en Wednesday appointed Imperial Grand Master of the °wage Society, in room of the late Lord Enniskillen. his father-in-law. Lord Aehbourne (Lord Chancellor) and Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimer were, with Lord Justice Fitzgibbon on Monday, sworn in Lord Justices for the government of Ire- land during the Lord-Lieutenant's absence. Forty-one of the Kerry Moonlightera arrived by train at Cork on Monday, under a strong escort. As they were naarcbed to the gaol a large crowd followed them, and Mr. John O'Connor, M.P., caused cheers to ba raised for tee prisoners. A solicitor who had been refused accommodatien at an hotel in Tralee—being boycotted because of his connec:ion with Lord Cork's estate—recovered £3 damages from the landlady in a trial before Mr. Justice O'Brien and a jury in DuWin on Wednesday. The arrest of Mr. Thompson (chairman) and Mr. Mon- cried (exedireetor), of the Ulster Land, Building. and In- vestment Company, on Saturday night, by order of the Vice-Chancellor's Court, in connection with recent disclo- sures as to the condition of that company, has created in- tense excitement in Belfast; although some such step was fully anticipated. On the Sheriff arresting Mr. Moncrief, who takes a prominent part in local religious matters, the latter quoted scripture extensively to prove the illegality of the proceeding. SIR R. flaminTort's SUCCIMOR.—GeneraI Buller's ap- pointment as under-Secretary for Ireland is, according to a Central News telegram, only a temporary engagement. He returns to the War Office early in March. The Government requires his services during the transaction of business inci- dental to Sir Robert Hamilton'sdeparture, and the reorgank ieation of the secretarial department. dividing the work It is in contemplation to recommend that the Under-Secretaryship should be filled by a member of Parliament, to relieve the Chief Seeretary in the House of Commons. DM/IAM' SritscHw3.—A meeting was held at Riverstown, on Sunday, at which Mr. O'Brien denounced the Govern- ment in strong language, and exulted in the the fact that they were able to overcome their unworthy schemes for re- pressing public opinion in Ireland. The police threatened to arrest Mr. O'Brien, but he de- fied them; and as there was only a small force of police in the place, the police thought it pru- dent net to take extreme measures. Mr. O'Brien subse- quently delivered two short addresses in other small towns in the neighbourhood, denouncing the trial of the Galway rioters in Sligo. In the town of Sligo the police did not allow any of the Nationalist leaders to address the people, and the streets were kept clear by the police and Lancers. Dr. Tanner, M.P., attempted to hold an open-air meeting in a field near the town, and had just commenced to de- nounce the tyranny of the Government and jury packing, when the police dispersed the crowd at the point of the bayonet.

JOHN DILLON IN COURT. In the Queen's Bench Division, Dublin, on Tuesday, be- fore Justices 1.40115013, O'Brien, and Johnson, Mr. John Dillon, M.P., appeared to answer a summons, served on him at Ballagbadereen, to show cause why he should not be called upon to provide bail for his good behaviour. There was a large attendance Inside the court, including several members of Parliament. Mr. Dillon was cheered as he en- tered the court in company with the Lord Mayor of Dublin. —Mr. Healy applied for an adjournment, on the ground that he bad only just been instructed, Mr. Dillon having returned to town late on Monday night. The affidavits for the Crown were exceedingly voluminous, and he required time to read them, to see whether they demanded an answer. He quoted the case of Seymour and Devitt as a precedent for granting a postponement. When Mr. Devitt asked for time to instruct counsel, the Attorney-General, for the Crown, admitted that the request was a reasonable one.—An argument ensued, in which Mr. Healy urged that evidence should be given not by affidavit, but orally.—The Attorney- General submitted that affidavits were customarily filed, and contended that the eastern must be observed in this case—Mr. Healy declared that the action of the Attorney- General was unfair and ungenerous. and intimated his in- tention net to file any affidavits, but to raise be question when the case came on again. The Attorney-General had tl4is Apposition lurking in his mind, and, considering that ' Mr. Dillon's liberty was at stake, it was ungenerous.—Judge O'Brien peremptorily directed the affidavits to be filed by Wednesday next.—The Attorney-Generel offered no objec- tion to a reasonable time being given.—After some discus- sion the Court fixed December 11th for the trial.—Mr. Dillon, on leaving court, was followed by the crowd and loudly cheered. Amongst others present were Mr. Timothy Harrington, M.P., Mr. Gill, M.P.. Alderman O'Connor, M.P., Mr. Cox, M.P., Mr. Dickson, and several Roman Catholic clergymen and ladies.
