He had no doubt that total ab- stinence societies throughout the world had great mime for thankfulness, and when they saw the remarkable diminu- tion that had taken place in the drinking habits of the people, it must give them great pleasure to see how the cause was progressing. They might depend ripen it that the time was not far distant when the people would become more convinced of the propriety, usefulness, and advantage of becoming sober people. There were many things conducive to habits of intemperance ; one was the lack :of good wives. He looked upon that as a question of the greatest possible im- portance, for many wives, net having been trained ia do- mestic habits, were incapable of makiug home comfortable, end as it should be, with the consequence that in many cases men went to the public-house as a more congenial place. (Cheers.)—The choir then sang '• Beautiful stream," and the Sisters Clarke sang the duet "The song of the fountain."—Mr. J. H. Musg., D. 8.5., of Manchester, in the course of a stirring address, said that Good Ternplers them- oelves went in for the "whole hog," but did not blame those who were not prepared to go quite to far as they did. Good Ternplare did not, in the strict sense et the word, eay that drinking a glass was a sin. They allowed everyone to be their own judge, but he thought that in his case, from the circumstances and surroundings of his life, it would be a positive sin to take intoxicating drinks. The great end and aim of Good Templar work was the overthrow of the drink traffic, though the realisation of it might be a long way off. They were battling against drink because they believed it to be in its broad results a great evil, for it stood in the way of social, moral, and national progress.—Mt. MoRRIS JONES, W.D.S., Liverpool, afterwards gave a prac- tical address, an 4 also proposed a resolution to the effect that the meeting deeply regretted to hear of the very serious condition of the Mayor of Warrington, and earnestly prayed that it be the Divine will that he might speedily recover, and so be able to discharge those duties for which be was so eminently qualified, and also that the meeting assured his family of it sincere sympatby.—The resolution was carried unanimously.—During the evening musical selections were rendered, and a collection in aid of expenses was made at the close.

DISTRICT MEETING. The quarterly district meeting of the South-West Lanca- shire Dtstrict Lodge, 1.0.G.T., was held on Saturday after- noon. in the lodge room of the Temperance Mission Lodge, Academy-street,Warrington. A large number of representa- tives and members attended the session, which was opened by the presiding officer of the district, Brother J. W. Hall. The various reports of the officers were read and adopted. That of the W.D.S. gave the statistical returns, and stated that the membership in the district numbered 2,500, work- ing in 65 lodges, and each lodge was fairly well attended. Many public meetings had been held, and a large amount of mission work had been done during the past quarter. The aggregate number of meetings, ledge sessions, and public meetings attended by the executive officers was 201. Tbe work connected with missioning various parts of the district had been well taken up, and would be well carried out durieg the winter months. The district treasurer re- ported a good balance in hand,which was very encouraging, as it is some time since the treasurer had been able to give such a good report. The district was free from debt. The superintendent of the juvenile branch was able to report good progress in connestion with the javenile work, and a bright prospect for the ensuing quarter. The following re- solution was passed unanimously :—" That this District Lodge exprestes its hearty approval of the course adopted at the late nonference, held at Boston, Mass., to secure the re-nuton of the two branches of 1.0.G.T., and trusts that this object may be speedily consummated, whereby the 620,000 members associated therewith slay be enabled, under God, to pursue the great work of raising rthe fallen and preventing others from falling, regardless if race, colour, er clime." On the conclusion of the meeting the members adjourned for tee,whish had been provided by the sisters of the Mission Lodge.

. LECTURE ON "DREAMING." On Monday evening, the Rev. J. A. Macdonald, of Birkenhead, gave a lecture on "Dreaming," in Bold- street Wesleyan Schools, Warrington. In the absence of the Mayor through illness, Alderman Davies presi • ded. There was a largo attendance. The Chairman having expressed the regret he felt at the illness of the Mayor, said he should not like to sit down with- out saying how pleased he was to take the chair that night. He was satisfied that all their various sect* were like the sidings on a railway: if they were going in the right dire'. tion they should all get on the right line. (Hear. hear.)— The Rev. J. A. Macdonald then gave his lecture, which was an extremely interesting one, and listened to with great at- tention. Dreaming was the result, he said, of the activity of the mind during the sleep of the senses. The dreams they remembered were those which occurred when sleep was broken. Those that they remembered frequently occurred either before one fell sound asleep at night, or just when one was waking from sleep in the morning, or if anything should disturb one's sleep. The ease of a gentleman who was the victim of dreams is reported. He consulted a phy- sician on the subject, and the physician asked him what he had hadlor supper the previous night. He replied that he bad for his supper half a mutton pie, and he dreamed aboet his grandfather. " Well " said the doctor. "if you had eaten the other half, you would have seen your grand- mother also." (Laughter.) Whatever was calculated te disturb the rest was likely to give rise to dreams. The lee- turer then referred to somnambulism and incubus or night- mare. The latter ha explained was a state in which the dreamer tried to act in his dream, but the muscles refused to perform their work. There was also such a thing as day- mars, the effect of which was that a person's muscles re- fused to work although be had perfect possession of his senses. Le dreams, the senses being locked in sleep, there was nothing to correct the vividness of the ideas, and these appeared as though they were realities. It was a well- known fact that people in a state of ab- straction bad very vivid ideas, and those who were remarkable for their clear ratiocination, and their profound thinking qualities were oftentimes what were called absent men. Those who had the power of abstract- ing themselves from the interference of the ewes had superior opportunities of cultivating the reflective ideas than ordinary persons. It was often found, therefore, that men of absent minds were men of deep thinking Powers. It was said of Archimedes that when Syracuse was attacked, in the midst of the noise and slaugh- ter of the capture, he was found by the soldiers trying to work out a geometrical problem. The soldiers dragged hien away from the work, but he still seemed to be unconscious of the uproar, so abstracted was he in the investigation of the problem. Sir Isaac Newton, and other men who were remarkable for abstraction in their thoughts, were also referred to. The moral to be drawn from this, Mr. Mac- donald said, was that they should anticipate the disem- bodied state in which, wben they were free from the intru- sion of their natural senses, the spiritual sense would come out into strong power. (Hear, hear.) Incongruity in re- lation to time often characterised their dreaming. Lave- leye, when in prison in 1315, dreamt that he saw a proces- sion of skinless horses which continued to pass him for several hours, but when he awoke he found he had only been asleep a few minutes. Dr. Abercromby also dreamt that he had crossed the Atlantic, and made a tour through the United States, yet when he awoke he raw by the clock that he had been sleeping no longer than ten minutes. When the freaks of fancy they were subject te in dreams, became fixed upon the mind, they were said to be possessed of an idea, aid that was incipient insanity, and if that became permanent they had a Case of permanent insanity. The finest minds were often the most nicely balanced, and it was often the finest strung intellects that were closest to the edge of insanity. He sometimes thought that some of our poets were just on the verge of insanity, und it was thrise parts of their poems in which their genius most appeared that indicated how finely their minds were balanced. In- tellectual feats during dreams, such as the composition of music and writing, were then referred to, and these achievements the lecturer ascribed to the freedom of the thinking powers from the in- trusion of the irreses during sleep. The memory also was extraordinarily powerful during sleep, and they might infer from this that when they left the body behind and passed into that state between death and the resurrection, they would have a wonderfully keen recollection of every- thing they did on earth Hence the wisdom of doing on earth actions which could be thought of with pleasure hereafter, and of avoiding doing the reverse. (Hear, hear.) The mind had alio excursory powers during sleep, and in- stances were alluded to of persons while asleep apparently wit- nessing things which were taking place at the same time is distant parts. For this phenomenon, Mr. Macdonald said, he could think of only one explanation,which appeared to be a simple one, and that was that the mind had the power of extremely rapid migration, and that when the oc- currences referred to took place the mind had actaally migrated during the sleep of the dreamer to the scene of the occurrences. Prophetic vission, and the wiping out, as it were, in the minds of some people of all remembrance of what had taken place in certain periods of their life were next referred to in an extremely interesting manner ; and, in conclusion, the lecturer said he was inclin•cl to think that after death they would not go untducated into the spirit world. He believed they should have gathered a lot of experience of that world during sleep, and that they would there find themselves in the midst of friends. (Loud aoplause.)—A vote of thanks to the lecturer was warmly accorded on the motion of the Rev. G. E. Cuttine, seconded by Mr. Silccck. A similar vote to the chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

people during the last few years, and this was brought about through the efforts of the mission- aries. (Cheers.)—The Rev. W. W. STEPHENSON, speaking on the success of missionary work in India, said some people sympathised with mission- aries because they imagined they were undergoing all sorts of penances; but, although they did not have the same comforts that the people of this country had, they did not want their sympathy on that account. They wanted it in order that they might be able to go on manfully with the work, and be made to feel their responsibilities. Mission- aries wanted to feel that they were only the ad- vanced guard—only soldiers on foreign service fighting for Christ Himself. The real difficulties missionaries had to contend with in India were custom, the unmitigated selfishness of the people, and their utter indifference in regard to the future. They were, however, getting through their difficul- ties, and the work was progressing as probably no other work had progressed in the world; and edu- cated Hindoos had told him that he would be aston- ished before long at the immense hold the mission- aries had obtained on the natives of India. (Ap- plause.)—The meeting terminated with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: GREAT MILL FIRE AT GOLBORNE. .£50,000 DAMAGES.
div.p: GREAT MILL FIRE AT GOLBORNE. .£50,000 DAMAGES.

About three o'clock on Tuesday morning what proved to be a most destructive fire broke out at the extensive paper-staining works of Messrs. Mit- chell, Arnott, and Co., of Golborne, near Newton-le- Willows. At the time the weather was exceeding- ly boisterous and wet, and few people wsre astir. shortly before two o'clock, however, a small fire was discovered in Mr. Kidd's chemist shop, and as the police and a few neighbours left the premises their attention was directed to the paper mill, which was then ablaze. The works were three stories high, and covered a large area of ground, the front por- ;ion being surrounded by the Legh Arms Hotel and a large quantity of valuable cottage property. Fortu- nately the wind was blowing south, anti the flames were thus carried from the surrounding houses where for a time, some scores of people were asleep. The ire, which originated at the Legh-street end,seemed to gain possession of the building in a very short time, for when the alarm was raised it had worked its way so into the works as to completely envelope the fire extinguishing appliances kept on the pre- 'wises. This means shut off, there was no source of available water except from the street mains, hose- pipes to which were immediately coupled. The force was altogether inadequate, and despite the efforts of the many willing hands who had now arrived the flames rapidly spread, and shooting up above the building lit up the sky for many miles. Meanwhile the Newton Fire Brigade had been tele- graphed for, but the officials being off duty the communication could not be effected. A large quan- tity of paper, varnish, and other inflammable material was stored, and this gave increased zest to the raging flames, so that within an hour from the outbreak the entire place was completely gutted, and renewed efforts were made to save the adjoining property. The walls fell in with a loud crash about five o'clock, com- pletely blocking up some portions of the surround- ings. About two hundred hands will be thrown idle, many of them being heads of families. The loss will be great to the inhabitants, as only lately large cotton mills in Golborne were closed. The greatest sympathy is shown for the firm, who will be put to irrecoverable loss, the fire having con- sumed all their books, valuable blocks, new season's patterns, Sze. From now onward for a few months is usually their busiest season, and every prepara- tion was complete for executing new designs for , the coming season. The damage to the plant, Sze., has-been estimated to be upwards of £50,000. The premises were insured in several offices. The origin of the outbreak is unknown.

div.head: ALLEGED ATTEMPTED FRAUD AT
div.p: ALLEGED ATTEMPTED FRAUD AT

EA.RLESTOWN. At Warrington County Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesday, a young man named John Fitzpatrick, who formerly worked for a contractor for the Newton Improvement Commissioners, was charged with having, on the Monday previous, attempted to ob- tain 5d by false pretences, from William Platt, at Earlestown.—Platt, a lad, son of Joseph Platt, Gas- street, Leigh, said that last Monday he was in Earlestown, going to the station with a basket of oat cakes, which he had been endeavouring to sell for his father. In the afternoon lie met prisoner in Queen-street. Prisoner asked him what he was selling, and he replied oat cakes. He showed them to the prisoner, who took a piece off the top of one and off the bottom of another and toasted them. He said he had taken Mr. Crabtree's place and he wan- , ted sd. Prisoner asked him if he had seen Mr. Crabtree, and witness replied that he had not. Mr. Crabtree was the collector of tolls for the Newton Commisioners. When he told prisoner he had not seen Mr. Crabtree, Fitzpatrick said "Well. I want 5d." Witness told him that he had only one basket of cakes, and then the prisoner said he wanted 20, but he said nothing about the tolls. He then took a book out of his pocket and appeared to write on a piece of paper; while he was ;doing so the paper blew down the itreet, and prisoner went after it. Witness then went up the street, where he Saw Crabtree and a policeman, to whom he gave infor- mation. He had never seen the prisoner be- fore. lie had given Mr. Crabtree toll on previous occasions. the charge being 3d for two baskets.— John Crabtree, market inspector and toll collector for the Newton Commissioners, said he had on several occasions received toll from last witness. Three or four months ago prisoner worked for a con- tractor who was under the Commissioners. He had not been engaged since that time in any work con- nected with the Commissioners, as far as witness knew. Ile had certainly never had authorithy from him to collect tolls.—P.C. Hunt, of Earlestown, de- posed that when prisoner was charged he said, "Crabtree told me to collect tolls for him." Prisoner

had a book, a piece of paper, and a pencil in his hand, and when searched the surm of la 12s 5d was found upon him. Prisoner was sober, but appeared to have had some drink.—Mr. Worsley (law clerk to the Newton Commissioners), said it was not a Com- missioners' but a police prosecution, and he did not think there had been sufficient evidence to show that the rights of the Commissioners were directly endangered, and that they should pay the costs (as suggested by the magistrates' clerk) if the prisoner was committed for trial.—Mr. Bleckly thought that if the Commissioners expected such an offence to be put down they should step into the breach and pay the costs.—Mr. Worsley consented to do so on behalf of the Commissioners, and the prisoner was then committed to the sessions for trial.

Wuxcx OW A Govauxxxarr Bartop.—lnformation has been received by the War Department that the barge Sul- tan, while proceeding down the Thames with a million rounds of ammunition for shipment on board the Duke of Buccleuch, was run into, off Tilbury Docks, by a steamer laden with fish, and sank. The ammunition, which was packed in 1,800 boxes, was bound for India, and the loss is estimated at nearly £7,000. MORN STRING/1i FOR THU NATT.—}lOr Majesty's ship Lizard, one of the two gunboats being built fer the 'Govern- ment by Messrs. Harland and Wolff, Belfast, was success- fully launched on Saturday. The new ship is a composite gunboat, and will probably be ready for the naval dock- yard in about six months. The sister ship Bramble, it is expected, will be launched early next month. The too-
pedo vessel Heela was the last Government ship built in Belfast.

ALLEM) Seniors FunwatnttaNT.—Much sensation was- caused on Monday in Hull by the report that the cashier of a firm in the town had absconded, and Oat an examina- tion of the books showed there were defalcations amount- ing to between £4,000 and £5,000. No particulars have been made public, but it is known that the police on Saturday evening made en extensive viznre of property said to have been purchased from proceeds of the embezzle- ment.

A noniron Love TRAOHDY.—A true lovers' tragedy has just occurred in Lyors. A young man 25, who had com- pleted his term of military service, finding that his means. did not enable him to merry tlaci girl of his choice, whose - parents were obdurste, wrote to her to sav that, as life was- intolerable without her, he intended to smother himself with the fumes of charcoal. The girl agreed to die with him, and they were both found lying dead in a room several days after they bed carried out their fatal plan. THE M MBES' CONEBRENCE AT MANCERSTBR.---Tbe Miners' National Conference nniehed its sitting, at Mane cbester, on Saturday. Two important resolutions were passed. The first advocated an effort being made at the earliest opportunity to eecure an:advarce of wages The !Second was that the Conference strongly conderancel the action of the Governmeut in taking away the mail con- tracts from English steamship companies, and giving tce German and French companies the mail contracts to America and Afriss. Tim Larcaserza Wive MIIMMITI CASE.—Thclmaq Bina- barn, framework knitter, was brought up at Leicester. on Saturday, and remanded, charged with murdering his wife. The evidence showed that the prisoner applied to the mag- istrates for a warrant against his wife for bigamy During a quarrel the previous night the prisoner shot his wife with a pistol. and then knelt upon her and almost cot her bead off. The prieener eagerly cross-examined the wit- neasee. When charged the prisoner replied, "I did it. I shot her and cut her throat." Drsarraous Cowsrox.— The Maggie Trimble, from Iquique, South America, anchored off Ryde Pier. on Satur- day, having been in collision in the English Channel with another vessel, name unknown. Under the fallen top gear one of the crew, a Dane, was crushed. An attempt was made to rescue him, but unavailingly. On the vesel ar- riving off Ryde assistance was afforded and the debris re- moved, the mart being found underneath quite dead. AN the head gear and the cutwater of the Maggie Trimble were carried away by the collision. M. J. MORLKY AND LORD RIPON AT HAWARDRN.-- Mr. John Morley Arrived at Chester on Saturday evening by the North-Western express from Euston due at 5.50. Mr. Gladstone's private carriage was in waiting and in this the right honourable gentleman drove over the interreniag eight miles to Hawarden Castle, arriving there precisely at seven o'clock. Mr. J. Morley dined with Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone. The Marquis of Ripon travelled by the night mail from London to Chester, having also driven from Chester. Earl Spencer is expected to join the party. MR. G LADSTONE AND CHURCH ESTADLTSIMENTB.—A

letter Is published from Dr. Parker of the City Temple, which that gentleman says that having written to Mr. Gladstone and asked him whether Church establishmeats did not now depend upon their usefulness for their duration, the right hon. gentleman replied as follows:—" Hawarden Castle, November 28.—Dear Dr. Parker,—You are quite right in supposing that I acknowledge and cannot forget the consistent and generous support which I have so long received from Nonconformists in ail parts of the country, and likewise that, in my opinion, which receives from day to day more and more illustra,ion, Church establishments cannot and ought not to continue uniess they prove themselves useful to the maintenance of the higher life of the nation.—l remain, very faithfully yours, W. SOME months ago, when Mr. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule Bill and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S federation proposals were being hotly dip. cussed, we ventured to argue that one way out of the difficulty was to unite the two pro- posals by giving a separate Home Rule Par- liament to England, to Ireland, to Scotland, and to Wales, with a federation which should furnish us with an Imperial Parliament for imperial affairs. Wider knowledge, and close attention to the facts of the situation, con- firm us in the opinion that, however long we may be about it, "to this complexion we must come at last." Ireland will have no- thing but Home Rule; it is the only thing which has the least promise of satisfying the peopie of Ireland, and that counts for some- thing in these days of universal suffrage. And now Scotland has formally put in her - claim. At a largely-attended Conference of- the Nation I Liberal Federation of Scotland, which was held at Hawick, on Tuesday, the following resolution, amongst others, was adopted That in the opinion of this Conference it is imperative alike in the in- terests of Scottish, and of Imperial affairs that a measure of Home Rule should be granted to Scotland which will place the entire manage- ment of all purely Scottish questions in the hands of representatives of the Scottish people." In the course of his speech in mov- ing this resolution, Mr. A. L. BROWN, M.P., said "he did not see that it was a very cii.lcult matter to take purely Scotch matters out of the control of Englishmen, Welshmen, and Irishmen, who knew nothing and cared little about them. The proper solution of that question was therefor,,, separate or local national government for each of the four na- tions, and joint Imperial government by all the four nations." As this is pretty much in the strain of our own contention, we need hardly say that we quite agree with the mem- ber for the Hawick District. Mr. CZIAMBER- - LAIN has a watchful eye, and ha will, of course, make himself familiar with the views. of the National Federation of Scotland. He- has shown himself to be, as a rule, resolute,: ' in insisting that the people should, as far as.. possible, be left to govern themselves ; and, as he has, moreovei, advocated federation, it will be of interest to note how he receives.- a proposal for federation based upon the setting up of four Home Rule Parliaments. People of the timid sort, who are influenced by names rather than things, are, we are quite aware, scared with any talk, about anther Parliament. The opposition to Home Rule to Ireland is due in a great measure to his grandmother y weakness. But practical statesmen should be above considera6ons of this kind. What is Parliament, after all, but a National Committee for managing the. affairs of the nation? And if it has become obvious, as we hold it has, that one Parlia-. ment is utterly incapable of getting through. the work assigned to it, why should we- shrink from sating that the work would be. far better done if, for minor business, there were four Committees, or four Parliaments, in- stead of one? We know that it is urged that much of the business of each country will be taken out of the hands of the Impe- rial Parliament when we get 3 reform of local self-government, and we do not deny the truth of this proposition. The difikulty is that local self-government as applied to-Ire- land will not be a remedy for the ills of Ire- land ; it will not get rid of Irish discontent. The machine may be set up, but the people of Ireland will not work it; or if they do put it in motion, they will use it as a means of forcing what they now ask for that is Home Rule. They are perfectly frank about this ; they make no concealment of their intention; and, this being so, we cannot understand why the Government, or the Dissentient Liberals, should wish under the circumstances to give them anything at all. Perhaps we do the Government an in-

justice in supposing they desire to bring forward a measure for the reform of the gevernment f Ireland; they are pledged to such a course it is true, and they are under- stood to be collecting information for this special purpose; but recent utterances of -Lord SALISBURY and Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL lead to the conclusion that they will do nothing for Ireland until they are compelled. It is different, we trust, with the Dissentient Liberals; they may have thought Mr. GLADSTONE'S scheme for set- tling the Irish question was not a good one; but they, too, are pledged to speedy reform of" Castle government,", and, as they are Liberals, we would fain think that they will be true to the traditions of their creed. What they have to ask themselves is, "Can we • propose any reform in the local government of Ireland short of Home Rule which will not be used as a lever for forcing Home Rule ?" 1f they answer this with a nega tive, and we do not see what other answer they can give, they may be constrained to say, "Since Home Rule is inevitable, let us have Home Rule all round, for we are de- termined not to give Ireland advantages ' which are denied to Scotland and Wales" This would be a sound and logical posi- tion ; it is a position, at any rate, which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN could take up ; for it would be perfectly consistent with his known desire to work on lines of federation. Those who look only on the surface are op- posed to any delegation of legislative power on the ground that it would lead to differences in law which would breed confusion and dis- order. These people do not seem to be aware, as Mr. BROWN remarked at the Conference, that so far as Scotland is concerned, "She had separate criminal and civil law from Eng- land; her bankruptcy law, education law and land laws, fishery and game laws, v-ere all different." It is pretty much the same as to Ireland, which is so far different from Eng- land as to have got rid of the Established •Church, and secured a better system of land tenure. Wales, too, has its points of differ- ence, as we see if we go no further than the Sunday closing question. We have in these cases different laws because of differences of countries and of peoples; and it is for the same reason that we require different Com- mittees, or Parliaments, for the direction and management of purely domestic affairs. Why, forsooth, should the business of the Imperial Parliament be blocked until Englishmen, _lrishmen, Scotchmen, and Welshmen have decided what should be done as to a tramway in some remote corner of Ifeland ? And so 'with regard to the smaller affairs of other Fortions of the United Kinfrdom. Let them in so far as they are Scotch be dealt with by Scotchmen in a Scotch spirit. How many English members of Parliament are there, for instance, that tnderstand the A B C of the connection be- tween Cliurch and State in Scotland? Not more than a score probably, and yet, unless a change takes place. Englishmen, Welshmen, and Irishmen will be called in to assist Scotchmen in deciding on a question which the Scotch could much more satisfactorily decide for themselves. Then there is the question of the English Church in Wales. As it stands it is an iniquitous burden upon Welshmen—a burden of which they are striv- ing to rid themselves, and from which they would soon be free if left to deal with the matter in a Parliament of their own, Look- ing at England, pure and simple, we do not hesitate to say—to give a recent and local in- stance—that an English Home Rule Parlia- ment would speedily brush aside such routine nonsense as that which demands double com- mittees of inquiry and the wasting of hun- dreds of thousands of ponnds before author- ity can be obtained to spend money in making a Ship Canal. Indeed, approach the question from any point of view, and it will be seen that sub-aivision of labour—for that is really what it comes to—is as good in matters legislative as it is in matters mechan- ical. The Imperial Parliament is so conges- ted that it can never even overtake its arrears. Asepatate Parliament for Ireland would relieve it of much, but separate Parliaments, in addi- tion, for England, and Scotland, and Wales would relieve it of a great deal more, and restore it to something like healthy action.

THE sad bolting fatality on the Mersey, at Latchford, on Thursday week, by which two men and a youth lost their lives, has naturally excited a great deal of attention. The in- quest was held on Monday, when the body of the third victim had been found ; but the facts disclosed do not add much to what was known last week, though they emphasise what the CORONER described as "the gross ignorance or foolhardiness of the men in going so near the Weir." No doubt men familiar with the sea, as some of those were who entered the fatal boat, felt that it was a small matter to take a spin on the river ; and it would seem that a visit to the Weir had a special attraction for them as having a spice of danger in it. How else can their rushing into what proved to be the jaws of death be explained? JOHN GARLICK one of thetsur- vivors, states that he saw the danger they were in when they got about ten yards from the Weir, and called upon the two who were rowing to stop. He was sneered at for his timidity ; the boat shot forward until Within three or four yards of the fall, when, as might be expected, it was instantly en- gulphed in. the whirling waters, The youth clang to the Man CARTY, and both were drowned. BURTON had the narrowest pos- sible escape; it was only by shaking himself free of DAINTETH—and that after a desperate struggle—that he was enabled to get to the shore. Indeed, it may be said to be a won- der that two of the five escaped ; for the whirlpool belew the Latchford Weir is per- haps the most dangerous spot in the whole course of the river Mersey. It will be noticed that none of the three bodies were carried down the river—that of DAINTETH having, in all likelihood, been whirled round and round the terrible pool for four days. The Coroner remarked that the catastrophe showed the necessity of all persons learning to swim. This is obvious, and it is to be hoped that it is not less obvious that special skill may be so abused as to be of no benefit. Bravery becomes bravado when it is displayed where there is no call of duty. There is a tendency at the present day, wh'ch cannot be too much condemn ,d, to do dangerous feats for the sake of notoriety. The trapeze is raised. higher and higher that the crowd may gape more and more; but the people who perform in this way have at least the excuse that they are earning a living whilst they run the risk of haying no life at all. We do not say that the railway men who went up the river last week intended to come back with a tale of a daring deed; the probability is that they thought, when they approached the Weir, that they would see how it looked from the nearest view they could take with a certainty of getting back again. They were ignorant of the full danger they encountered, and fool-

hardy in running any risk for so small an advantage. We cannot, alas, bring back life, but we can sympathise with those who sorrow for the lost ones, and profit, it is to be hoped, by the lesson which the accident so sadly and yet so forcibly teaches.

Miss Nellie Farren has recovered her jewels; they were found in the cab which took her from the theatre to her hotel. She was positive—oh, SO DOSitiVe—mat she had placed them on the sideboard in her sitting- room. Tne ladies, bless them ! are never so positive as when they are entirely mis- taken.

The Bishop of Manchester, after saying disagreeable things of Nonconformists, has succeeded in making himself offensive to the teetotallers. He cannot in these matters be described as liberal-minded; a change of climate seems to have changed his mind. And there is no help for it; Bishop Moorhouse is not Bishop Fraser.

It is not every fire bjigade that can cope with a fire ; but they can at Copes. The " firemen" at the celebrated cigar factory are women ; and they recently showed what they can do in the way of applying the ex- tinguisher. Let the inferior sex, as Long- fellow says, "take care"; Copes' girls can either strike "a spark" and kindle a flame, or put him and it out.

Let footballers. beware. The Mon mouth- shire court Lord Raglin, of the Ancient Order of Foresters, on Monday, passed a resolution as court law not to allow any sick pay to any member who receives in- jury by playing football. This is not un- reasonable. Footballers should join an extraordinary Accident Fund rather that an ordinary Sick Fund.

It has been decided that the chief memo- rial to the late Canon Barclay, of Runcorn, shall take the form of a church chancel, which, it is estimated, could be built for £1,350. This is all right so far as Church- men are concerned; but what of Noncon- formists? The Church is a great "sponge," but it must not expect to draw on Dissenters under the pretext of a memorial to the late vicar.

The Tary working-man would seem to be alive and disposed to kick, strange to say, at the Tory Government. Several Conservative working-men's clubs have passed resolutions condemning the conduct of the Government in subsidising a German line of steamers to carry the Southampton mail to America. What are the members of Liberal Clubs do- ing? Are they playing at " Nap ? "

The blundering of the Government in the matter of the American mail contract has not been explained away either by the Postmaster- General or Lord Salisbury. The "Globe," which is a Tory organ, says "No satisfactory answer has been given," and adds : The German Lloyd's ships are subsidised by the German Government to enable them to compete with English vessels enjoying no such advantage, and, as the manager of the Cunard Company points out, they call at Southampton in order: to divide with our own shipowners the profits of the carry- ina trade to America. If they can afford to outbid the o- Tners of English steamers, it is because of the assistance they derive from the State of which their proprietors are citizens. Competition under such circumstances, whatever else it may be, is assuredly not Free Trade.

Mary Thompson, of St. Helens, has singu- lar ideas of fun. She was brought before the magistrates on Monday for breaking a plate- lass window, at the Prince of Wales Inn, the value of which was estimated at L 4. zs 6d. She told a policeman that she did it for " a bit of fun." What she would do when she was in the humour for a lot of fun, it is be- yond imagination to conceive. It is to be hoped that "two months with hard labour" will take some of the fun out of her.

It is stated that when the accounts of the International Exhibition are finally made up it will be found that the net profit of the four "shows" will be almost, if not quite, £30,000. This should be something towards the Imperial Institute, and might be taken as a contribution from the provinces; for it is visits of the "people from the country" that have made the Exhibitions a success. As to sending up money to celebrate the Queen's Jubilee, that is too absurd. In such a matter charity should indeed begin at home.

The Travelling Tax Abolition ComMittee is an organisation for getting rid of the Rail- way Duty, which ought, long since, to have been knocked on the head. Singularly enouzh, a tramway driven by steam, that is a Street Railway, is held to be exempt from the duty. The Committee have put to various Chancellors of the Exchequer the question—Why is this thus? but they cannot get a satisfactory answer; and an appeal is now being made for justice at the hands of the public.

The Nottingham Chamber of Agriculture has passeda resolution declaring Free Trade "a fail- ure as far as the producer was concerned, while the consumer only benefitted by excessive cheapness obtained at the producer's expense." This is sheer nonsense. The cheaper every- thing is and the better it is for everybody, ex- cept the monopolist. It is absurd to suppose that all producers sell at a loss; the weak go to the wall and the fittest survive. Free Trade is not a failure; but it wouldn't be safe to say as much of the 'Nottingham Cham- ber of Agriculture.

It is considered advisable for a Mayor, as well as a dog, to have a chain. It is stated that when the Queen visited Liverpool, and was about to be presented to the big-wigs, an official exclaimed—" Now then, you Mayors without chains—stand back ! " This it is, may be, which has suggested to the people of Preston the advisability of having a chain of the greatest magnitude. They are about to spend £7OO in one as one way of celebrating the jubilee, and already more than half the money has been subscribed. "Proud Pres- ton "does not mean to "stand back."

Sir Michael Hicks-Beach spoke as a humane and sensible man when he said— ' " There is no greater foe to the rights of pro- perty in the whole world than he who attempts harshly to exact its rights and fails to perform its duties." It would seem to be an expansion of the axiom that "property has its duties as well as its rights ; " but no matter. The point of interest just now is to observe how the Secretary for Ireland will make his observations fit in with the policy of harsh exaction upon which the Government are obviously bent.
Mr. John Monet with the keen insight which distinguishes him, was quick at the Liberal meeting at Hawick, on Tuesday, to

point out the inconsistency and instability of the G:;vernmeltt. The Irish Secretary had said that there were many laws in Ireland that could be amended with great benefit. Lord Salisbury, on the other hand, said the salvation of Ireland was not to be wrought by the alteration of the law. Again, with regard to the promise of legislation for Ireland, Mr. Morley put the case in a nutshell when he said :—"The Government but a fes weeks ago—a few days ago—were urged to forget that and to violate it, because Ireland was quiet. To morrow they will be urged to forget and violate it, because Ireland perhaps will not be quiet."

A GOLDEN WEDDING.—Mr. and Mrs Giles Owen, of South Bank Cadishead, attained the 50th anni- versary of their wedding on Sunday last. They are the only couple living in Cadishead at present that were married 50 years ago. They have ten children living, namely, five sons and five daughters. Mr. Owen is Well known in the Warrington district amongst the members of the M.U.1.0.0f Oddfellows, who two years ago presented him with afi illumin- ated address for his past services. THE FAILURE OF A ST. HELENS Ex-MA.Yon.—At the Liverpool Bankruptcy Court, on Monday, before Mr. Registrar Bellringer, the public examination of Edward John Eon, grocer, St. Helens, and at various other places in the neighbourhood, an ex-Mayor of St. Helens, and formerly a. colliery proprietor, was ordered to be closed. Mr. Cornett appeared for Mr. . George lahon, the trustee, and stated that he was satisfied that th 6 bankrupt had fully disclosed his affairs. The official receiver also expressed himself satisfied. THE SHIP CANAL.—On Wednesday, at a meeting of the Barton Rural Sanitary Authority, a letter was read from the directors of the Ship Canal Com- pany asking whether the Authority would be,will- ing to accept paid-up shares for the amount of compensation required by them in the constructim of the Ship Canal,which will practically cut in two the Authority's sewage farm at Flixton. The clerk was instructed to reply that, as a corporate body, the Authority had no power to accept such shares, otherwise they would be willing to do so. PERVERTS FROM THE ESTABLISHMENT.—The Liberator says:—" Much indignation has been ex- pended by Protestant journals on the action of the Rev. C. H. Moore, a Roman Catholic priest, in secretly receiving a married woman into his Church, as a convert from Protestantism, without the knowledge of her husband. But none of them have called attention to the fact that this priest was nurtured in the bosom of that Church which boasts of being the bulwark of Protestantism,' and that for some years be was one of its ministers. Not only so, but Cardinal Mannimf, who, as the ecclesiastical superior of Mr. Moore, has vindicated his proceedings, was also a conspicuous member of that Church. The 'Staunch Churchman,' who has so bitterly complained of the domestic misery which has followed, may therefore be, in some, respects, likened to the struck eagle. who
Viewed his r,wn feathers on the fatal dart 77 Which winged t.:e tiaft thtt quivered in his he ca. _

And, if he will inquire, he will find that the Romish Church has received hundreds more perverts from the same source. It is alleged that if the Estab- lishment disappears Rome and infidelity would be its legatees. One of these legates, it appears, is cominc, into part possession before the demise of the institution." .

THE BEDFORD LEIGH EXPLOSION.—A special re- port has been presented to the Home Secretary by Mr. J. Dickinson, Inspector of Mines, on the explo- sion of fire-damp which took place at Wood End Pit, Bedford Leigh, in August last, when 38 lives were lost. The Inspector deals specially with the nature and sufficiency of .the safety lamp which was in use in the mine at The time of the explo- sion. lie states that the Davy lamp without a shield will not resist an explosive current exceed- ing certain velocities, and this was known to the owner of the Bedford :Colliery. In continuing to use the lamp under such circumstances he was not alone, there being still a large majority of the owners of the district who use them exclusively in all their pits, and others who use them in some pits. Therefore any condemnation which may fall upon him on that account must be shared by manyothers in the district. Mr. Dickinson concludes that the terrible lesson taught to miners by the explosion is to observe the rule.which requires ttem to give in- formation if they notice any fire-damp or any cir- cumstances likely to produce danger, and not to think the danger insufficient to report; and to ow- ners and managers the lesson is to have such safety lamps in use as will not pass the flame in the event of a miner losing his presence of mind. _ .

DEATH OF PLAINTIFF IN A LIBEL ACTION.— Tucker v. Mackie .a,.d Go.—On Monday, this action was dealt with before the Lord Chief Justice and a special jury. Before the jury were called in the case, which was an action for libel brought by a solicitor, named John Tucker, against a newspaper company, Mr. Cyril Dodd, who appeared for the defendants, said that since the action was set down for trial the plaintiff had died, with the result, as he understood, that the cause of action did not sur- vive to his executors. The action had therefore come to an end, but in the course of it his clients had brought money into court as security for inter- rogatories, and in the same way the plaintiff's solicitor had also paid money into court. In addi- tion, the defendants in the present action had paid £25 into court in satisfaction of the plaintiff's claim, having pleaded that they had published a sufficient apology and the usual statutory defence. He there- fore asked his Lordship to strike out the action, and give liberty to his clients to take the money out of court. —The Lord Chief Justice: Does any one ap- pear on the c ther side ?—Mr. Dodd: No, because the action has abated, and no one has now an interest in the suit. The action arose out of this circum- stance. There were two solicitors of the name of John Tucker, and in the report of the proceedings against one the address of the plaintiff, who had nothing to do with the transaction, was by mistake wrongly introduced.—Ultimately an order was made to enable the respective solicitors engaged in the action to take out the money paid into Court.
RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH CHORAL SOCIETY.

The members of this saciety gave their first concert of the season on .Monday evening, in the National Schoolroom, Runcorn. The audience was •of en- couraging proportions, but was not so large as the attractive items provided, merited, Although only in the second year of its existence the society has made considerable progress, and the choral work on Monday evening was admirable. The parts were well balanced, and in each of the four glees essayed, there was evidenced intelligent appreci- ation, taste, and ptecision. The solo and chorue, " Now tramp o'er moss and feil," was deservedly encored. Miss Harwood, who sings with great care and ex- pression, took the solo: Liter, she won a hearty recall for her contribution " Cherry ripe." A similar honour was awarded Miss Harnpson for her pleasing interpretation of " Side by side to the better land." These lady vo- calists were associated in the duet " Two merry hearts," which they rendered with much success. Miss Ooodwell contributed•the song " Janet's choice," but she failed to dis- play hr vocal abilities to the best advantage. Mr. Caygill gave two of Dibdin's sangs—" Down amongst the dead men " and " Heaving the anchor." " The haven aloft " and " Queen of my heart " were retv'ered by Mr. James Littler with much taste and expression, and on each occasion be was loudly applauded. Mr. Littler and Mr. %V. Pownall, jun., were associated in the duet "Albion," which was a pretty piece of vocalisation, acid well merited the encore awarded. Mr. F. Joule contributed "Nancy Lee" and " True till death" ; he was heartily re- called for each effort, and responded with fresh items. Mas- ter Clarke sang "Our boys," and was also encored. One of the most enjoyable items was a pianoforte solo by Mr. Wadsworth, who has undertaken to conduct the society, and officiated as accompanist. A most skilful performance secured an enthusiastic encore, to which Mr. Wadsworth responded. The programme closed with the chorus singing the National Anthem with variations.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONER. cra The monthly meeting of the Board was held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road. Mr. P. SOeakman presided, and there were present Messrs. R. Shaw, H. J. Grice, W. Hankinsgn, W. Mellor, J. Dobson, J. Pritchard, W. Fisher, J. W. Light- burn, F. A. Lake, H. White, W. H. Linaker (law clerk). E. Marshall (secre,ary), M. Barker (surveyor), and F. McDou- gall (medical officer). MR. SHAW ON STREET LIGHTING.—RATEPAYERS'

MONEY WRONGLY SPENT. Upon the minutes of the last monthly meeting coming up tor confirmation,—Mr. R. Shaw objected to the minute of the General Putposes Committee recommending that lamps should be fixed in Okell-street, Clarence-street, and Porter- street. He objected to the minute, sot because it was in- correctly stated, but because it was illegal according to the 150 and 152 sections of the Public Health Act. He asked the law clerk whether the public rates could be made chargeable for the lighting of any street that had not been completed according to the sections he had named. The streets mentioned had not lieen so complet,ll. These sec- tions also applied to Norm in-road, but that matter would come up when the accounts were to be passed by the auditor. —The Law Clerk said in his opinion it was not competent for the Board to spend money out of current rate for the oerpose of lighting unfinished streets No responsihilitv attached to the Comtnisaioners until those streets had been completed and were taken over by the Ccmmissioners as public streets.—Mr. Grace inquired what had been the cus- tom in regaad to such streets. There were scores of streets lighted up that were not finished.—The Chairman said the procedure of the Board had been wherever there was any property erected, and light was needed whether the street was made or Let the Committee always recom- mended that lamps should be placed where required. —Mr. Shaw agreed that the Board had always done as Mr. Grief, stated ; the qaestion was whether it was in accord- Ince with the powers given to us, or whether the Board had been making a great mhtake in compelling the ratepayers to pay money that the owners of property should have paid. (Hear, hear.) He objected as a private ratepayer and it ought to have been obj.cted to before.—Mr. Lightburn said they could not begin too early to remedy a wrong, but he pointed out that the 146Lh section of the Public Health Act stated that the Commissioners might pay a sum of

*** SITEET ALMANAC.—On Saturday, December 18, there will be presented to each of our readers a • large sheet Almanac, printed in two colours, and containing a large amount of local and general information. It will be adorned with a beautiful -view of Winmarleigh House and an excellent por- trait of Lord Winmarleigh. Presente,d on Satur- day, December 18. Order early of newsagents. .Examiner and Almanac—price one penny.

APPOINTMENT OF LIBRARIAN AT WIDNES.—MiSS Proc- tor, schoolmistress, Halebalik, has been appointed librarian of the Widnes Free Public Library, at a salary of £65 per annum. LECTURE AT RUNCORN.—In St. John's Presbyterian Chapel, Runcorn, on Monday evening, the Rev. John Wil- , Hams, of Chester, delivered a lectbre entitled " Chairs." Mr. J. Meadowcroft presided, and there was a moderate at- -I.tendance. / POPULAR CONCERTS AT RUNCORN.—The third of the ad- mirable series of concerts arranged by the Mill Brow Brass Band will be held this (Saturday) evening. ['he programme contains some very attractive items, and the price of admis- sion is on the lowest scale. VOLUNTEER CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—As announced in our advertising columns, the annual concert in connection with the Earl of Chester's Rifles will take place on Wednes- day night next, in the Runcorn Publie Hall. An excellent programme has been arranged, RUNCORN GYMNASIUM.—Thi9 m st valuable institution has now been operose for the winter season at the Drill Hall. To procure a sound mind in a sound body no exercises can be more effective and agreeable than those in vogue at this gymnesium, and new beginners have the aid and advice of coemetent leaders. PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAND OF HOPE, WIDNES.—A pub. Ho meeting in connection with the ahove society was held in the Hutchinson-street chap,l on Wednesday eveuing, when vocal and instrumental music, dialogues and recit,- tions, were given by the members. Mr. 1). Lewis presided, and there was a fair attendance. Wfberes POLICE COURT.—(TaesdAy. Before Mr. F. H. Gossege.)—Drunk and Begging: Richard Hennessy, of Warrington, and Edward Hancock, of Wavertree, were each. fined 53 and costs for being drunk at Widnes on the previ- ous evening. James Roach, of Widnes, and Patrick O'Brien and Robert Johnson, tramps, were each committed to gaol for begging. CAMDEN BAND OF HOPE. RUNCORN.—The members of this society on Monday evening gave an entertainment in Camden School. An interesting item was " The Flower Queen," intelligently performed by 20 little girls, who were tastefully attired an I embellished with flowers. Songs, recitations, and dialogues were also given, and a pleasant evening was spent. CASUALTIES TO RUNCORN VESSELS.—The Ethiopian, bound from Fowey to Runcorn, on Monday put into Holy- head, leaky. The schooner Rebert, with clay bound to Run- corn, has also put into Milford Haven, leaky. The scUooner Unicorn, bound from Port Leven to Runcorn, with forefoot damaged and making water, having struck off Platte Rocks has also put into Holyhead. LACROSSE.—Sefton it. Widest—Played at Sefton Park, on Saturday. Sefton were short of two good men in Rankin and Fay, but this loss was made uo by Widnes playing one, man short. After a good game Wines left winners by five goals to nil. F. Wylde in attack and Sayce in defence were the pick of the winne.s. All Sefton played fairly well, but were decidedly on the lieht side. RUNCORN Y.M.C.A. LIBRARY.—The library of the Run- corn Young Men's Christian Association has been entirely disposed of. On Wednesday night, the books which had not been transferred to the Free Public Library were sold by auction, the lots realising fair prices. Mr. S. Yarwood acted as auctioneer gratuitously, and at the close was ac- corded a hearty vote of thanks. WznerEs•C.E.T.S.—The juvenile section was responsible for the entertainment on Thursday evening, and an enjoy- able programme was gone through. Mr. H. Wade Deacon presided. and spoke of the advantages to be obtained from gymnastics, and drew attention to the Free Public Library, remarking that the completion of the building was being pushed on as quickly as possible. It would be an institu- tion where, if they liked, they could get a great deal of knowledge and pleasure. NATIONALITIES BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.—We Would again remind our readers of the " Wegld's fair, or Nationalities bazaar," which is to be held in Bethesda Schoolroom on Wednesday and two following days. Mr. Robert Verdin, M.P., will open the proceedings on the first day, and Mr. P. Speakman, chairman of the Board of Commissioners, on the second day. The decorations will he of an original and unique character, and altogether the bazaar will be of a useful and interesting character. The object of the bazaar is one that demands support. A WORKMAN SEVERELY SCALDED AT WIDNES —A man named Edward Garner, who resides at Runcorn, and is em- ployed at the Widnes Alkali Works, was emptying the con- tents of a wheelbarrow into a jigeer at the works on 'FLIT day, when .the barrow slipped, and, coming violently against him, knocked him backwards into a pan of hot liquor, where his left hand and both legs were severely scalded. He was taken to the Accident Hospital, and his injuries were attended to by Drs. McDonnell and McCam- bridge. He is now progressing favourably. UNLAWFUL SCALES AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court on Monday, Mary Brook, an elderly woman, was charged with having in her possession a pair of scales which were unjust.—Superintendent Hollingworth stated that on the 22nd November he visited the coal yard kept by the defendant off Greenway-road. He found the scales balance with a piece of iron piping weighing 22ilbs. He did not think there was any intention to wrong the custom- ers, but it was against the law to have loose pieces of ken about the scale—The defendant, who said she was not aware she was doing wrong, was ordered to pay the costs, 103. 63. LECTURE ON THE LAND QUESTION At' WIDNES. Mr. McGuffie Ureaves, of Manchester, who was a candidate for one of the divisions of Glasgow at the last general election, attended at the National League Hall, Widnes, on Monday evening, and delivered an eloquent address on the land question. Dr. O'Keeffe presided, and there was a good at- tendance. The lecturer pointed out the anomalies of the land tenure of England, and asked if Englishman could not manage their own land, how could they expect to manage land in Ireland. On the motion of Mr. Laughlin, a resolu- tion condemning the policy of coercion adopted by the present Government in regard to Ireland was passed unani- mously CONCERT AT RUNCORN.—A concert was given on ;Thurs- day night, in Bethesda School-room, in connection with the Mersey Missions to Seamen, by the members of the drain and fife band, assisted by several friends. The chair was occupied by Mr. S. Coventry, who alluded in high terms to the progress made by the band to the value of the training received by the members. The programme included selec- tions by the band, and songs were given by Messrs. E. Hob- son, A. Bratt, P. Shaw, S. Bate, J. Wilkinson, J. Hampsnn, J. Shaw, and F. Mack. Songs were also contributed by Miss Howard, Miss M. Holland, Miss Hampson, and Mr. R. Morris. The prograngme was gone through with excellent taste, and reflected great credit on many of the younger members of the band, several of the pieces being encored. Miss Jukes accompanied with ability. Votes of thanks were accorded to the chairman and to those who had assisted in the evening's entertainment. ALARMING FIRE AT HALE.—Shortly titter eight o'clock on Tuesday night flames were seen issuing from the farm buildings at Halton Towers, Hale, by a teamsman named Andrew Moody. On the arrival of the fire brigade, tinder the command of Major Williams and Drill-Sergeant Price. the fire, which is supposed to have originated in the beiler- house, had spread to the loft over the stables, in which was a quantity of hay, to the roof, and to the stables themselves, where there were six horses. Fortunately, however, the animals were got out in time. There being a plentiful supply of water the brigade, assisted by a number of willing hands, after about six hours' ircessant labour, succeeded in extinguishing the flames, but not before the roofs of the buildings, together with the contents, were completely de- stroyed. The amount of damange is not at present known, but we believe it is covered by insurance. The buildings are in the occupation of Mr. Thomas Charnock. WIDNES FETTY SESSlONS.—(Thureday. Before Mr. F. money to assist in making a road, and did not say anything about that the road should be adopted by theloatn.—Mr. I Mellor pointed out that Norman-road hed been made and ' adopted by the Board.—Mr. Shaw replied that Okell. Clar- ence, and Porter-streets were new and not adopted by the Board, and he understood that no expense could be in- curred by the Board until these st-eets had been paved, [legged, and lighted.—Mr.Grice inquired how long Porter- street had been built.—Tfee Surveyor : It is not a proper street.—The Chairman agreed that the Board was placed in this dilemma by the Law Clerk, who ought to have advised them before that it Was illegal to erect the lamps as recom- mended, and pointed out that the Law Clerk had an agenda 6 days before the last meeting.—The Law Clerk said suppos• ing he had the agenda as stated there was nothing to show that thene streets were not public streets which had been adopted by the Board. He had no knowledge of every street in the town.—Mr. Pritchard was inclined to accept the Law Clerk's explanation, an 4 conclude that he was not responsible for this matter. The responsibility of the question ought to be laid upon the committee which had had it under consideration for some weeks. With regard to Nerman•road, that minute was objected to by a member of the Board on the ground that it had not been legally adop• td by the Board, and was referred back for further conside- ration, along with the other rereets,and the committee ought to have dealt fully with every poiet. The committee cell- sisted of eleven members—a majority of the Board, and at the second meeting held not a single member of the com- mittee took .any notice whether the erection of the lamps was legal, just, and proper. The committee was highly blameable,—Mr. Grice stated that the cost of making Nor- man-road was passed by the auditor as a legal expense, and who did the road belong to if it did not belong to the town. Mr. Shaw : 1 hese streets • are out- side Norman - road. I sall have something to say about Norman - road if it is discussed.— Mr. Lightburn expressed his disapprobation of the remarks made by Mr. Pritchard, and aslaed him why he did not make them at the committee meeting, at which he was pre- sent.—Mr. • Pritchard said he was not a member of the com- mittee, and informed the members that they had the right to request the law clerk's attendance at a committee meet- ing if they were in a difficulty.—Mr. Dobson, as one or the memners of the committee, said he understood at the time the road was made that it was adopted by the town. Mr. Linker Was the law clerk at the time, and the members were guidul by his decision. Two-thirds of the members voted for its tdoption by the town, and they thought it was legally conveyed. On that ground .£4OO was spent upon the road, and they never thought they were acting illegally. The law clerk was present at the last meeting when Mr. Shaw raised the question, and the Board expected him to aid tham in all these matters, and not allow them to get into such a dilemma.—The Law Clerk said he had previously stated that although the Board had spent a curtain slim of inoney on Nerman-toad lee had grave doubts as to the lia- bility of the Board for it.—Mr. Dobson had no recollection of such a remark. The Law Clerk replied that the Board made the reed on the understanding that Lord Cholmondeley would make a road to Frodsham. Mr. Lake said it was quite evident that the property owners would not have given the land for Norman-road had there not le-.,en some understanding that the Board was to make it. If it did not belong to the town the owner of the land could block it up, and the least said about it the soonest mended —Mr. Shaw said there was the greatest difficulty in getting the auditor to pass the account for making Norman-road. The committee at the last meeting had their attention called to the possibility of tbe illegality of the act in the past, and surely they did not expect the law clerk to do their work.—Mr. Grice said he was unaware until tbat morning of the illegality of fixing lattips in those streets.—Mr. Shaw (earcestically): And Mr. Grice, the chairman of the committee having the lighting of the streets under their centrol, did not know anything about what the Act required him to do!—The Chairman: He went according to procedure.—Mr. Shaw said they insisted upon the expenditure, and when it turned out to be wrong they would not take .the blame upon themselves.—The Chairman stated that the Law Clerk did not sit at that Board to watch them get into a dilemma. Mr. Linaker was certainly not present at the second meeting. He sim- ply stopped away. He thoueht he should have excused himself for his absence.—The Law Clerk : In justice to myself, I must say that as I left the Boardroom I told the chairman thet as the meeting was in the evening I did not think I could be present, and he made no objection.— The Chairman replied that be could not be expected to hear every remark that the law clerk might make as he left the room.—Tlae minutes of the Board were tbeu confirmed.— Subseqwently, on the motion of Mr. F. A. Lake, seconded by Mr. Shaw, the following resolution was carried unani- mously :—'' That the correspondence, minutes of committee of this Board relating to the formation and maintenance of Norman-road be referred to the Legal and, Parliamentary Committeefor report as to the present ownerehip of such road and the liability for the maintenance thereof."

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

The Medical Offic; reported that "The number of deaths registered during toe past month amount to 22. Of these deaths two were due to inflammation of the lining of mem- brane of the brain, two to disease of the heart, two to con- sumption, two to senile decay, and one each to apoplexy, conjeetion of the liver, acute bronchitis, failure of the heart's action, convulsions, disease of the brain, inflammation of bowels, chronic disease of the brain, disease of the hip joint, conjestion of the brain, enteric fever. peretonitis dentition, and one to disease of uncertain origin. The above 22 deaths show an average death rate of a little over 15 per 1,000 of the estimated population. During the Christmas holidays of last year the public schools within the sanitary district of the authority were fumigated with a disinfecting acid with, 1 believe, good results, and I am of opinion that it would be an advantage to have the like process repeated sometime during the forthcoming holidays."

HIGHWAYS AND BUILDINGS COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee recommended the approval of the following plans :—Mr. John Thomason, for the erec- tion of three houses in Norman-road; Mr. W. Chadwick, for the erection of wash-house at the rear of house in Leinster- gardens ; Mr. S. Webster, for the erection of two houses in York-street.—The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Dobson, seconded by Mr. Grice.

FINANCES. iThe minutes of the Finance Committee stated that the receipts for the month amounted to £9OO 193 101, and the expenditure to £561 153 4d. The committee recommended that the sum of £228 Is 91 be transferred from the general fund to the sinking fund.—Mr. Fisher, in moving the adop- tion of the minutes, said there was now a sum of £373 183 33 in the sinking fund. By transferring the sum of £226 le 9d it would make a total of £6OO, which they pro- posed to apply to the paying off a loan of £6OO to the Rose of Sharon Lodge of Oddfellows. '1 his would effect A sav- ing in interest of about £24 per year.—ln reply to Mr. Pritchard, Mr. Fisher said the total liabilities of tbe Board were only £8,700, which he regarded as very satisfactory.Z

THE QUEEN S JUBILEE. A letter from the Prince of Wales, atlciressel to the chair- man, was read by the Secretary. It WAS a copy of the letter sent to various authorities throughout the country, urging the claims of the Impmill Institute.—The Chairman inti- mated that he would call a public meeting shortly to con- sider how the Queen's Jubilee should be celebrated.—There was no further business.

THE PROPOSED BARCLAY MEMORIAL. The adjourned meeting to consider what form the memo- rial to the late Canon Barclay, vicar of Runcorn, should take, was held in the National School on Tuesday night. Mr. F. A. Lake presided, and amongst these present were essrs. E. :L_Cho, I ton, W. B. Holland, H. White, A. Jordan, J. Johnson.*. Meredith, H. J. Grins, T. Kirkham, E. Imi- son, W. Hankinson, J. Latter, W. Mellor, J. Davies, G. Moss, E. Marwood, J. Torkingten, G. Bell, J. W. Light. burn, G. Summer field, J. Craddock, W. Pownall, junior, M. Barker, C. Pow rail, F. Joule, E. Kay, J. Horsfield, H.Coward. and W. Sutton (sec. pro tern). The Chairman explained that at the last meeting there was a proposal that a mural tablet should be erected to the memory of the late Vicall in the Parish Church, and that money be raised to finish St. Michael and All Angels Church te farther perpetuate his memory. A second pro- posal made by Dr. McDougall was that a scholarship should be founded at one of the leading Universities. The former meeting ,was adjourned so that the feasibility of these schemes could be considered before coming to any de- cision. Mr. Sutton read a letter from the Rey. A. Anderson, of St. Mark's Vicarage, Dunham Massey, stating he should be happy to become a subscriber. He also read a communica- tion from Dr. McDougall, who, after stating his inability to be present at the meeting, added that his scheme had been misunderstood by some, and others were of opinion that not enough funds could be got together for such a purpose. His own views were unaltered, but, in deference,te would with- draw the suggestion made hy him at the first meeting. Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele wrote that if it was agreed to raise a fund sufficient to clear off the existing debt on the new church in Greenway-road, and to complete the building so as to enable it to become consecrated and open for service, the firm would have much pleasure in assisting. (Applause.) Mr. Mellor asked what amount it would take to pay off the debt on the nave and what it would cost to complete the church so far that it could be consecrated. The Chairman replied that if the sum of £365 lent by the Chancel Committee to the Nave Committee was included they would have to raise something like £1,200. If they allowed that debt to continue he saw no objection to allow- ing that until they commenced to build the chancel, they would have to raise about £850.—10 reply to Mr. Chorlton, the Chairman said the church could be consecrated without the chancel. the Rev. R. Edwards said if they wanted to raise a suit- able memorial, build the chancel and let the nave look after itself. A gentleman of very much experience in building had told him that week that the chancel could be built for LI 350. If so only a net sum of abeut £9OO would have to be raised for that purp)se, as they had about MO in hand and promised. Mr. Lightburn proposed that a mural tablet, with a bust of the late Canon in marble at a cost of £7O or LSO should be erected in the Parish Church, and the balance to go to- wards the completion of the new church in Greenway-road. It might be argued that they could not expect Nonconfor- mists to subscribe to that object. but he contended that there was a broad sympathy with the Church of England and the late Canon amongst the Nonconformists of Run- corn, and that they would willinely subscribe. Mr. Gates suggested that a public park or baths would be a suitable tribute—(hear, hear)—and claimed for his propo- sal that the Nonconformists would subscribe. After some further conversation. Mr. W. Mellor proposed that a mural tablet be put in the Parish Church, and that

I he chancel be added to the church in Greenway-road as a memorial to the late vicar. He argued that to wipe off the debt on the nave would not be any memorial to the vicar, whilst the chancel would be a memorial chancel. There was no fear that the gentlemen who had pledged their word for the debt twhich was on the nave would at all suffer in consecieence. (Applause.) . Mr. Marwood seconded Mr. Mellor's motion. After a discussion, Mr. Mellor agreed to leave the cost of the tablet open in his proposition. Mr. W. Pownall, jun., seconded Mr. Lightburn's proposi- tion. Mr. Davies said he had it en the highest authority that Mr. Hayes' donation was intended for the chancel only. Mr. Lightburn withdrew his proposition, and that moved by Mr. Mellor was carried unanimously. On the motiou of Mr. Moss, seconded by Mr. Torkington, it was decided to appoint a committee of 12. Numerous names were suggested, and a complaint was made that in- fluence was not represented. Mr. Chorlton thereupon proposed that Mr. Robert Verdi'', M.P., and Mr. J. T. Brunner should be added. (Laughter.) Mr. Summetfield secondtd Mr. Verdin's nomination. Mr. Brunner bad said he would do nothing for the church. Mr. T. Kirkham : We won't ask him. (Laughter.) Eventually the following committee was formed : Messrs. J. Brundrit, J.P., Charles Hazlehurst, J.P., W. Hayes, W. Whittaker, W. Hankinson, M. Barker, W. Mel- lor, A. Jordan, Goodwell, G. L. Wigg, G. Summerfield, and J. E. Meredith. Mr. W. Sutton and Mr. G. Moss were appinted joint §ecretaries, and Mr. E. A. Charlton 'accepted the position of treasurer.
