ACTION AG %INST THE BAILWAY COMPANY. E. V. Greathatch, merchant, Stoke-on-Trent, brought an action against the London and North-Western Railway Company to recover the sum of 17. 6d, damages alleged to have been sustained by the plaintiff by reason of the company having lost part of a consignment of horn piths during transit from Runcorn to Merple.—Mr. J. B. Ashwell, solicitor, Stoke-on- Trent, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Preston represen- ted the cornpany.—Evidence for the defence was called to prove that during transit the piths would lose weight both by evaporation and by reason of the rubbish being shiken out of them.—His Honour considered the defence a goed one, end give a verdict in favour of the company. • £5 FOR A. DcG BlTE.—Rohart Ainsworth, a boy, sued by James Ainsworth, his next friend, to recover £lO from Seined Moss, farmer, Micbeldale, near Overton, damages alleged to have been sustained through bites inflicted by the defendant's dog. A jury, of which Mr. U. Bellamy was the foreman, had been empanelled to hear the caae. Mr. J. Barton appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Linaker for the defendant. Mr. Burton stated that on the 16th Septem- ber last the boy went to the defendant's farmhouse to in- quire for his father's horse, which was impounded. When .)e) got two or three. yards inside the yard, a large liver- coloured dog belonging t ) the defendant broke loose from its chain, sprang at the boy, and knocked him down. The animal bit him on the arm, hand, and thigh before it was driven off by a man in the defendant's employ. The wound on the thigh was a most serious one, and he lost a great deal of blood,and suffered much pain and anxiety. The tame day Dr. Weaver dressed the wounds. The boy had since been unable to follow his employment. It was clear that tbe de- fendant was aware of the ferocity of the done, as in January, 1834, the animal bit a boy named Tiley, and on the 13th September, three days before it attacked Ainsworth, the dog bit a man named James Whitby.—Evi- dence in support of this statement having been given, Mr. A. Linaker for the defence contended that while the father of Ainsworth was employed at the farm, the boy, who had been in the habit of visiting there regularly had continually teased the dog by hissing at it and throwing stones into the yard.—Evidence was given as to the boy teasing the dog.— In reviewing the case, His Honour said the chief question for the jury was whether the boy did anything to bring this attack upon himself. Did they think that the throw- ing of stones at the dog six ,months before had made such an impression upon a savage dog's disposition as to cause it to attack the boy, and inflict the injuries described.—The jury feund for the plaintiff, and fixed the damages at £5. His honour allowed costs.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

_ The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall,Water- loo-road, yesterday. Mr. J. Pritchard presided, and there were present Messrs. W. Handley, E. Imison, and F. Rigby (clerk). THE SCHOOLMISTRESSES AND IGNORANT CHILDREN.— Miss Hutchinson, the mistress at the Greenwav-road Board School, recently refused admission to two children, aged respectively eight and eleven years. on the ground that they did not even know the alphabet, and that no grant would be paid for their attendance. The children were tben taken to tke Mill Brow Infant School by their parents, who ware however told to take them back to Greenway-road School, and allow them to continue in attendance there. The Board being of opinion that it was the duty of the teacher of the Green*ay-road School to admit every child that presented itself, regardless of its attainments, when there was room, gave instructions to that effect, and had received from Mr. Hynnereley, Her Majesty's Inepector, the following memor- andum, which confirms their policy in every respect : " The Mill Brow School should ba regarded primarily as an infant school, and the children in standard I. who are ad- mitted here should not be of an age or size to interfere with the infants proper. A boy or even a girl of ten years, though tectinically ai iniesable, woeld be exceedingly objection- able. In the Greenway-road Mixed School all cnildren over seven must be admitted. Ignorance is no excuse for refusal to admit. Tne school was origiaally entered for the benefit of the canal boat children who have hitherto been neglected at home and have been coldly received, or even refused, at the other schools in the town. Any children ad- mitted in an entirely ignorant state shonld be noted in the log-book and should be placed in the primer class. If, on the day of inspection, they have not made sufficient progress to enable them to be presented in the first standard, they should be entered en the exception schedule with reason for backward condition." SCHOOL ArTENDANCR.—Mr. Handley, chairman of the Attendance Committee, stated that during this month there we.e 16 more on the lolls than last month and 7 more in average attendance. The percentage bad decreased from 79 to 78, because the attendance was not au good in the infant schools owing to the approach of winter. The attendance was, however, satisfactory. and were it not that the Board's actioa was clogged by the boat children, the percentage would be over 80. In July the percentage of attendance was only 66, and now it was 78, so that the vigorous action of the committee had had very satisfactory reeults.—Toe Clerk said for several years past there had been epidemics of measles and scarlet fever, and at the re- quest of the Commissioners the children had been kept away. These epidemics had kept the attendance down con- siderably. The percentage of attendances for the various schools was as follows :—Greenway-road, mixed, 71 ; last month, 69 ; girls, 63; 67; Mill-brow, infant, 80 ; 80 ; National, boys, 86 ; 83 ; girls, 82 ; Si; infants, 80 ; 82 ; Trinity, boys, 89 ; 90; girls, 82; 83 ; infants, 80 ; 85 ; Wesleyan, boys, 86; 83 ; girls, 79; 78 ; infants, 72; 80; Catholic, mixed, 62 ; 66; Newtown, infants, 73 ; 79. Percentage throughout the town, 78; last month, 79. There was nothing further of public interest.

div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY AT WIDNES.
div.p: SHOCKING FATALITY AT WIDNES.

The works of Messrs, Gossage and Son were the scene of a deplorable accident on Tuesday afternoon. The victim was William (lough, a wheelwright, 53 7eAri4 of ace. It appears that Clough and another man named Peter Etagui,y. of Lugsdale-hin-, were engaged in repairing the silicate " hoist et the brio k., and after doing so they caused the CATI to be moved upwards and downwards to see if the rep,irs , had been properly executed. Afterwards tt.e deceased es- cended a lander to ascertain if the bolts that had been re- placed were all right. Whilst be was ou the ladder about 12 feet above the ground, the hoist descended, and jatnned his bead against the framework. He bias fearfully bruised, and one part of his face was almost taken off. He was conveyed to the Hospital, where his injuries were attended to by Dr. McDonnell and Dr. Richards. The unfortunate man, however, succumbed to his injuries on Wednesday evening. Yesterday afternoon, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroaer, held an inquiry into the cir- cumstances of the accident.—Clara Ann Grough, the daugh- ter of the deceased, deposed that her father was not deaf nor near sighted.—Miss Downie, matron at the hospital, said she asked the deceased how the accident occurred, and he replied that he did not know.—Peter Baguley, who was the deceased's fellow workman, said he did not know for what purpose Gough ascended the ladder. When the cage descended, the deceased was bending forward a little, and he was caught on the back of the head. He was held fast by the cage until it was again hoisted up. When the repairing job was completed he told Owen, the enginetnan, to lower the cage, to see whether it winked to their satisfaction. It was found all right. It was about five minutes afterwards that the deceased ascended the ladder. The deceased would not have been in any danger if be had not been bending his bead forward. The attention of the man who attended to the engine was drawn to the fact that theloist had to be lowered or higbered by means of a gong, the rope of which was in close proximity to the deceased when he was on the ladder. Witness did not hear the gong sounded, as there was a great deal of noise at the time.—Joseph Owen, the engine " tenter," stated that on the first ocOesion he lowe:ed the clge according to the inattuctions of last witness. He heard the bell sound distinctly afterwards, and he lowered the cage. That was the time the accident happened. The jury, after a few minutes deliberation, returned a verdict of accidental death. They suggested tkat the sig- nalling for the hoist should, be put in the hands of a more responsible person than it appeared to have bean in the past.

CONVERSAZIONE AT LATCHFORD.—On Tuesday evening a well attended conversazione was held in St. James's School, Latchford. A kelection by the string band was given at the commencement, and the choir then sang two Christmas carols. The choir sang other carols, and magic lantern exhibi- tions were given during the evening. Songs were given by Mr. Warburton, Mrs. Slater, and Miss Green. Mr. Stirrup's bawl played for dancing, and refreshments were served at intervals.
THE VISIT OF THE MARQUIS OF
RIPON TO RUNCORN.

On- Monday afternoon a conference of Liberal delegates will be held in Runcorn Public Hall, under the auspices of the National Liberal Federation. Sir B. W. Foster will preside, and besides Mr. Schnadhorst, the organiser to the Federation, other prominent politicians will take part. In the even- ing a public meeting will be held at the Public Hall, under the presidency of Mr. R. Shaw. The principal speaker will be the Right Hon. the Mar- quis of Ripon. In addition to the gentlemen al- ready advertised to be present, there will be Mr E. R. Russell, M.P., who will move a resolution. His Lordship will arrive at Runcorn from Leeds at 31-36, and will at once proceed in Mr. Shaw's carriage to the Highlands, Higher Runcorn, where he and a number of other gentlemen will be entertained. His Lordship and Mr. Schnadhorst will be Mr. Shaw's guests during the night; and will depart next day for London.

MEDICiL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. Sephton reported for the month ending Novernb,r 30th that the number of births was—males 17, females 21; deaths—males 4, females 4 ; the exczss of births over deaths being 26. and the death rate from all causes equal to 10•3 per 1,000. There were no deaths returned from preventible causes, which spoke well for the esaitary condition of the district. An outbreak of measles had occurred at Padg,te. There had been in all about 30 cases in Padgate,Fearchead,and Woolston, most of them, however, being now convalescent. The epidemic was of a very mild type, and simple in its form, being in most cases uncomplicated witu chest or other affections. Three cases of scarlet fever of a mild cbaractor wen reported at Win- wick Quay. div.p: LEC IUiE UN SPIUTUALIST AT WARRINGTON.

At the Workmen's Club, on Tuesday evening, an "inspirational discourse" on "Spiritualism: Its facts, philosophy, and principles," was given by Mr. E. W. Wallis, of Manchester. Mrs. Groom, of Birmingham, was also advertised to speak, and give clairvoyant descriptions of the departed friends of those present, but from some cause Mrs. Groom was not able to attend. As showing the interest taken in the subject, there was a very large attendance, the large room being filled. The chair was taken by Mr. John Pemberton, of Blackburn, and the pro- ceedings having been opened by the singing of a hymn, that gentleman said they did not ask the audience to believe all they heard, but they did ask them to use their own judgment, and not allow themselves to be led by any,)ne. There was ridicule and scorn thrown upon Spiritualism, but this did not affect those who had had evidence. Having re- ferred to the correspondence that had taken place in these columns, he remarked that in connection with things of this sort there was always an uphill fight, and the greater their opponents the greater the struggle; but the greater also would be the results.—Another hymn was then sung, and a prayer offered up. Mr. Wallis gave his discourse. There had been, he said, an instinctive desire for information respecting the death- change. It was unquestionably true that the faith in continued existence after the change of the body had grown with the growth of humanity. Whilst they might admit that there were some savages so low in the scale, and so ignorant, that they had little or no conception or desire for an immortal state of being, that was simply the ex- ception which proved the rule; and as humanity had climbed higher in the scale of being of organic enfoldment, and of spiritual development, so there had been an increasing growth of this instinctive desire for information, and of an affirmation of im- mortality for the human race. This being so, it was natural that there should be an increasing heart hunger on the part of those who had cultiva- ted their affection, who had known the beauty and blessedness of life, and who had felt the stirring of diviner possibilities than they have ever realised in their earthly pilgrimage. There was undoubtedly a naturalness in the question "If a man die shall he live again?" What answer was given to that out- side of Spiritualism? He made bold to affirm that there was no answer except that they were called upon to have hope for immortality, to believe that there was another life. But the life which was pictured for them after the change called death was so difft:-.7ent and so alto- gether out of accordance with their precent nature, intellectual faculties, capacities, and spiritual powers that they were ofttimes compelled to ques- tion whether the life that was pictured for man after the change called death was a desirable one after all. The claim on! behalf of the Christian was based on the spiritual appearance of Jesus after death, but if Jesus was God His resurrection was no proof of theirs. If they dfitid Jesus His appear- ance after death had no an.ogy with human im- mortality. If on the other hand they claimed that Jesus was a divinely-inspired man then, in His re- appearance after the death of the body they might claim to have an analogy which went, on all fours, and they might assent that as he lived they shali ' live also. At all events spiritualists held that ! Christians founded their hope of immortality upon a spiritual manifestation. Spiritualism was solely an affirmation that man was a spiritual being, and that under certain favourable conditions the dwel- lers on earth may have evidences of the presence of other spiritual beings who had passed through the change called death ,li ad been divested of the body,and who in the spiritual bodywere living a real and an intelligent conscious life. The question then really resolved itself into this: Can man have any evidence that he survives death? He claimed thaf spirit- ualism was established upon demonstrated evi- dences of spiritual presence which not only in modern times, but in all ages of the world, had been vouchsafed to humanity. The speaker then referred at some length to the facts in regard to spiritualism, and dealt with the objections of opponents. . At the conclusion of the discourse, the Chairman invited written . questions, and the first paper handed up contained a request that the lecturer might explain the passage of the Psalm of David. which stated "That the dead know not anything." To this Mr. Wallis replied that of course if there were any dead they would not know anything, but if they were not dead, but living in a spiritual state, they would not only know, but be in a bitter position to know, than those on earth. (Hear, hear.) The fact was there was no dead, death was only in seeming. The speaker was next asked if lie could give instances in which spirit messages had been received regarding something out of the. knowledge of the persons present at the time, and in response he alluded at length to a number of instances of the kind. Some other questions with regard to passages in scripture were also put and answered, but the chairman at length ruled questions of this sort to be out of order. Mr. Acton then inquired how it was that a table could not be moved independent of animal magnetism. - Why should not the table move without hands being put upon it? In answer to this, Mr. Wallis explained to the effect that the animal magnetism was the .force utilised by the spirits to make known their information, just as steam was utilised by an engineer to drive a loco- motive. But that the movements of the table were not due to animal magnetism, Mr. Wallis argued, was shown by the fact that intelligent messages were conveyed which must of necessity be sent by something. endowed with intelligence. During the lecture the speaker was listened to with marked attention, but without any demonstra- tions .of assent or dissent. In the course of the questioning, however, the audience became more demonstrative, and many of the points made by Mr. Wallis were warmly applauded, and in conclusion a hearty vote of thanks was accorded him on the motion of Mr. H. Whitham, who had been one oE the questianers. The meeting was finally closed by the singm of a hymm,

SATIMDAY.—Before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, A. C. McCorquodale, and W. G. Gooch. DRUMEEZINESS.—Bernard Coffey, summoned for being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown, on the 12th ult., was fined 5s and costs.—A like penalty was imposed on Thos. Mannion, for a similar offence an the 14th November.— Patrick Conroy was fined 5s and costs for being drank and disorderly on the 20th ult.—Henry Charnock, summoned far drunkenness on the 20th ulc, was fined 10s and costs.— John Mahan, was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly at Earlestown on the 16th ult.—Lambert Heaton was summoned for being drank on Sunday, the 14th ult., in Olipsley-lane, Havdock, and was fined Sc and costs.—A similar penalty was imposed on Francis McAdam for bou drunk and disorderly in Kenyon-lane, Haydock. on the 13th salt —Patrlck Charles and Frank Charles were each sum- monad for being drank and disorderly in Queen-street, Golborne, on the 19th November, and they were each fined 5s and costs. DISORDHRLY Bmravtoun.—John Bradley was summoned for being disorderly on the licensed premises of the Ram's Head Inn, Earlestown, and refusing to leave when requested on the 13th November. WARRINGTON BLUE COAT SCHOOL.

The annual distribution of prizes to the scholars of this school took place in a room of 'the institu- tion in Winwick-road, on Tuesday evening. There *as a numerous attendance a friends of the scholars and of townspeople who take an interest in the in- stitution, the room in which the proceedings were conducted being crowded. The scholars were ' dressed in the costume of the school, and looked extremely neat and well cared for.' Indeed, their appearance reflected great credit on Mr. and Mrs. Rose, the master and matron, who seem to have the entire confidence and trust of the children. The programme arranged for the evening commenced with an anthem "I will always give thanks," which was followed by the sacred song "Evening prayer," and a second anthem "Beheld how joyful." The children sang well, and i excellent tune. Mr. Rose ably wielded to conductor's baton. The prizes were then distributed by Alderman Pickmere, who in a few words addressed to the scholars ad- vised those who had not succeeded in winning prizes to be encouraged to try to succeed next year, Whatever they did he urged them to try and do well. They must strive to do their best while at the school, and when they grew up they would take a delight in thinking they had been at the old Blue Coat School of Warrington. After the distribu- tion the programme was proceeded with as follows: Part song, " Pretty river ; ' recitation, "The Inch- cape rock," G. H. Young; part song, "Woodlands ring ;"- solo (Edith Gerald) and chorus ;" "The old familiar place ;" recitation " Something to do," Elizabeth Weedall ; song and chorus, " The valleys of Cashmere ;" glee, " Ye mariners of England." The first part of the programme was concluded with selections by the band, which was under the con- ductorship of Mr. Armstrong. Throe selections were given in a manner that pleased everyone, the playing of the boys being of a really high standard. The second part of the programme comprised : Part song, " Xmas ;" recitation, "Tom and his cruelty," Joseph Gleave ; round, "Hark to the rol- ling drum ;" cornet duet, Fred Rose and Albert Bar- low; dumb-bell exercises, with musical accompani- ment; part song, "Echo chorus ;" recitation, "Sunshine and shower," Alice Hemmingway ; song and chorus, "The old brigade " (solo by Albert Bar- low) ; part songs, "Those evening bells * and "The mellow horn." Master Fred Rose presided at the organ. On the conclusion of the programme Alderman PICKYRRE, thanking Mr. and Mrs. Rose for the entertainment that had been given, said that a great amount of time and attention must have been bestowed upon the pupils to tiring them to the state of perfection they had attained. (Hear, hear.) He proposed that a vote of thanks be accorded Mr. and Mrs. Rose. The proposition was seconded by Alderman WEBSTER, who remarked that it was impossible to over-estimate the quality of the education given in the Blue Coat school. its effect on the future of the pupils would no doubt be of the most excellent kind, and tend to make them all good members of society. The motion was heartily carried, and Mr. Rosa expressed his thanks. A vote of thanks to Alderman Pickmere for distributing the prizes was passed on the proposition of Mr. C. WHITE, seconded by the Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON. The following is a list of the names of the pupils who took prizes : Ellen Smith, Rachel Barton, Alice Hemmingway, Mary A. Ward, Sarah Rawlinson, Mary Massey, Edith Gerrard, Letitia Cundall, Ruth Hayes, Eliza- beth Meedall, Elizabeth Hazlehurst, George 11. Young, Frederick Marsh, Joseph Gleave, Frank Wallwork, W. Burgess, Albert Barlow, Henry Poole, W. A. Foden, George Smith, Alfred Scholtze, and James Lowe.

ALLEGED ASSAULT BY:A PUBLICAN CLAIM FOR DAMAGES. James Murray, a farm labourer, brought an action at Warrington County Court, on Wednesday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes, against William Whit- low, landlord of the Red Lion Inn, Preston Brook, to recover damages or injuries received through an assault alleged to have been committed by the de- fendant. Dr. Cummins, M.P. (instructed by Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington), was for the plain- tiff, and Mr. Fletcher, solicitor, of Northwich, ap- peared for the defence. In his opening statement Dr. Cummins explained that on the 26th of May last the plaintiff, with some companions, went to the Red Lion Inn, where they had some beer, wait- ing for the weather to clear in order that they might go to work. As plaintiff was leaving the house at about twelve o'clock, the landlord, who ap- peared to be in a bad temper, shouted out "Yes, you had better go, or I shall shove or kick you out." Plaintiff replied that he would go, and defendant, calling upon his sons to strike plaintiff's companions, knocked plaintiff down the steps into th o yard. in consequence of which the latter's leg was broken. Plaintiff was after the lapse of some time removed to 'Warrington Infirmary, where he remained an in patient until the 23rd of June. He was still an out-patient, and. would not be fit for work for six or eight weeks to come. When in the Infirmary plaintiff instructed a solicitor to demand compensation from the defen- dant, who, in a somewhat peculiar manner, replied by issuing a summons against plaintiff for being disorderly in his house. Plaintiff was afterwards fined at Daresbury for that offence. Plaintiff had thus had his remedy at the hands of the magis- trates. Dr. Commins said that the excessive force ' used was not only illegal, but was brutal. Plaintiff had been out of employment 28 weeks, at what was practically the best part of the year for him to ob- tain wages. He was entitled to compensation for that, even if the pain he had • suffered was not taken into consideration. Evidence was then taken.—Dr. Richmond, house sur- geon at the Warrington Infirmary, said that he I saw plaintiff at that institution on the second of IJune. . Plaintiff, who was suffering from a fracture of both bones of the right leg, just above the ankle, was an in-patient, and remained in the Infirmary for some weeks. He must have suffered consider- able pain from the injury. He would not be able to re-commence work for a month.—Plaintiff was then called. He said that on the morning of the 26th of May he and his brother, and Michael and Roger Maloney, went to the Red Lion Inn, Preston Brook. It was a wet morning, and his master had said that he mast not go to work until the weather was fine. At about twelve o'clock witness seeing that the jrg that had contained beer was empty, said to his companions that they had better be mov- ing. Defendant, looking through the bar window, told them to get out of the house, or he would "shift " them. As witness was going towards the yard door to get out defendant followed him and struck him with his fist in the ribs on the right side. Plaintiff was knocked into the yard-by the violence of the blow. As he fell he could feel his leg break, and said that it was broken. Defendant, in reply, said he would break his neck, and struck him a second blow, which knocked him down again. Defendant and his two sons beat the other men with hoes as they ran from the yard to the highway. Witness was left lying in the yard for an hour and a quarter, defendant refusing to allow assistance to be ren- dered. One of the tons of the defendant cut John Malony's head open by a blow. After remaining for about an hour at the station at Preston Brook, witness was taken to the Infirmary at Warrington. He had since been kept by his friends, as he had no money of his own. In answer to Mr. Fletcher, plaintiff admitted that he and his friends were singing in the house, but denied that he struck at Mr, Whitlow over Malony's shoulder. —Corrobora- tive evidence was called on behalf of the plaintiff.— For the defence, evidence was given to show that a disturbance took place between plaintiff and his companions. Defendant called upon his sons to assist him in ejecting the plaintiff and his com- panions. It was contended that the plaintiff, while aiming a blow at someone over the shoulder of one of his companions, fell backward off the step into the yard. It was given in evidence that defendant did not strike Murray, and that he did not use any unnecessary violence in ejecting the men, who had refused to quit the house.—His Honour, in review- ing the evidence, said that it was difficult for any witness to speak exactly as to the facts, as the affair seemed to have arisen out of a public-house brawl. He thought that plaintiff brought the trouble upon himself, and that Mr. Whitlow was not at fault. lie gave judgment for the defendant.

EARLESTOWN COLLIES. Before Mr. R. Houghton and ther magistrates, at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, James Forster, of Earlestown, formerly a' collier at the Edge Green pit, was charged with stealing a collier's drill, value 5s 6d, the property of John Thornlv, at the colliery mentioned, on the 3rd May. —Evidence was given, showing that the drill was missed from the smithy, and that the prisoner had disposed of it, to a man at Aston. Prisoner, who acknowledged the offence, was fiued 101 and costs, or in default of payment, 14 days' imprisonment.

GOOD TKII:PLAIIT.—The weekly session of the Hope of E,rlestown Lodge of Good Temp tare was held on Monday evening, when Brother George E. Warburton, P.W.C.T., presided. There was a good attendance of members. After the opening of the session, two candidates were initiated. Arrangements were made for paying a visit to the Crow-lane Band of Hope and giving them a friendly entertainment. A report of the District Lodge Session at Warrington,on Saturday last,was submitted by Bro. George Clarke, and was adopted. The evening's programnae was "Roll call and question box," and the roll of members was considered, and arrangernecn made for visi- ting the absentee members. In accordance with ' the latter part of the programme, a variety of questions affecting the Order were handed in and answered. This concluded a very successful session. Giant TnatPASO AT NNWTOIf. Before Mr. R. Houghton and other magistrates, at the Newton Town Hall on Saturday, John Handley, a middle-aged man, living at the Vulcan, was sunimoned for trespassing in search of game on land in the occupation of Thomas Kerfoot, at Newton, on the previous Sunday morning.—Mr. Thomas Stone, of Newton Park said a little before eight o'clock on the pre- vious Sunday morning he, accempanied by Thomas Pen- nington, were walking along Hermitage-lane, when, from in- dications they obaerved, tr.ey went into a wood about 100 yards from Winwick-.-road. They saw two men bring up from near a tree and make the beat of their way out of the wood. He followed thern, and caught the defendant, whom he charged with poaching. He said he was doing no herrn, but witness replied "Come on beck, and we will see." They afterwards found a net and a rabbit, and the defendant said he and his companion had been drunk at the Hermit, and had been sleeping in the wood all the night to escape from the police.—Mr. Thomas Pennington gave corroborative test imony.--P S. Comtnins stated at a quarter-past twelve on the Sunday morning in question he saw the defendant at his own house at the Vulcan. He was not then drunk ; nor was he hiding from the police.—The Bench implied a fine of 5s and costs.

SELLING AI:tur,TI3BATED WIIIEZY.-At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. It. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, A. C. McCorquodale, and W. F. Gooch, George Navior, landlord of the Swan Inn, Newton Common, was summoned for selling a pint of whisky, not of the nature and rerbstanee demanded.—De- fendant said he wool.' plead guilty, but he did not know it. —P.S. Dunn, stationed at Leigh, said that on the 18th October he visited the defendant's house, and asked Mrs. Naylor, who was there, for a pint of whisky. She served him and he paid her.2l for it. He then informed her that he had purchased the whisky for the purpose of having it analysed. A sample of the whisky was afterwaris taken to Dr. Campbell Brown for analysis.—Superintendent Weir said the certificate hom Dr. Brown stated that the whisky was a mixture of whisky and water, upwards of 30 per cent under proof, which was upward.) of 5 per cent too weak.— In reply to the defendant, P.S.Dunn said shortly after he had paid for the whisky the defendant came in and said it was not the best whisky, and he hoped it would be found all righr.—P.C. Rutter c,ifroborate4.—The defendant's ex- planation WV, that on the day in questiott he was away from home, and his wife ran short of whisky in the bar. She mixed up a quantity during the day in his absence, and the officers called before he (nefendant) had tested it. He afterwards found it was deficient of the proper standard.— The Bench inflicted a fine of 20s and costs.

ADULTIIIIAII9 Burrpn.—At the Ne;vton. Petty See- alone on Saturday, John Howe, wholesale and retail grocer, provision dealer, dre. , Market street, Earlestown, also at Wigan, and other places, was summoned for selling an article as butt-r which was not of the nature and quality demanded by the purchaser. Defendant said he would plead guilty so as to enable him to give an explanation.— P.S. Dunne (Leigh) deposed that on Monday, the 18th ult., he viaired the defendent's shep in Market-street, Earle's- town, and asked for a pound of butter. The young man in charge asked him what sort he wanted. end witness replied that he wanted " good butter." He offered him some at a shilling ):I.r pound, end witness replied that would do. It was marked "Prime, is." He informed the young man that he intended to send the butter for analysis, and the reply was that it was not pure butter. That was said in a rather lower tone so that a woman who was in the shop would not hear IL—P.C. Rutter corroborrated.—P.C. Spen- cer said he served the defendant with the summons and asked if he was willing to sign a paper nquiring the at- tendance of the analyst as a witness. The defendant de- clined to do so.—The Clerk ( Mr. Buckton) : The certifi- cate says that the sample contained foreign matter As under: —ll per cent of water and 68 per cent of foreign fats.—The defendant said he had changed his manager at the time in question. One left on the Saturday and another came on the Monday. He always gave instructiors for labels to be pasted on cards denoting that it was Untterime, but with having a new manager on the Monday he had not then done so. He gave strict injunctions to sell nothing as butter an— less it was strictly pure butter.—The Chairman remarked that the sample appeared to be sold as pure butter, whether by accident or wilfully it was not very material, and the de- fendant would be fined 40s and costs.

The Home Secretary on Thursday reeeived a deputation repreeentirur local authorities of the Metropolis, who urged the desirability of a reform of municipal government in London. The tlrst departure of the American mails under the new arrangement took place on Thursday evening, when the North German Lloyd's steamer Eider left Southampton for New York with a heavy mail. Two MEN DROWNED IN TIM Mneasier.—A heavy gale, with terrible showers of hail and sleet, prevailed in Liver- pool during Wednesday night, succeeded on Thursday morn- ing by keen frost. During Wednesday night two men in charge of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board Light- chip, in Tranmere Bight, were either going or returning to tbe lightship in their punt. when It capeizerl and they were drowned. The capsized punt and the bodies of the two men were found on the beach on Thursday morning. MR. Joule Monmtv LT Efavercx.—ln connection with the visit of Mr. John Morley, a conference of the National Liberal Federation of Scotland was held at Hawick.on Tues- day. There was a large attendance of delegate., and among the speakers were Mr. A. L. Brown, M.P., Mr. Provand, M.P., and Mr. Gilbert Beith. Reeolutione were passed ex- pressing confidence in Mr. Gladstone and his policy, in fa- vour of Home Rule on purely Irish matters for Ireland and on Scottish questions for Scotland. It was also resolved that reform of the land laws, religions equality, local option. free education, and other urgent questions be pressed forward. A crowded demonstration in connection with the conference was held in the evening in the Corn Exchange. Hewlett, when the chair was occupied by Mr. Laing, of Lindean, president of the local Advanced Liberal Associa- tion. Among those present were the Right Hon. John Morley, M.P., the Earl of Elgin. Mr. A. L. Brown, M.P., Mr.Provand, M.P., Mr. Donald Crawford, M.P., Mr. Gilbert Belli), and others. Mr. Morley said he was glad to find that in the south-east corner of Scotland the Liberals were t organising in support of the principle of justice to Ireland. The condition of that country was grave, not only for Minireers, but for those who led the Opposition. He stood to his declaration at Leeds : and Mr. Gladstone who was in excellent condition, had no languor in his heart, nor weakness in his •word, but was still prepared to adhere to his Irish policy. Mr. Morley said he did not perceive any evidence that the present Government had the slighteet in- sight into the Irish question. They renounced the policy of blackmail in Parliament, though they had carried it out in Ireland, until it failed. The Chancellor of the Exchequer said Ireland would receive great benefit from legislation. but Lord Salisbury stated that her salvation was to come from firm administration of the law. Mr. Morley appealed to the Liberal dissentiente to join with the Liberals in asking the Government to free Ireland from the nightmare of confusiun and distraction in which she walked. THE COLIN C'AMPBELL DIVORCE Casa.—The court was again crowded on Saturday morning. when Mr. Justice Butt and a special jury resumed the hearing of the consolidated snits of Campbell v. Campbell, and Campbell y Campbell. Marlborough, Bird, Butler, and Shaw The same counsel appeared as on the opening day.—Lady Miles having iden- tified the Prayer-book referred to in her previous evidence, Mr. Finlay continued his address on behalf of Lord Colic Campbell. Prefacing his remarks with a brief epitome of the matters to which he referred on Saturday, the learned counsel said the charge of cruelty against Lord Colin was never breathed to anyone until Lord Colin had intimated to Lady Colin his suspicion of her inftdelity. In reference to the application made by Lord Colin to the Paris municipal authorities, Mr. Finlay pointed oat that at the time the summons was applied for he firmly believed that his wife was living with Lord Blandford as his paramour, but in point of fact this incident was totally irrelevant to the issue before the court, and it was only introduced by Sir Charles Russell to prejudice Lord Colin in the eyes of the jury.— On Monday. Mr. Finlay concluded hia opening statement of Lord Colin Campbell's cese. and evidence was then given to show that the accusation broeght by Lady Miles against Lord Colin in reference to Mary Watson could not possibly be true. Mary, or rather Amelia, Watson was then exam- ined, and gave information as to visits paid by Lord Bland. ford, Captain Shaw, and Dr. Bird to Lady Colin Campbell, and also denied that Lord Colin had at any time been un- duly intimate with her. The case was adjourned till Wed- needay, when Rose Fisher, wee Baer, formerly Lady Colin Campbell's maid, was examined at great length. She stated that Lord Blandford was a frequent caller upon Lady Colin; that he stayed about an hour; that he had accompanied her home at three in the morning and then entered a room with her ; and that Lady Colin very frequently wrote to him. Sharp, living in Lrgh-street, Ear'esteem, was summoned for assaulting a girl named Caroline Adams, on the 12th Nov Mr. P. Davies (Warrington) appeared for the defendant, who pleaded guilty, and Mr. W. Swift (St. Helens) appeared for the complainant. Mr. Swift, after expressing surprise that the charge against the defendant was not one of lade- cent assault, proceeded to say that the girl was under 15 Years of age, and was a kind of assistant or help at the house of the defendant's mother, where she used to go two or three hours each day and help to clean. About three o'clock en the afternoon of the date in question, she was cleaning the windows of the back kiichen, when the defen- dant entered the house, and after having his dinner, gave some corn to some pigeons in the yard. He afterwards en- tered the kitchen again, and pulled her off the box upon which she was standing, and behaved indecently towards her. The complainant then left the house and went home, where she complained to her mother, who visited the de- fendant's house the following day and complained. The girl, however, returned on the Friday, Saturday, and Sun- day, and on the Monday when she was drawing her wages she was discharged—The complainant then gave evidence in support of Mr. t•wift's statement, adding, in reply to Mr. Davies, that she had been working at defendant's home for seven or eight months. She denied having thrown any water upon the defendant, or that she had thrown a dish- cloth at bith.—For the defence Mr. Davies pointed to the gsod character borne by the defendant, who, he said, was in a respectableposition, and in the employ of Mr. MolY- neux, of Earlestown, who had sent a certificate as to his character. while Mr. Urquhart, tailor, of Newton, and the Vicar of Earlestoen, would also speak as to his character. He submitted that the complainant had thrown some water upon the defendant, and that he merely seized her arm to shake her and caution her about doing so in the future. The defendant never dreamt a charge of assault would be brought against him, and he (Mr. Davies) thought the girl must have been wicked to make the complaint she had done. If there was a doubt in the case the defendant should have the benefit of it.—Mrs. Alice Callender said about the date stated she was nursing defendant's mother who was ill in bed. div.head: BOATING FATALITY AT WAR-
div.p: THE BOATING FATALITY AT WAR-
RINGTON.

In connection with the sad boating accident on the Mersey, near Latchford weir, on Thursday of last week, the dragging of the river for the body of Richard Dainteth, one of the three persons drowned whose body had not up to Friday night last been found, was continued over the week end without result. On Monday morning, however, about half-past ten o'clock, it was discovered by one of the grapplers close to the weir, and within a hort distance of the scene of the fatality. It was at once conveyed to the Patten Arms and lodged in the same building as the other two which had by that time been placed in coffins ready for burial. •

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

On Monday morning an inquest was held at the Patten Arms by the deputy coroner, Mr. W. T. Hus- band, as to the death of the three persons, Thomas Carty, John Woods, and Richard Dainteth. John Mackenzie deposed that he lived at 14, Castle-street, Much Wooiton, was a joiner by trade, and was in the employ of the London and North- Western Railway Company. Ile identified the bodies of the three deceased who had all been in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company. Thomas Carty was a sailor about 29 years of age, and lived in Wittier-street, Smith- down-road, Liverpool. John Woods was about 15 years of age, and was employed to a great extent in running messages. Richard Dainteth was 24 years of age, lived in Selby-street, Warrington, and had been employed as a time-keeper and a labourer. William Burton, 27,11opesmith-street, Liverpool, formerly a sailor, and now in the service of the North-Western Company, said he went for a sail up the river on Thursday afternoon last during the dinner hour. Ile was accompanied by John Gar- lick, John Woods, Richard Dainteth, and Thomas Carty. They started from the iron bridge at Arpley, where they were all employed. All the men were in the service of the company. The boat was what might be called a "gig.' They went close up to the weir, when the boat was sucked in by the water and swamped. Witness was rowing at the time. Witness and John Garlick swam ashore. Carty was a splendid swimmer, but was drowned, he believed, owing to Woods clinging to him, because when the two bodies -were found Woods was clinging round the neck of Carty. Dainteth was rowing with him on the day in question, and Carty was steering. They were about ten feet from the weir when the boat began to be sucked in, and he heard some one sing out " Look out for yourselves." Witness had been in boat accidents at sea.

John Garlick, 28, Wendell-street, off Smithdown- road, Edge Hill, Liverpool, joiner, in the service of London and North-Western Railway Company, said he was at work at Arpley Iron Bridge on Thursday, and during the dinner hour he went with the others named for a row on the river, as far as the weir. Burton and Dainteth were rowing when they got to the weir, and Carty was steering with an oar. When they were about ten yards from the weir wit- ness shouted to the rowers to stop, but they did not do so. l'ifo reply was given, but some of the men sneered at him. The back current caused by the falling water then drew the boat in, and it was swamped. Witness and Burton succeeded in swim- ming ashore; but the other occupants of the boat were drowned. In answer to a question, witness said that when near the weir he said to the others in the boat," Do you see that froth ; if you go into that you are done;" but there was no reply. The boat was swamped twice, and after the second time he did not see any of the other inmates. William Patten, filesmith, Howley, deposed to finding the bodies of Carty and Woods on Friday last about quarter-past eleven o'clock, about 50 yards below the weir. Woods had his arms round Carty's neck, and their legs were "twisted round each other as if they had been tied, they were so fast together." .

William Bennett, locomotive fireman, living at 9, Allen-street, said that he found the body of Dainteth that morning, about a quarter or twenty minutes past ten o'clock, about five yards below the weir.

The Coroner, in summing up the evidence, said it was a very absurd and foolish thing to have rowed up to the weir. Three of the five persons in the boat were good swimmers. Two got ashore, and the jury had heard why the other men did not do so. If all the men had been swimmers they might all have been saved, and that showed the necessity of learning to swim when they had the opportun- ity. Nothing in his mind could excuse the gross ignorance or foolhardiness of the men in going so near the weir. The two men who had been sailors fancied they knew a great deal about water, but evidently they did not understand the water at this weir, and they appeared to have sneered at the warning which was given them. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

LT-crunn ort "A Pic e op Coar.."—Ort Monday even- ing, under the auspices of the Haydock Reading Room, a public lecture entitled " The history of a piece of coal "was given in the St. James's schoolroom by Mr. T. R. Burnett, Fellow of the Geological Society, and one of the lecturers connected with the Manchester Working-men's Clubs As- sociation. There was a good attendance, and Mr. A. H. L. Evans presided. Among those present were Dr. J. W. Wat- kins (Newton), Dr. T. E. Hayward, Rev. H. Kearney, vicar of Haydock, Messrs Thomas Jackson, J Taylor, John John- son, G. Weldon, R. M. Prescott, J. C. Westworth, lac. A number of ladies also attended. The lecturer commenced br giving the various ideas of coal entertained since the 15th century up to the present, and proceeded to trace how coal was formed millions of years ago, before man was created, from vegetable matter. He commented upon the systems of coal mining, and by a series ef diagrams and illustrations added considerable interest to his instructive ; lecture. The Chairman moved a cordial vote of thanks to the lecturer, which was seconded by the Rev. H. Kearney, and carried with acclamation. In responding, the lecturer moved a similar compliment to the chairman, which was seconded by Mr. John Jackson. Dr. J. W. Watkins (New- ton), in supporting the motion, said the lecturer had re- called to his mind the great Hugh Miller, and he promised to give to the Haydock Reading Room a copy of Hugh Miller's "Red Sandstone." (Applause.)—The Lecturer re- marked that Dr. Watkins had forestalled him as he had in- tended making a similar offer, but he would supplement it by giving a work cm geology by some other author. (Are- plause.)—Mr. R. M. Prescott proposed, and Mr. Taylor seconded a vote of thanks to the trustees for the loan of the schoolroom, and the motion 'wee passed.—The Rev. H. Kearney acknowledged the compliment, and said it was highly gratifying to have a Sunday school placed at the disposal of a man of science, who came there not only to give scientific education, but to harmonise science with re- ligion, which he (the vicar) thought was better than many sermons that were preached. (Laughter and applause.)— The proceedings then concluded.

Princess Henry of Battenberg is said to be gaining strength with rapid strides, and Ethelcourt will now be able to remove to Osborne for Christmas, The funeral of Mr. 0. E. Coops, member for Brentfo.d Division, took place at South Weald, Essex, on Thursday, the Bishop of St. Albans officiating. A large number of men employed at the Liverpool docks held a meeting on Wednesday to protest against the changes In the American and African mail arrangements. A" Daily News " Dublin telegram says :—Another mem- ber of the Irish Parliamentary party is to be summoned to the Queen's Beneh in connection with a speech delivered in county. Gal way.
On Wednesday the Kentish Knock lightship was run into by a strange barque and nearly cut in two. The crew were taken off by a passing barque, and the lightship went down in three minutes.

ALLEGED ROBBERY PROW TUB PBRSON.—Rebecoa, Airhe, a middle-aged wom,tti, of no fixed residence, was. chatgA at the Police Coma, on Wednesday, with being drunk and disorderly, and farther with stealing 7s from the person of Roger Hughes, a collier, living in Edward- street. Prisoner, who said she came our of Scrangewaya Gaol on Saturday, pleaded guilty, and said she was in drink. She was committed to Walton Gaol for one month with hard labour.

A TEOUBLRBO2daI BOY.--At the Police Court, on Wednesday, Joseph Critehley, of Peasley Cross, who on the. 17th ult. received nine strokes with the birch, fer stealing his father-in-law's watch, and on the following (lay received twelve strokes in Liverpool for stealing a watch from a public-house in Miller-street, was charged with stealing four brass weiptta from the shop of Thorns Hampton, Raven-street. Inspector Keighley expkined the boy's previous character, and the magistrates (Alderman M'Bryde and Alderman Harrison) committed him for fourteen days' bard labour. Tun ALLEGED ROBBERY ON TUB RATIMAY.--George Clifford, alias Charles thiffiths, of Leamington, remanded. on a charge of stealing a puree containing 9s 2-1 d and a railway ticket from Mrs. Mary Bold, of Pemberton, while she was travelling from St. Helens to Wigan, on the 23rd alt., was again brought before Dr. Gaskell at the Town Hall on Wednesday. Mr. Terrand, for the London and North— Western Railway Company, asked for a further remand, saying that inquiries into prisoner's character were being made, but replies bad not yet been received. Mrs. Bold having repeated her evidence as to being alone with prisoner in a compartment, and after saying good-bye to her sister missing her purse, the prisoner was remanded until next day.

tSrAnviTrom ROI3BIIIIY.—At the Town Hall, on Monday, before Messrs. W. Blinkhorn, R. Pilkington, and A Walmsley, Elizabeth Gaskell, an elderly woman living at 14, Mount-street, Eccleston, was charged with stealing two pinafores, value 13 6d, from a stall on the Market, the property of Joseph Abrams.—Prosecutor sail he lived at Manchester, and kept a draper's stall on Si. Helens Market. On Saturday afternoon from what he was told he followed the prisoner and found the two pinafores produced under her sh‘wl, and which had been taken from his stall.—P.C. Massey' said he apprehended the prisoner, who in reply to the charge said, "Yon did not see we take it. If I had not 4 been drunk I would not have touched them."—Superinten- dent Johnston informed the Bench that the prisoner had , been formerly convicted for similar offences.—The primmer pleaded guilty, and said it was starvation that made her commit the offence.—She was committed to prison fcr six weeks, with hard labour.

THE Sr. HELM'S HAERIDES.-3feesrs. H. Wardman and H. Rigby officiated as hares on Saturday. To deceiin the pack the hares very acutely laid the trail, on starting from head quarters at 3-22, as if making for Most Bank, but by a sharp turn they brought it through Cowley Park, down No.tharoad and Church-street, the countenance ef the " hares " being highly expressive of their inward ezulta- tion at the deceptive trail they were laying. The appear- ance of the hares in Church-street attracted much atten- tion, and a large concourse of people assembled, apparently enjoying the sight very much. The pack also received a most cordial greeting whilst passing through the town. The run was continued along the canal bank, Sherelley Park, Thatto Heath, Eccleiton, and Windle. The hares reached home at 4-35. The pack started at 3-32 and returned at 5-0. Distance, eight miles. The pack comprised the following members :—R. H. Mather (deputy captain and pace), A. Makin (pace), W. Webster, H. Harrison, J. J. Davies, P. Phythian, W. A. Orglev, Joseph Wood (whip), W. G. Burrill, J. S. Mather (captain), J. Parr, and F. Wilson. BRBAZING A WINDOW ',Eon FUN."-At the Town Hall. on Monday, before Messrs. W. Blinkhorn, R. Pi,king ton, and A. Walmaley, Mary Thompson, a girl whose fre- quent appearance at the police court has given her an mien- viable notoriety, was charged with wilfully breaking a Wats glass window, and doing damage to the araunt of 2s ad, at the Prince of Wa'em Inn, Ormakirk-street. The prisoner pleaded guilty.—P.C. Bell said that at about four o'clock 1 he was on duty, and saw the prisoner near the Prince of Wales Inn. He suspected ber,and in a few minutes returned. He then found that she had broken a plate glass window. He saw her coaling away, and apprehended her, whereupon she said she bad broken it for a bit of fun. She added that if he would let her go she would break all these windows.— Mr. Griffiths, landlord of the Prince of Wales, sail the damage had been estimated at £4 2s 61—The Chairman said the prisoner's previous character was so bad, and she bad been there for a similar offence before, that they felt bound to give her the full penalty of two month's imprison-. naent with hard labour.—The prisoner, who exclaimed "Thank you," was then removed, smiling, from the deck.

PRIMROSE LEAGUE MEETING. A public gathering in connection with the Gerard Hab tation of the Primrose Lsagoe was held at the Conservative Club, Hall-street, on Tnnrsday evening. The proceedings took the term of a cancert, interspersed with short speeches. Mr. Joseph Robinson (Ruling Councillor) presided, and amongst the large attendance of knights, dames, and associates and members of the party were Mr. W. Pilkington, J P., Mrs. Pilkington, and the Aims Pilkington, Roby Hall, Mr. Thomas Pilkington, and Mrs. Herbert Pilkington, Mr. Lee Pilkington, Major Windris. Mr. W. Longton, and Mr. W. J. btewart, Liverpool. The Chairman said they did not wish those gatherings to be stiff and formal affairs. They. went there to have some de. gree of pleasure, as well as discharge the duties allotted to them. The league was a combination which he was sure would assist the Cons-rvative and constitutional cause, and he sincerely hoped that that habitation, which had commenced in a favoarable way, would ate on and propper. (Applause.) Mr. Stewart said it had been said that imitation was the sincerest forma of flattery, and therefore he would say that if there was no. thing else to recommer d the league, they had it from the mouth of the other side (who had attempted to form an or- ganisation of ladies and gentlemen, bat could not agree) that there was something in the system which they had ID-. angurated which was worthy of being followed by their political opponents. They were clearly and truly a national party; unity was their mottt-, and lIDIOR their aim. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Stewart proceeded to deal with the objects of the Primrose League and the way the work was to be carried out. The real work which led to success in elections, he said, was not that work which was done at the eleventh hour or in the last month, but work which was carried on week after week and year after year in the shape of registtation, and keeping a watch on and influencing neighbours.

THE PARR KICKING CASE. Before Messrs. W. Blinkhorn, R. Piikington, and A. ' Walmeslev, at the Town Hall, on Monday, James Seddon, a yeung man, residing at Parr Stocks, was charged, on re- mand, with unlawfully wounding Joseph Pennington, at Parr, on the 18th September last.—Mr. R. W. H. Thomas appeared for the prosecutor, and Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the prisoner.—Mr. Thomas stated that the prisoner Was charged with kicking tha prosecutor on the leg, and bre.alee ing his knee-cap. He remarked that it would be some months before the prosecutor would be able to walk.—The Prosecutor, who had to be carried in and out of court, said he was a collier, and lived at Fleet-lane, Parr. About half. past eleven on Saturday night, 18th September. he was going home from St. Helens, and when he had passed the prisoner's house the prisoner ran after him and kicked him. He was knocked down, and he cried that his leg WAS ' broken. The prisoner said, I'll kill you, you b I've had a payment a good while for you." When he fall he begged the prisoner to let bins alone, but the prisoner kicked him from one side of the road to the other. He did , not give the prisoner any provocation, and had not seen him before then on that night. Some women then came up and stopped the prisoner, and he (prosecutor) was carried home, and a doc- tor set his leg the same night. Ha had known prisoner for two years, and he was quite sure it was the prisoner who , kickec: him.—ln reply to Mr. Swift he said he did not call Mrs. Seddon a bad name and hit her. He did not see his ' (prosecutor's) brother George Lit her and knock her down. At St. Helens he was in two beerhouses, and had a few bot- tles of cider and three glasses of beer. The prisoner had his hat and coat off, his shirt sleeves rolled up, and wore a pair of pit clogs.—Mrs. Deacle, wife of Joseph Deacle, liv- ing at Albert-terrace, Parr, said on the night in question be was standing at her door, when the prosecutor and two men passed. They had got only a few yards past, when the prisoner came out of the entry leading to his house, and af- terwards ran towards the prosecutor. She heard a noise, and then she heard some women cryiog to Seddon " Let him alone, you've done enough and you have broken hie leg."—ln reply to Mr. Swift witness said she had formerly summoned the defendant and his wife for assaulting her, and she bad also been a witness against Mrs. eeddon in • another case.—Mrs. Hannah Heyes, a resident of the neigh. bourhood. said she saw the prosecutor pass her door, and another man ran up to him and kicked him. The prosecutor then fell to the door. He could not swear that the Man who kicked the prosecutor was the prisoner.—Mary Flowers wife of George Flowers, deposed that she saw the prisoner kick the prosecutor.—Dr. Casey, of Sutton, said he attended the prosecutor on Sunday, the 19th September. He found him suffering from a fractured knee-cap. A. kick would cause the injury. It was extremely unlikely that a fall would Cause the injury.—In reply to Mr. Swift, witness said there were several bruises on prosecutor's face, and the prosecutor said another man, not the prisoner, had caused them.—P C. itatcliffs sail he apprehended the pri- soner at his residence, and charged him with the offence, whereupon the prisoner replied, " Oh, tha charges me, and Inc in bed."—For the defence, Mr. Swift submitted the evi- dence for the prosecution was full of discrepancie, and con- tended that his client had been in the house from ten o'clock on the night in question, and he did not again go out that night. tie meted that the prosPcutor had sustained his in- juries in a free fight, and that the case had been brought all through spite.—The .13inch decided to commit the prisoner for trial, and the prisoner eaid. he was not guilty, and that he never saw Pennington that night. He went to bed at ten o'clock, and never went out again.

CONGREGATIONAL BAND or Horn.—On Tuesday even- ing a very good meeting was held in connection with the above. Rev. J. Johnstone was chairman, and there was a good attendance. CHURCH OF ENGLAND —The customary fortnightly tem- perance meeting was held on Monday. The R.v. F. R. Lee occupied the chair, and there was an excellent attendance. The Rev. W. H. Hunt gave an address, and a good pro- gramme was gone through. THE VICARAGE.—The Rev. Harry Mitchell, M.A. (Em- manuel College, Cambridge), vicar of Pemberton, to which he was appointed in 1831 by the rector of Wigan, the Hon. and Rev. Canon Bridgeman, has beea offered the living of Prescot by the Provost and Fellows of King's College. Cam- bridge, in whose gift it is, the present vicar. the Rev. H. A. Macnaghten, having been appointed by Lord Fitzwilliam to the living of Tankersley, near Barnsley. It is stated that Mr. Mitchell will accept the offer, and will take charge of the new parish early in the new year. His removal from Pemberton will be much regretted.

TO have and to hold—The baby. A retired editor—One who is in bed. Up the spout—The plumber's profits. ON TIIR DOCTORS.—" I am feeling very ill," said a patient to his physician. "Let me see your tongue," said the doctor. "It's no use," responded the patient, "no tongue can begin to tell how I feel." • MEANT FOR A GAG.—" Maria, I wish you would keep still," said Brown, trying to write. "Your tongue is like Tennyson's brook, it goes on forever." " Humph!" answered Mrs. 8., indignantly. "I suppose you think that's a joke." "Well, I meant it as a sort of gag." No Go.—The attempt to introduce the tailless evening coat has met with about the same success that the tail- less morning coat enjoyed when associated with a tall hat. The wearer always looked "curtailed," and the dignity of the high hat was lost by the scantiness of the body covering. "Mr. Jones," said the end-man of a certain black minstrel troupe, "can you tell me how to invest money so that it will go the farthest ?" "No, Mr. Thompson, I am not aware that I can. May I ask how you invest money so that it will go the farthest ?" "Why, I buy postage-stamps, to be sure." A NIOT WATEnimo-PLacn.--Scene---A Scotch railway- station; porter notifying passengers requiring to change carriages. Porter: Change here for Stevenston, Salt- coats, Ardrossan, and flurry up !—Old English lady': Porter, where is " Hurry-up? '—Porter : Speir the cap- tain o' the steamer when you get to Ardrossan, mistress. RHTENGE.—She was re-headed and vindictive; he was mild and fobearing. After a dozen years of matri- mony he was a ruin. One day she had been unusually belligerent. "I hate you," she screamed. "I hate you worse every day, and I hated you the first time I ever saw you." "Then why in heaven's name did you marry me?" he asked, with unusual emphasis. "Because I hated you," she answered; and much wisdom fell upon the husband, so he knew why he suffered. LOOKED FOR TURNIP Fip.si.—An old policeman sel- dom gets fooled on a street gamin. Yesterday, when a woman ran out of her house on Fifth-street and in- formed a passing officer that a boy was lying dead in the alley, the officer didn't hurry any. If the boy was dead hurrying wouldn't do any good. If dying the officer couldn't save him. He walked slowly around and found the boy stretched out on the ground, very much alive but still making no efforts to get up. 'Somebody run over him, and the wretch ought to be discovered and punished!" exclaimed one of the crowd. "He may have shot himself," added a second. "I think he fell from that shed," put in a third. "Or some larger boy has almost killed him," chimed a woman. The officer paid no attention to these remarks, but after a look up and down the alley he bent over the hop and inquired: "How long have you had it ?" "Half an hour." "How many did you eat ?" "Two." "Well, you'd better get up and keep moving, and it will go away the sooner." "What is it ?" asked five or six voices. The officer crossed the alley and picked up a half-eaten turnip and held it up to view. Everbody nodded and said, " Urn !" and the crowd quietly dispersed.
IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE_.

On Sunday afternoon a meeting of the local branch of the Irish National League was held in the League Hall, Orford-street, Warrington, at which a lecture on "The Progress of the Irish Cause" was delivered by Mr. J. G. Taggart, of Liverpool. The chair was taken by Mr. F. Loughlin; and he was supported on the platform by Mr. Taggart and other gentlemen. There was a large attendance. The CHAIRMAN said the present brutal Tory Govern- ment had once more declared war against the liberties of Irishmen—in the words of one of the victims, they had struck the first blow. They would, he thought, be wanting in their duty as Irishmen if they did not pass a resolution condemning the action of the Government and offering words of sympathy to the people at home under their present sufferings. He therefore moved "That we beg to express our contempt and disgust at the coercive policy about to be adopted by the present Tory Government, and we would warn them that it can ' but end as all coercion has ever ended, in utter failure; and would at the same time exprtss our ' opinion that there can be no real, true, or lasting lunion between Great Britain and Ireland until the people of Ireland obtain their oft-demanded rights of self-government." (Applause.) Having spoken to the resolution, the Chairman said he would like to say a word or two about local matters. He had often heard the desire expressed by Englishmen who were favourable to the Irish cause that there should be established an English Home Rule Asso- ciation. He was of opinion that by doing so a great amount of good would be done, and he could not understand why those Englishmen who professed to be the friends of Ireland—and he would not doubt what they said—did not do something. The reason of their defeat last July was the want of education upon the question of the English electors, and be was perfectly certain that if a few lectures were got up in the town upon the Irish question they would turn the " No " of last July into a "Yes." In Mr. Crosfield they had a candidate who, he be- lieved, was a genuine Home Ruler; and if ' they and the English Liberals.' would but set to work he was convinced that they would certainly put Mr. Crosfield into the :position he deserved to be in, namely, that of re- presentative of the town. (Applause.)-'--Mr. M. CHAMBERS seconded the resolution.—Mr. TAGGART then gave his lecture, and supported the resolution. He contrasted the position of the Irish party and Irish cause in 1879, when the League was formed, with the position they held at the present time, and remarked upon the great advances that had been made. When. they considered that at the for- mer period only four English members of Parlia- ment voted even in favour of an inquiry into Home Rule, and that recently 212 English Liberals voted for Home Rule itself, he thought they had a great deal to congratulate themselves upon. (Applause.) He expressed the opinion that the Tory Government would not -venture upon coercion, but if they did he felt certain that it would end in their overthrow and the bringing back into power of Mr. Gladstone. (Applause.)--The resolution was then carried unani- mously.—A vote of thanks to the lecturer was after- wards proposed by Mr. STIRRUP, and seconded by Mr. WILITEHRAD, the latter expressing a wish that such sentiments as those uttered by Mr. Taggart could be brought more under the notice of English- men.—Mr. WHITHAM, in supporting the resolution, said Englishmen, Irishmen, Scotchmen, and Welsh-j men had one common enemy, and that was the landowner. What they were striving for in Home Rule was to make it possible for the worker to live a comfortable, happy life. He was in favour of some method being adopted in Warrington, and all over the country, of bringing Englishmen and Irish- men more together, so that they could work shoulder to shoulder, and look upon each other as friends. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks to the chair- man brought the proceedings to a close.

The pain was so great that I could not remain more than a few seconds in one position. I lost flesh, and my face and body assumed a worn out a,nd deathlike appearance. I consulted two physi- cians, and paid them each a guinea, simply to hear that I must die; my own doctor gave me up. 59, BURTON CRESCENT, LONDON, W.C.—Ever since my child was born, some seven years ago, I have suf- fered very much from uterine disorders, which have rendered me very miserable and have confined me to my bed a large portion of the time. I suffered intensely from violent headaches, with a great deal of pain in my back, and became very much reduced in flesh and spirits. What was to me, in addition to this, a very peculiar thing, was that I gradually lost my hearing. I consulted a number of physicians in London, and one and all advised me to take a sea voyage; I did so, without deriving much benefit from it. When I arrived at New York, I consulted two of the best known physicians who make a speciality of diseases of women, and received only temporary relief from their treatment; and I came back to London very much discouraged. During these years I have, from time to time, consulted many prominent physicians, both in England and on the Continent, but none of them were able to give me more than temporary relief. The terrible head- aches, awful bearing down pains, and great ner- vous depression, seemed to come round with wonder- ful exactness, even when under the doctor's care. In fact I was laid up in bed from nervous prostra- tion and debility about one half the time. My liver was torpid and sluggish, and I had no appetite. Doctors called it female complaint, but could give me no permanent relief. Hearing "Warner's SAFU Cure" highly recommended, I gave it a thorough trial, and am now in good health, all the previous troubles having left me. It is now some five months since I have taken any of the SAFE Cure, yet I have had no return of my old disorder, and I consider myself permanently cured. div.head: LAT FST NEWS.
div.p: LAT FST NEWS.

Messrs. Hodgkinson- f-i-nd Codlings' cotton mill, Blackburn, was partly destroyed by fire on Friday morning. The new law for the suppression of gambling has just come into operation in Paris clubs. No loans or playing on parole will. be allowed. Several games are prohibited. The Public Prosecutor at Brussels on Friday received a communication from a leading inhabitant of that city accus- 9ing two persons residing in Brussels of complicity in the recent mail robbery. Mr. J. 13igwood, whe contested East Finsbury at the general election, has been selected as the Conservative can- didate for the Brentford division of Middlesex. The Liberals have not yet selected their candidate.
FATAL Ica ACCIDENT.—On Friday afternoon a fatal ice accident happened at Middleton. A number of children were skating on a pond when Peter Smith, aged 13 years, fell through the ice and was drowned.

SHOCKING TUNNEL EXPLOSION.—On Friday morning a man named Richardson was killed, and sev- eral others injured, at Rybal, by an explosion of blast- ing powder in a tunnel being made in connection with the Thirimere Waterworks. Richardson was driving a charge home when the explosion took place. He received terrible injuries. FRIGHTFUL EXPLOSION AT GATESHEAD.—Two MEN KILLED.—A sad disaster occurred at a tar works at Gateshead on Friday afternoon. A still became choked, and took fire, Mr. Chine'', managing proprietor, rushing to the place ; the still exploded and caught him in a volume of flame. He was so badly burned that his life is despaired of. Two other men, George Patten and Robert Porthouse, were burned to death. The engineman, John Clark, was also fearfully burnt.

Tine WIFB MURDER AT LEICESTER.—Thomas Bloxham, framework knitter, was charged at Leicester on Friday, with murdering his wife. Shocking details were disclosed, showing that the prisoner had shot her near the heart, stabbed her five times right through the lungs, and then cut her throat to the vertebrae on each side. The prisoner be- trayed no emotion whatever in the dock, and appeared well satisfied with himself He was committed for trial on the capital charge.
THE CAMPBELL DIVORCE CASE. SHOCKING REVELATIONS.

On the bearing of the Campbell divorce suits baing re- sumed on Thursday, evidence was given by tbe Hon. R. F. Villiers, Mr. Mark Pleydell Bouverie ; Cornelius Calling. ham, who has been employed as a waiter at the Royal Hotel, Purfleet; and Albert Derocbe and James O'Neill, both of whom have been in Lord and Lady Colin Campbell's ser- vice. The last-named witness, who testified to adultery with Captain Shaw. was under cross-examination when the court adjourned.—On Friday the witness O'Neill was fur- ther cross-examined by Sir. C. Russell. Questioned as to what Sir C. Russell called the keyhole performance," witness repeated the whole story.— By his Lordship: He did not tell Rose Baer about the key- hole affair. He allowed her to be dismissed for saying cer- tain things, although he knew Lady Colin had committed adultery with Captain Shaw.—Elizabeth Evans, formerly in the service of Sir Philip and Lady Miles, at Leigh Court, said she remembered the ball at Leigh Com t at Christmas, 1881, and seeing Lady Colin and Mr. Bird pass into the study together. The Marquis of Blandford and Mr. Bird were there at the Easter visit. The Marquis occupied bed- room No. 37, and Lady Colin No. 38. Lord Blandford went on the same day and left on the same day as Lady C3lin.—Mrs. Duffy, a professional nurse, said she was engaged to attend on Lord Colin in September, 1882. While at Leigh Court Lady Colin took no notice of Lord Colin. Mr. Bird was at Leigh Court, and witness had seen him in Lady Colin's room more than once.—Elizabeth Wright, nurse ta Lord Colin previous to Mrs. Duffy, said prior to the marriage she had several conversations with Lady Colin and her mother as to his lorqehip's health. Witness caustd a sensation by declaring that, prior to the consummation of the marriage, her ladyship was suffering from a certain die. ease. She did not mention this V.) the surgeon who was attendiag Lord Colin, because it was so disgusting. She also admitted she had never warned Lord Colin.—The case was then adjourned.

div.head: MINISTERIAL CEUSIS IN FRANCE. .
div.p: MINISTERIAL CEUSIS IN FRANCE. .

Pests, FRID&Y.—ThO French Chamber to-day rejected by 13 votes the motion of the Government with reference to sub-prefectures. The sittihg was adjourned till to-mor- row. M. Freyeinet has declared privately that the Uovern- ment will certainly resign. The Berlin debate on the military bill commenced in Reichstag on Friday. The Secretary for War atated•that there was no imminent danger of war.
DISASTRoUS COLLI ERY EXPLOSION.
5 LIVES LOST AND 20 MEN ENTOMBED.

A colliery explosion occurred about three o'clock on Thursday morning at Elemore, near Durham. There were 38 men in the mine at the time, mainly thifters, preparing the mine for the day-shift men. A number of other men were waiting to descend when the pit fired, and the shaft became blocked with the cages. Communication was opened at six o'clock with the men in the pit, when it was ascertained that 13 of those impri- soned were certainly safe. Three bodies much burned were afterwards brought to the bank, and exploring parties were at once organised. The manager, Mr. [Ashman, was soon in attendance with his staff of workers, as were also Mr. Wil- liam Crawford. M.P.. and Messrs. William Patterson, John Foreman, and John Wilson, miners' agents, who had been summoned from Durham by the workmen. A large num- ber of people congregated during the morning at the pit head, and great excitement prevailed. Tbe damage to the colliery is large, and the shaft, owing to the explosion, is blocked by the cages. The first man the exploring party found on reaching the Low Main seam was Thomas Charlton. Toe), then travelled along the return airway to the Lady seam, where the dead body of Thomas Spence, furnaceman, was found lying near the furnace, also that of Ralph Lawson, whose occupation was to watch the electric light. At the end of the drift throe men named Appleby, Luke, and .Johnson, who had been enlarging the in-take airway, were found lying alive. but all very badly burned. They were at once seat to bank, but Appleby died almost immediately. It was not advis- able to venture further into the workings, and the explor- ing party returned to the bottom of the shaft. A consultation was held in the pay office of the colliery, and the exploring parties were arranged and set to work. From time to time the entombed miners were reached and sent to bank, where they were attended to by the doctors, and afterwards taken to their homes. Most of them were suffering from shock, and were badly burnt. Up to three o'clock 20 had been got out, three of whom, as already stated, were dead. A heavy fall prevented the explorers reaching the other 18 men entombed. The last exploring party heard a rapping, but it was impossible to commu- nicate with the men or to ascertain whether they were all alive or not. The following is the narrative of one of the rescued men: —Tbomal Charlton. residing in the Brick Garth, Essington Lane, said: "I have been 39. years employed at this col- liery, and lam now 61 years of age. I sin employed as a master wasteman, and went down to work this morning. I first felt the shock at ten minutes before three o'clock, as near as I can tell. The shock took my senses away com- pletely, but I recollect shouting to be taken to the Lady Low Main, from where I started. There I met Luke, and managed to get hold of the tabs. After I got hold of the tubs I pulled myself together and assisted Luke to the bottom of the shaft, where we remained until we were rescued by Mr. Lishman and Mr. George Johnson." A Sunderland correspondent says :—During Thursday night a large party of explorers were hard at work en- deavouring to reach the entombed men. Another body, that of Ralph Fishburn, was recovered, and it is believed 20're- main in the workings. Roads are being made over tbe falls, but the work is slow and dangerous, owing to frequent falls of stone. Of 50 ponies in the lower seam all but 16 are dead. The falls in the Hutton and Low Main Seams are very heavy.

A later telegram says :—Soon after noon another body, that of George Johnson, was recovered ; life had been ex- tinct some time. This makes the fifth death. The gloomy forebodings which had seized the friends and relatives of those entombed below grew darker, and none but the most sanguine entertained a hope of seeing any of the nineteen lost colliers alive. As the work went on, and little progress seemed to be made, it began to be felt that the recovery may not be made for two or three days yet, the men having been at work about a mile from the bd'tom of the shaft when the disaster eccurred and the falls having been enormous. Up to the time of telegraphing the persons have not been reached.

WARRINGTON HARRIERS.—The above harriers had a splendid run of about eight miles on Satur- day, twelve members taking part in it. The hares, J. Burke and G. Stokes, were despatched with the bags at 3-20, as well as a slow division at 3-30, com- prising J. Waterworth, T. Gleave, H. Maddock, J. Bellian, J. Chrimes, 'and T. Eden% and a fast division at 3-35. The trail I.ay along Legh-street, and the road to Bewsey, thc.ln across the fields to Dallam, and along the canal to Hulme Locks. Then, cros- sing the canal, th e trail lay over some splendid country and canae on the road at Winwiek Church, over the fields to the left, and came on the road again at Lon.gford. Here the fast division overtook the slows, and all joined in the run home, arriving at 4-30., The fast division was composed of R. Sherlock, D 0 Walsh, and A. and G. Ratcliffe.
