div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER

LONDON. THURSDAY. I hear that the Queen has at last decided to over- come the aversion to London, and, when Parliament meets, to take up her residence at Buckingham Palace. Very little was gained by the capital from these hurried rushes from Windsor, a three days' installation of the ugly pile in Belgravia, and then the return to Windsor before the week had passed its centre. The Great-Western Railway was the rnetst considerable recipient of the Queen's money. • The account for special trains was large, and the money easily earned. Residence at Buckingham • Palace involves much outlay, and the coming win- ter season may be gayer and brighter. I hear the Queen intends to open the next sess;on of Parlia- ment in person, and that the ceremonial will be carried out with full splendour. Year after year it has been more and more prosaic. The Jubilee is to be the occasion for important changes. These have, however, only to do with ceremonial. A far more important matter is the opening of the session a month before its wonted time. The osten- sible object of this move is to give time for consider- ing the procedure rules, but I believe it will really end in a common sense arrangement by which the House will rise every July and re-assemble in Octo- ber. :ieeds the strongest patriotism to persuade member to endure Pall Mall in August. And it is quite unnecessary. As a result, we shall probably have a very early London season. But the new move means even more than this. It is really a step in the direction of paid members. If the people's delegates have to be in the calaii,al from January to July, and then from October to Christmas, they will have little time to mind their own business as well as the country's. But the debate on the Address and the consideration of the procedure rules will occupy much more than the two or three weeks gained by an early opening day. The Irish question increases in importance and perplexity every hour. I hear that the conference at Hawarden has mainly been occupied with a reconstruction of the Irish policy so as to meet the views of the advanced Eng- lish Liberals. There has been an apathy in the ranks, mainly due to the want of a programme. The want will soon be supplied. Mr. Raike's fais pas is still commented upon, and wondered at. There is a view of it taken hero which rises above local interest, and which has to do not with mere commercial considerations, but with more various questions of statesmanship. Ger- many subsidizes the Southampton liners in order ' to develop not so much our commerce withe America as the establishment of a line of ships that may at any moment become a line of trans- ports. She has scarcely any mercantile marine, and the tonnage of her vessels average small. Our recent actual wars, even our recent scares of war, have shown the State the value of our ocean-going vessels. Private companies have kept up a fleet of transports ready for use whenever the War Minis- ter chose to charter them. Germany actually pays a subsidy to nave this dcne for her, and to this subsidy England is contributing by handing over the carriage of the mails to a nation that may nt any moment, if a Russian war were to break out, become our enemy. I know, a4a matter -of fact, that the White Star . Company was comtemplating adding to its fleet and building sister ships which should surpass the swiftest and largest of the present vessels. There is little inducement to sink money in such a ven- ture now. But I should not be at all Sur- prised if the North German Lloyd people added to their fleet. Now the result of this would be that England would have two ships less, and Germany two ships more. and that the German ships would practically have been paid for with British money. 1 am not touching the question of the claims of the Cunard and White Star as against those of the Guion and Oceanic. I believe that this part of the question will, in the end if not in the beginning, right itself. In the meantime we owe to Mr. Raikes, what rarely rights itself, the deflection of British trade into a foreign channel. It is no wonder that Germany is elated. The Drury-lane pantomimes go on increasing in magnificence and cost. Sixteen thousand pounds is to be spent on the next. The sum seems almost incredible. But the amount of good done is incred- ible also. We are approaching a period of great destitution. Now Mr. Augustus Harris is the pay- master of a very necessitous class. As 1 pass up Russell-street and through Covent Garden of an afternoon, I meet, thronging out of the stage door, a whole army of his ragged followers, carpenters, Scene shifters, supers, ballet girls. In a few weeks we shall be in the dazzling halls of fairy land, but the poor fairies in frowsy ulsters, trapesing through the slush and the fog, look like the denizens ot a very hardworked world. I know much is said about the morality of the theatre, but anyone who passes the Covent Garden just before rehearsal is called will have no doubt that here is a question not of luxury and vice, but of poverty and hard work. I mentioned in my last letter that a plaster cast of Mr. Boehm's statue of the Duke has been set up opposite Apsley House. The week's criticism has been directed partly to the work itself and • partly to the site it at present occupies. They have already changed it from one posi- tion to another. Criticism on the cast is of no great practical value. The statue will follow the model. The site is more important. It seems not a well cl- osen one. Of course the statue must be set up somewhere very close to the spot which the model now occupies. It must be opposite Apsley House, and near the arch which acted as a pedestal for its predecessor. The Campbell case has lost none of its interest. It is true the barricades are down in the Strand, but by this time the public have learned that neither money nor interest can avail those who want seats in the Court and have no business in it. Nothing is more remarkable than the patience of the audience. Those who get in make a day of it, and during lunch time the Court looks like an aristocratic pic- nic. There was great interest amongst the Bar to see how Mr. Finlay would cross-examine. He has never been engaged in a case like this before. His hard grinding voice and Scotch downrightness and persistence were very telling, and no cross-examina- tion could well be more irritating. It is a sad thing, indeed, to see how many ladies of birth and posi- tion have tried to gain their way into the Court. Sir Charles Butt is more lenient than Sir James Hannen. Some of the details that have come out are very degrading to listen to. But at this trial so many persons Of mark in society are interested that to have been present at it implies distinction. " Been to the Cohn-deries ?" one hears asked as a question in a light-hearted way—as if evidence ad- duced of the alleged adulteries of Lady Colin had the same kind of social interest as a private view at the Grosvenor, or a State concert at Buckingham Palace. - _

At he exhibition of the British artists in Suffolk- street, which opened this week, the crowd collects round Lady Colin's picture by Whistler, which even in the judgment of its painter is admitted to be "un- finished." Mr. Whistler might have plenty of time to finish it. But then, by that time, Lady Colin would not be as interesting as now. I think the saddest face I have ever seen is that of old Mr. Blood, and one of the handsomest. The mother manages more easily to constrainther feelings. The Bloods were well-known on the continent. It is only a few years ago when I used to hear it said at Florence that the three most beautiful faces in the city were those ot the Miss Bloods and their father.

November is the season for hairdressers' con- gresses, and the fashions of May and June are j settled solemnly and irrevocably when the fogs be- gin to come. It is a curious thing that there is a J parallelism between dress and hair cutting in this respect, that the French still settle both questions for women and the English for men. Latterly, how- ever, there has been much give and take. The male j fashion of having the hair cut away from the temples, and in a full short wing on the forehead was the celebrated invention of eapoul, the French tenor, who took as mueh interest in his own eheve- lure as Oscar Wilde did in his own great coat. We have latterly begun to adopt this Capoul cut. But I hear that short hair for girls is to go completely and rapidly out of fashion. It may indeed go completely, but it can scarcely go rapidly. There must be an interregnum while the short hair is growing, and the difficulty of the members of the Hairdressers' Conference has been how this matter is to be settled. They have settled it. We shall have a short season of curled hair, of little imper- ceptible wigs, and then gradually we shall revert to the fashions of four years ago.

WARRINGTON WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVE- MENT SOCIETY.—A meeting of the above society was held in the large school-room, Bold-street, on Wednesday evening, the Rev. J. Howell Jones pre- siding. In response to invitations, several local societies availed themselves of the opportunity of taking part in a debate on ." Home Rule." Mr. Charles Plinston, who brought the subject forward, moved the following resolution, which was seconded by Mr. Hunt :—" That the best interests both of Great Britain and Ireland imperatively require that the great effort to give a better government to Ire- land which was begun by Mr. Gladstone should be firmly persevered in until a durable settlement is arrived at; that such a settlement must meet the views and wishes of the Irish electors, as expressed by their constitutional representatives in Parlia- ment; and that the only plan whiCh will satisfy either the justice or the policy of the case is that of an Irish legislative body for the management of what Parliament shall decide to be distinctly Irish affairs." Mr. Arthur Bennett moved an - amend-

ment, which was seconded by Mr. J. E. Richardson, to the following effect :—" That this meeting, whilst disapproving of the proposals of Mr. Gladstone, is in favour of the gradual extension of the principles of local self-government on lines which shall be applicable to every part of the United Kingdom." The following gentlemen took part in the debate : Messrs. T. Birchall, C. Travers, W. H. Butler, W. J. Calvert, E. Wright, and Rev. R. Pilcher, B.A. On a vote being taken the amendment was lost by a large majority. van4-nrio OF EVERY DESCRIPTIOII, executed by John S. Green, Printer. Intelligent messages are spelt by a code of signals through the movements of the table, and the fol- lowing is one which has eccurred in the town of Blackburn ; the statement is taken from the " Blackburn Standard." A widow who was earning her living by washing, hearing of spiritualism, from curiosity sat at the table, and information was spelt out from the table, which was " Your brother John is alive and lives at 28, East-street, Waymeuth ; write to him." PROPOSED MEMORIAL TO TELE LATE CANON

BARCLAY. Sir,—l am afraid the few words which I made use ef at the meeting on Tuesday evening last conveyed to the minds of several gentlemen present an erroneous impression— namely, that I did not fall in with the idea of handing the balance over and above the cost of a mural tablet to the new church in Greenway-road. I entirely agree with this view, but at the time I thought that, as the subscription list was thrown open to all, irrespective of creed, a memorial to per- petuate the memory of our late vicar, such as public baths or a park (after the completion of the mu-al tablet), would be more in harmony with the feelin4s of the Nonconform- ists and the general public, and would be no more expen- sive, perhaps, than the founding of a scholarship, whilst at the same time they would be equally as advantageous to the people of Runcorn.—l am, yours truly, J. GATES. Runcorn, December 1, 1896.

div.head: LIBERALISM IN COUNTRY DISTRICTS.
div.p: LIBERALISM IN COUNTRY DISTRICTS.

Sir,—Will you allow me space. as a country Liberal, to offer a suggestion as to the best mans of reversing the re- cent Liberal defeat. Some of us in out-of-the-way places hardly feel the stir and throb of political life, and we are ungenerously left to our dulness and our Inactivity. The efforts of the leaders and lecturers of the party seem to be expended in converting the converted, while those nes of the country where faith is weak, and the fight is hardest, are left without a much-needed stimulus, and no Liberationist lecturer deigns to notice us. What we want is to see these gentlemen oftener, and to be roused by meetings where other than lo.sl celebrities air their oratory. It is in New- toe-le-Willows and such like places that a robust tone of political life is wanted, and names are of the first impor- tance. A little patronage from those who are gre.:t in name and wisdom would perhaps be more usefully expended in such parts than in large towns, where good speeches can often be heard, and an enthusiastic audience can be assured to cheer to the echo an incisive attack or a vigorous state- ment of policy. Unless something i done to enomrage those doubtful places Lord Salisbury may be left in office to carry out his policy as long as he pleases.—Yours, w. G.
Newton-le-Willows, November 30, 1336. /
MORE LIGHT IN THE STREETS.

Sir,—l should like to complain through the colernes of your valuable paper of the wretched manner in which some of the streets in Warrington are lighted. There are some which have had every attention paid them, abate there are others that are at the present Laid in a state of comparative darkness ; indeed, what little light they have is of such a pool; sort that its presence is hardly felt. I don't profess to know how often the gentlemen whose duty it is to leek after this business go their rounds, as I understand they have to at certain periods, but I am persuaded to think there are some streets in our town that have very rarely, if ever, re- ceived a visit fromt nem, or else surely, they would be in a better lighted condition than they ar at the present time. There is one street in particular that I have noticed for a long time new (having had to pass alonz it at all hours), which is wretchedly deficient in light, via., Eustace•street. There are but two lamps in the whole streeet, and these have to serve the purpose of lighting some portion of two ether street, one at the top of Walker-street and the other at the top of Gladstone-street, thus leaving the ends of it at night in great darkness, more especially the and of the street nearest Froghall-lane. I centend that two lamps are not sufficient to light up any street the length of the one under notice, and many have been the complaints I have heard the inhabitants make against the poor way in which the street is lighted. Again, in consequence of the prevailing darkness at night it is a place which is made a great convenience of, as afford- ing a hiding place for all sorts of bad-looking persons, who come creeping up the street, and standing about at the corners in the gloom, alarming anyone who may be passing at the time and not able to see them hefore they are at the place where they are standing. More especially on Sunday nights is the great want of more "light " felt in this street, as on this night, when all is gale. the place is literally be- sieged with innumerable bad-looking individuals, who make it quite a resort wherein to pursue their trade. In fact, there are many persons living in this street who are frightened of going out of their homes after a certain hoar, for fear they should be accosted by some ugly piece of humanity asking for alms and who is quite willing, upon a refusal being given him, of using some of his brute force, knowing he is in a place well suited for any violent action he may choose to indulge in. With one of those large lamps, each as there are in some parts of the town, placed at the Froghall-lane end of this steeet a great boon would be given to the people who live therein, and for which I am sure they would be very grate- ful.

SPIRITUALISM V. CO IJURING.

Sir.—l had hoped that in your lest week's Issue we should have come to some reasonable grounds for argument, but your corresponderat "Clifford Dix," seems to have got so much steam up that he must open the valve and let it out with a rush. He seems to fr-t at the fact because we desire to get at the truth; and it tickles me to see how conceited he is, for if I read him aright he thinks that no one is able to judge but himself. What a pity he ctnnot take all the credulous people and endow them with wisdom and lodg- ment! In regard to slate-writing he says why put a piece of pencil inside ? I say to him why take up his pen? Is it to fence with words? If it ie, he will have to and another foe, for I catt put my time to a better use. He also seems to think that if the phenomenon does occur people would not believe. I say would that alter the fact? He wishes the Spiritualists to make a display of their phenomena and he will go and look at it. I say if the fruit is not worth the finding it is not worth having, so we will leave "Clifford Dix" and hope to come across him at some other time when he is in a cooler mood. Now with regard to the proposition I laid down in my last note, Mr. Acton says he will accept my challenge, which I will give you again, not coupled with a number of Traditions which can almost be turned any way. Mine is plainly as follows : That Mr. Acton shall arrange with Mr. Eglinton, of London, mid she' hold a seance with him either in Warrington or London, or anywhere he likes, and that he will prove that the phenomena which occurs in Mr. Eglinton's presence is done by a trick, and that he (Mr. Acton) who claims to be a clever conjurer, will perform the same trick under the same conditions, then I will forfeit ' £5 to any charitable institution in Warrington ; and if Mr. Acton fails he shall forfeit the same amount. I thinlr the above is plain. I tie him to no committee or conditiens, but those above. The editor has my name and address, and I think I am good for the above amount. When he is pre- pared to have the seance I will then ply down the money. 'I he only committee I ask for is Mr. Acton, myself and the e4itor of this paper. If Mr. Acton is willing to pay half the cost of bringing Mr. Eglinton to Warrington, if we can get him to come, I will pay flee other half. Now, with regard to the evidence of the gentlemen I named in my last note, he states that however clever Harry Keller may be in sleight of hand business be might not he a chemist. I say then what of Professor Crooks, who is one of the finest chemists of the day? And I ask again, are men like Mr. W. E. Gladstone so gull,Able that they have not judgment sufficient to guide them as to whether they &re being tricked or not. It is rather amusing to see how • clever some people think they are. div.head: FRODSHAM-
div.p: FRODSHAM-

Tar Rim R. P. BORWICK attended at the Liberal Com- mittee-room, Frodsham, on Saturday evening, and read an interesting paper, entitled, " How to rise in the world." Mr. Peter Riley presided. OPENING OP A NEW ORGAN AT HELSEL—On Saturday afternoon the new organ which has recently been erected in St. Paul's Church, Helsby, by Mr. C. H. Whiteley, Chester, was opened by Mr. A W. Dolby (Fellow of the College of Organists), of Chester.—The Van. Archdeacon Barber, Canon of Chester, delivered a Short address from the text Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms." After the ad- dress Mr. Dolby, in an able and very appreciative manner, gave an organ recital, from which a good idea of the power and tone of the organ were obtained. ANNUAL VOLUNTEER DINNER —OR Saturday, the mem- bats of the I Company (Frodsham) Earl of Chester's Rifles were entertained at their annual dinner at the rown Hall by their officers, Captain H. Harrison and Lieutenant T. B. Ashton. There were about 70 persons present, the visitors being Colonel Ashton. commanding the battalion; Mr. J. Hurst, Mr. A. A. Harrison, Mr. D. Ashton, Mr. G. H Dan- by, and Mr. G. F. Ashton. During the evening the band of the corns, under the leadership of Mr. James Garner, played selections. Various toasts were given, and several members of the corps enlivened the proceedings by singidg. SHOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT.—OR Wednesday afternoon a fatal accident happened to a man named Samuel Hulse, of Five Crosses. It appears that he had ben sent with a load of wheat, which was in a one-horse spring cart, to Frodsham station, from Mr. Herbert Frith's farm, at Newton; and whilst going down the hill in Red-lane, a part of the harness—the ridgeworth—gave way. The horse then bolted, and the driver, in attempting to stop the ani- mal, was knocked down and one of the wheels went over tiis stomach. He was conveyed to his home as soon as pos- sible after the eccurrence, but the injured man died two hours later.

ACCIDUNT TO A POLTCH OFFICER.—The other evening, between six and seven o'clock, whilst Police-Sergeant Whal- ley, of Froctsham, was returning from a coursing match which had been held at Ince, in company with Messrs. W. Youd, A. Bate, and S. Dutton, also of Frodsham, the horse of the trap in which they were riding, when coming down the Helsby new road, suddenly took fright, and ran at a furious pace until it arrived by Proffit's Pit, when it came into collision with a drove of cattle. The occupants of the conveyance were thrown out, and it is considered that the clothing of the sergeant mast have caught the trap by some means, as he was dragged a short distance. His head com- ing in contact with the curb stones, was cut and bruised very much. Strange to say, the other persons only received a few slight cuts. The horse then continued its wild flight until it collided with one of Messrs. T. Rigby and Son's lurries at the end of Main-street. The trap was smashed and the animal was captured. The officer was conveyed te his residence shortly after the occurrence, and oa examina- tion it was ascertained that he had sustained grave injuries. It is pleasing, however, to know that he -is progressing favourably.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING.

On Wednesday night a public meeting was held in Prod- sham Town Hall under the auspices of the Liberal Associa- tion of the Eddisbury Division. The room was crowded with an audience that exhibited much enthusiasm. In the centre of the platform was a table made from portions of a tree cut down by Mr. Gladstone, and a bust of the eminent statesman occupied the top of the piece of handsome furni- ture. Mr. W. Parish, J.P., of Helsby, occupied the chair, and he was supported by Mr. Tomkinson, the Liberal can- didate for the division; Mrs. Tomkinson, Mr. W. Summers, M.P. for Huddersfield ; Mr. D. J. Sweeney, the organiser of the Lancashire Branch of the Irish National League ; Messrs. W. IL Linaker, J. Beckett,T. Handley (Riaucorn), A. Cameron (Runcorn), W. Rhodes, I'. Rigby, jone, J. Jeffe, B. Kniveton (secretary), &c.—The Chairman, in open- ing the proceedings, referred to the defeat which the Liberals of the Division sustained at the last election, and said they believed that Mr. Tomkinson would go some day not far distant to Parliament, and that he would make a very excellent member when he got there. As politicians they were now entering upon a serious era. The Government of Lord Salisbury, of wham it was predicted long ago that they would either have to pass some measure of justice and conciliation for Ireland, or to resort to the effete and abomi- nable system of coercion, had, he was sorry to say, mitered upon the policy of coercion already. By and bye we should be in the midst of a very serious time, because the Govern- ment would not do what their great leader, Mr. Gladstone— (applause)—proposed should be done, namely, to extend to Ireland what had been extended to all the colonies, and even to the little Isle of Man. (Applause.) He was sure they were all, with him, pleased to see Mrs. Tomkinson once more. (Applause.) She was truly a helpmate to her husband, and he ventured to say in ber presence that there were few braver women in the country than Mrs. Tomkin- son. (Applause.) Mr. Tomkinson, who had a most cordial reception;moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting expresses its unswerving adherence to the principles of Liberals as expounded by our leader, the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, both in his home and foreign policy, and looks forward with hone and confidence to the time when ke shall return to office at the bead of a united party." (Applause.) In the course of his speech, Mr. Tomkinson alluded to the marvel- lous change of front in the Tery policy, as enunciated by Lord Randolph Churchill, and said the Dartmouth pro- gramme was not got up with a view to remedying abuses. (Hear, hear.) If the people thought to get reforms on the land question or any other great question they would be doomed to disappointment. (Applause.) The Tories only adopted reforms because they knew the people of England would have them, and only so far as they were necessary to keep themselves in office. Alluding to the Irish question, Mr. Tomkinson said the Liberal party had nailed their colours to the mast—(applause)—and whatever concessions of detail they were prepared to make in order to bring back their erring brothers, the principle of self-govern- ment for Ireland would be adhered to most strongly, and they were prepared to stty in the cold shades of Opposition for an unlimited period rather than withdraw one iota of that proposition. (Applause.) Alluding to the &TIM land question, Mr. Tomkinson said speaking generally the people of England bad been driven off the soil, and diverced from it in a way unjust and cruel to them, and most hurtful to the best interests of the country. (Hear, bear.) Three-fourths of the agricultural depression, and In a great measure the depression of trede, h"d come from the system of having immensely large holdings. Some politicians said the only remedy was emigration, but Perliament must find some way of restoring the people to the soil, and to make it possible for every man who was able and willing to cultivate a piece of land, and to pay a fair rent for it, to have an opportunity of doing so. (Ap- plause.) Reform of the land and the temperance question —less drink and more land—(applause)—thqse were the two great principles lying at the root of our national pros- perity. This was a glorious thing for every well wisher of his country to work for, and he hoped the people of Frod- sham would work for him te aid in attaining that end. (Applause.) Mr. Summers, M.P., in seconding the motion, dealt with the Irish question, and said Home Rule had been inscribed upon the Liberal banner, and he for one hoped with some degree of confidence that even in the lifetime of Mr. Glad• stone this policy would be crowned with success. (Ap- plause.) The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. W. H. Linaker moved "That this public meeting of the electors and non-electors of the Frodsham Polling Dis- trict of the Eddisbury Division of Cheshire hereby expresses its profound regret that Her Majesty's advisers have again resorted to the effete and barbarous policy of coercion in the government of Ireland, and calls upon all patriotic and liberty loving Englishmen here and elsewhere to use every effort to reinstate Mr. Gladstone and his late colleagues in power, so that that Christian Liberalism of which Lord Aberdeen spoke at Glasgow, on Monday night, may be fully carried out, and we may be enabled to do unto our fellow subjects of the green isle what we would they should do unto us." (Applause) Mr. Linaker said they could not I help admiring the strong purpose of the Irish people when for the last 80 years they had been fighting for the restore- Con of the right of self-government, which they possessed prior to the union. Until the English Government disposed of the Irish question to the satisfaction of the Irish people there would be no hope for legislation for this country which would tend to restore cenfidence and advance the progress of this country in the future as it had been built up in the pact. (Applause.) Mr. J. Jeffs seconded the motion.

Mr. Sweeney delivered a long speech in support of the proposition. He showed the utter fallacy and foolishness of supposing that Ireland could, if she would, separate her- self from England under Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill, and drew a bright picture of Ireland under reformed land laws and governed by an Irish Parliament employed in de- veloping the imdustrial resources of the country. Three cheers were called for the "Young Irish orator," and given with great enthusiasm. The resolution was carried unanimously. Mrs. Tomkinson, who was received with great cheering, moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Summers and Mr. Sweeney for their excellent addresses. She said the Tories had been taunting them that they (the Liberals) were doomed to be in the wilderness 40 years like the braelites. Considering that the Tories were dabbed the religious party, end had a general idea that nobody read the Scriptures but themselves, their parables were not so apt as they might b.. They should remember that if the Israelites were 40 years in the wilder- ness they increased and multiplied while they were there— (laughter and applause)—and also that they heat all the strong tribes, and when they left the wilderness they carrh-d all before them. (Applause.) She thought they would ac- cept their comparison. (Hear, hear.) I here was one thing which she had no doub the Tories would most heartily wish

to occur, Ixt which she did not believe would occur. They would like their (the Liberal) Moses to die within sight of the promised land—(laughter and applause)—but she was thankful to say that she believed that that part of their his- tory would be different from the Israelities. ¶lbey would keep on until he had led them into the promised land. (Applause.) Only about ten days since she had the great pleasure of staying at Elawarden with their Grand Old Man, and she never saw him look better or rnre vigorous. He looked as if be might live for manye a long day, and go back triumphantly into power to carry his great Home Rule Bill. (Applause.)
Mr. Beckett seconded the proposition,•which was carried enthusiastically and acknowledged. A similar compliment having been paid the chairman, the National Anthem was sung, and the meeting concluded.

div.head: PLEA. FOR IRELAND.
div.p: A PLEA. FOR IRELAND.

Sir,—Will you be so good as to put my letter in the columns of your good Liberal newspapers, as it is very necessary and pressing at the present time for Irishmen of all shades of opinion to speak out in a fair and practical manner. It is the duty of all friends to aid and assist the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone in the next session of Parlia- ment by all means, for, as I h .lieve, the time is close at hand when Mr. Gladstone will be Prime Minister again. I would venture to say that in the next session of Parliament Lord Salisbury will not be able to lead the British House of Commons, backed by Lord Randolph Churchill and Sir Michael Hicks• Beach, who is doing no good in Ireland but watching the poor peasantry turned out wholesale by cruel and bad lendlords, who very well know that, through bad harvests and stagnation in trade the poor peasantry are not able to nay. Still the present Lord Lieutenant of Ireland and under officials are doing nothing to stop this sad state of things. Homes are broken up, and people thrown from sick beds on the road side in all kinds of weather, while thousands are leaving their native land through bad ruling and bad government. wow. sir, I will come to the root of all the evils. Ireland, after 1691, was completely subdued; all Ireland was again confiscated. Under Elizabeth one million acres bad been taken away ; under Cromwell three millions additional, and under William eight millions. Nearly twelve million acres had been taken, and there did not remain a single Catholic proprietor on the island. They were allowed to expatriate themselves. Forty thousand Irish soldiers were allowed to join the armies of France and Spain. Young people had been kidnapped to the Barbed() Island, and the whole coun- try was thus crushed c)mpletely. What was the conduct of England with regard to that land I' Scotland was united to Englandin 1707, and Scotland has become a pronerous land. Hence many people have ag eed that since the Scotch could gain by union the Irish could have gained also. Let us see what was given to the Scotch, and what was given to the Irish. I would ask all sensible men who love liberty to read some true accounts. Four things were granted in Scotland that enabled that land to rise. Even Scotch historians admit that up to, the period of the Union Scotland was far behind Ireland. 'yet Scotland roee out of all that misery to become a great country, and how? First, because the Church of the people was recognised in eh:Union as the Established Church of the land. The Kirk of Scot- land b.carne the Established Church of Scotland, and so the people, identified with their national church and guided by it, had no bitter memories to call up. There were no prose- cutions except of the Episcopalians. In Ireland. it was the very contrary. The church of the majority was crashed to the ground ; nine-tenths of the Irish people were Catholics, yet the Catholic Church was banned and her priests were taken from her, her abbeys were ruined, her churches despoiled, and her people threatened with the penalty of felony if they should I-sten to a priest of their faith. The result was that the Church had to bide as in the ear - days of Christendom. Consequently, the people who I the Church were obliged to hate the law that be- ad the Church, their consciences that obliged them to submit to the faith of the Catholic Church, made them feel that the law that banned fleet Church was not law that should be obeyed. All the property of the Catholic Church was handed over foreign Bishops. There were actually Bishops of Ireland who never saw their diock ses in a score of years, yet they drew from the starving people—from the nine-tenths that were crushed to the earth—their tithe and incomes, and all went to England.

The next thine was that parochial schools were estab- lished in Scotland, and her people were educated. The &itch people bad not to sacrifice to conscience when they went to the Scotch schools. Hence young Scotchmen soon found places in every position in life. They rose in their own land and they rose in foreign lands hecanee they had education. With the Irish people it was different. No schools were allowed in all Ireland. It was felony to keep a school, five pounds for the head of a schoolmaster and for the head of a priest. Not only were they forbidden to have Catholic schools in Ireland, hut the people were forbidden to be educated. The Catholic who sent hie child forfeited all claims to his property and to his child. and the chili lost all claims to any in.ieritance. This is a sad subject. The hirr.orian tells us that even as late as 1800 he saw an old Irisnman pass one of the Charter schools in Dublin and call down terr:hle maledictions upon it. The next point on which Scotland was benefited was in the lead taws. There are hundreds of cases which I might lay before you, sir, and the public, if space would permit, showing the great necessity for Home Rule,in our oppressed and much abused land. Yours, otc.. PHILIP O'BRIEN.

Fir,—Once more I am reluctantly compelled to take up my pen in answer to the charmingly inaccurate epistle. si,2ned "W. E. S." It may be the nroduction of a Metho- distictl mind; it is certainly the offspring of a malevolent disposition, and I do not hesitate to designate it as a tissue of misstatements, misrepresentations, and scurrilous fabri- cations, from beginning to end. This is strong language, but it is not penned in that petty spirit of "personal spite and sple4n." which "W. E. S." so much condemns in "Garrick'" letter, although it is so conspicuous a charac- teristic of his own. It is rather he language of indigna- tion, which is the only kind that can fitly be used, when an opponent condescends to adopt such questionable con- troversial tactics.

Apparently to use "W. E. S.'s " own words "the thun- derbolts" which I and one or two others have ventured to "throw at his diminished head" had almost " annihilated " him. But, alas! that portentous vote of confidence in the secretaries, which was the spontaneous expression of a feel- ing, that those individuals must be supported in the stand which they are making, on behalf of the Society and not due to any "misgivings of conscience "on their part, ap- peared in your columns, and acting as a red rag does to a bull, roused once more the latent faculties of this doughty champion of truly moral and religious principles, who, as Shakespeare has it "scrowing his courage to the sticking place," and fortifying himself with a copious digestion of Webster's dictionary and other ittellectual food, essays again to enter the arena of newspaper controversy. And here let me apologise for an amount of repetition . _
which lam un Able to avoid in re-assertinz my position. I am sorry that this anonymous individual has taken so

, much trouble to build up an exhaustive argument upon a . mi•quotation of my words. He says—" Mr. Richardson disposes of the main issues ofothe question in the most re- markable and summary manner, by summing up all in the statement that theatre going lies between God and a man's conscience.'" A copy. of my letter lies before me, but lam unable t o discover any such 'broad and unqualified statement. which may well be termed "summary and remarkable" to a degree. What I wrote wee—That "the right or wrong of theatre going is a matter for a Christian, Methodistical or otherwise, tO settle between his conscience and his God." A very trivial distinction in words, but one that makes all the difference in the world to my assertion. I abide by that statement, and would add that a Christian will, naturally, take "the Word of God" into consideration in forming his opinion thereon. TQ my mind, it does not require a life-long "study of human nature" to discover the fact, which is too patent to most minds of ordinary in- telligence. that "men of the world" attend the theatre with- out considering any of these things. Your correspondent is afraid that my " string of figures" concerning the camposi'inn et the class is slightly '-mis- leading," as it included "the ladies." Unfortunately for W.E.5.," the ladies were to me "the unknown quantity," if I may use a 'mathematical term and, wherever any doubt existed as ta their member.hip in the Wesleyan Society, were put down as merely nominal members ; so that I arki able to give, if anything, a more favourable list in support of my contention by excluding the "fairer sex." I can vouch for the accuracy of the following statement :—Total number of male members to date 79, members of society 51, nominal Wesleyans 18. other denominations 10. These figures include the thrJe ministers, nine local preachers, eight class leaders, five Sunday school superintendents, and 13 teachers, besides eight others holding various official positions as "trustees, stewards, leaders, ctc ." in Wesleyan Methodism. Yet this is the society of "theatrical young men"! Taking these facts and figures into consideration, I can hut conclude that " W.E.S." was very "far from the mark " and, what is more, very ignorant of the facts of the, case, when he penned with such an apparent show of author- itative information his remarks about the society "or whom many are not Methodists, and the majority of the re- mainder only nominal ones." Again, I certainly do question "W. E. S.'" remarks about the attitude of our Sunday school superintendents towards us. and that on evidence derived, where necessary, from personal interviews with these gentlemen and not by the more circuitous and leas reliable channels, which a want of manliness. I presume, compels this anonymous individual to favour. Klatt is the result of those interviews? One doubtful one? No. Thank heaven, there are many in their ranks that take honourable exception to such narrow- minded Christianity. Further information lam unable to give in a newspaper controversy, without compromising individuals, but as I Dromieed before, if " W. E. S." will only "play the.man," I am prepared to give him incontro- vertible evidence that his channels of communication have be.n very misleading. In conclusion, let rue say with regard to the gross imputa- tion conveyed in "W E. t3.'e " inuendees about the "meta-
